title: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
author: Terrence O'Brien
body:
It feels like Apple’s Welcome Home event just happened. And the iPhone Duo announcement isn’t all that far in our rearview mirror, either. Yet, the company is back with another launch, focused on the MacBook Pro, it looks like. Its “Pro and tell” event is scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles. While obviously nothing is confirmed yet, it sure seems like we’re finally going to get that long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro.
What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
Apple’s long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro, an OLED iPad Mini, and more.
Beyond that? There could be an OLED update for the iPad Mini, plus M6 updates across other devices, following the M6 debut with the Mac Mini in August.
A touchscreen MacBook Pro
A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen has been a fixture of the rumor mill since at least early 2023. But now, in late 2026, it may finally come to fruition. The name MacBook Ultra has been floating around, but Apple is unlikely to rebrand its flagship laptop line.
This will be the first touchscreen laptop and the first OLED laptop from Apple. It will supposedly feature an iPhone-esque Dynamic Island, but don’t expect a dramatic revamp of the macOS interface — The touchscreen MacBook isn’t going to be some sort of iPad hybrid. It may include a few flourishes, like a magnification effect when you touch the screen or new gesture controls in native apps. But that’s it.
It’s also going to stick with the M5 series of chips for the time being — specifically, the M5 Pro and M5 Max. There might not be an M6 Pro or Max, even. Instead, Apple may wait to upgrade its higher-end processors until it introduces the M7 next year.
M6 MacBook Pro
That doesn’t mean there won’t be an M6 MacBook Pro, however. The base model of the MacBook Pro could be getting a bump from the M5 after the M6 debuted in the Mac Mini earlier this year. It might also get a slight redesign, including a hole-punch style camera. Unfortunately, they’re also expected to come with a price increase as component shortages reverberate through the Apple lineup.
M6 iMac
The iMac is also expected to get an M6 update, nearly two years after its last revision. Apple’s all-in-one desktop appears like it’s going to skip right over the M5. Don’t expect any real changes beyond that, though. But at least we might get some new color options, just like we did with the M4 model.
OLED iPad Mini
Another long-rumored device that might finally be making its debut on Wednesday is the OLED iPad Mini. Other than the iPad Pro, the tablet lineup has stuck with LCDs until now. The new OLED iPad could kick off a broader transition for the product line. The screen upgrade may add $100 to the cost, though. Otherwise, it likely won’t be a significant redesign, but expect a processor upgrade from the aging A17 to the A20 that debuted with the iPhone 18.

title: RJ Mitte's beloved opens up about life after heartbreaking loss
author: Web Desk
body:
Published October 25, 2026
RJ Mitte’s sister, Lacianne Carriere, is finding it hard to accept life without her older brother.
The Breaking Bad actor died on October 12 at the age of 34, and his death has left his family struggling with a loss they never expected.
Carriere recently shared a series of old photos with Mitte on Instagram. Along with the pictures, she wrote about the little things that now remind her of him.
She remembered how his strawberry Fanta was still sitting on her coffee table when she received the news. Even that small detail has become a painful memory for her.
Mitte was not just a brother to Carriere. He also helped raise her and became like a father to her after their mother was left unable to walk following an accident.
READ MORE: Bryan Cranston chokes up sharing regret over RJ Mitte: 'I just wonder'
Carriere said her love for music, films and video games came from the time she spent with him.
At his memorial in Texas last week, she broke down in tears while talking about their bond. She also shared how much they still had planned to do together.
Mitte became famous for playing Walter White Jr. in Breaking Bad. His co star Bryan Cranston also shared his sadness, remembering the time they spent together.
Carriere has now promised to keep trying to heal, even though she does not know how life will feel without her brother.

title: Saturday Sports: The World Series; the WNBA finals
author: Scott Simon
body:
Saturday Sports: The World Series; the WNBA finals
NPR's Scott Simon and sports reporter Michele Steele discuss the World Series and the WNBA Finals.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST:
And now it's time for sports.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
SIMON: The Brew Crew take Game 1 in the World Series, and the NFL prepares to play near Paris amid nationwide unrest. Michele Steele, who writes the Steele Cut Substack on sports and economics, joins us again. Michele, thanks so much for being with us.
MICHELE STEELE: Good morning, Scott.
SIMON: The Brew Crew defeated the Tampa Bay Rays three runs to two. William Contreras was the star of the night - three at bat, two hits, one walk, one RBI. None of these teams has ever won a World Series. This is an extraordinary matchup, isn't it?
STEELE: It really is, Scott. You might not know this, but I got a confession to make.
SIMON: Yeah.
STEELE: My favorite mascot in baseball is Bernie Brewer...
SIMON: Aw. I can understand.
STEELE: ...Mainly...
SIMON: Yeah.
STEELE: ...Mainly because he used to slide from a chalet in the outfield into a literal mug of beer. And he might get to be in a championship parade, finally, if the rest of this series goes the way that Game 1 did. Milwaukee has waited 57 seasons. Tampa Bay, 29.
SIMON: Yep.
STEELE: Game 1 was a nail-biter. It was tight kind of all the way through, but the Brewers' star, Christian Yelich, set the tone early. He tripled in his first World Series at bat. Now, the Rays almost crept back in the ninth when what looked like a game-ending double play was overturned on review. But the Brewers' closer, Trevor Megill, got the last out. And let's not forget Milwaukee also gave us another World Series first last night, the sausage race.
SIMON: Yes.
STEELE: I spoke to a former sausage this week. I'm not kidding you. He told me the races are real. So the fact that the Italian sausage won Game 1, that's an honest outcome. We'll get more sausage racing and more baseball tonight.
SIMON: Well, lots to look forward to. Look, let me ask you about le foot americain. Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints are scheduled to play near Paris tomorrow. France has been roiled by protest. Is it wise to play an NFL game when the French police might have to protect the Louvre, not the Saints and Steelers game?
STEELE: I can tell you, Scott, I've been checking in with some folks around the league, and at least people who work for other teams are looking at this game and have their mouths agape a little bit that this is still happening. The NFL just closed its NFL house in Paris today, and this is a day after closing its NFL pop-up shop amid security concerns. The Saints said that the Saints' house has been postponed until Sunday. The Steelers canceled their fan event today outright. So not quite safe enough to sell T-shirts, apparently, but the NFL says...
SIMON: Yeah.
STEELE: Its security chief is on the ground. They've beefed up security for the game itself. French president, Emmanuel Macron, met with Roger Goodell, the commissioner of the NFL, and the owners of the Steelers and the Saints this week for two hours. Lots of unrest in France, but in a world of splintered media, sports is a very potent political messenger, and France wants to proceed with this game as much as the NFL does, Scott.
SIMON: WNBA Final - finals Game 4 tips off today. Atlanta 2 to 1 edge over Golden State. But so far, the story has been about Atlanta's Angel Reese, hasn't it?
STEELE: It really has, Scott, and it's a little bit of a Chicago story too.
SIMON: Isn't everything? But go ahead. Yes.
STEELE: It all - all roads lead back to what I still call the Sears Tower. But she was drafted by the Sky. She was traded to Atlanta. She's the youngest in finals history with three straight double-doubles. The Dream have never won a title. So she's chasing Atlanta's first championship, as well. And her take on the series is that, quote, "it's a mental game." That is something that other athletes have echoed, right? The talent is so high once you hit the pros, it really is the mental side of all this that tends to separate players from champions. I interviewed her her rookie year, and I came away so impressed by her composure and her will to win, but Chicago's loss...
SIMON: Yeah.
STEELE: ...Is ATL's gain. We'll see how the next game goes.
SIMON: All right, I'll try and be happy for Atlanta. Michele Steele...
STEELE: Yeah.
SIMON: ...Writes the Steele Cut Substack on sports and economics. Talk to you soon, Michele. Thanks so much.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: The three-part plan to cut the carbon cost of flying
author: Branded Content By
body:
Flying makes the world smaller. It brings distant communities together, and means doing business across borders is quick and easy. But 80 per cent of the world’s population have never been on a plane before, and as that changes, the aviation industry has a big challenge ahead if society is to continue to reap the benefits of air travel.
Right now, aviation accounts for around two per cent of global emissions of carbon dioxide. But, with the rise in disposable income in developing economies, the number of passengers could double to 8.2 billion by 2037. By 2050, air travel could account for between four and eight per cent of global emissions – perhaps even overtaking cars, which are rapidly shifting away from a reliance on fossil fuels.
It’s a big problem, and there isn’t going to be a “silver bullet” solution, according to Duncan Van Bergen, vice president for Nature Based Solutions at Shell. It’s not as simple as switching jet engines for batteries. There’s plenty of research and investment going into those areas, but the added safety requirements of aviation mean that in all likelihood they won’t be ready to carry passengers for many decades. We need change more quickly than that.
The aviation industry is facing an “existential issue,” said Rickard Gustafson, the CEO of Scandinavian Airline SAS, at a recent panel discussion hosted by Shell Aviation at the International Air Transport Association’s AGM in Seoul, South Korea. “We need to demonstrate that we have the right to grow,” he said.
Potential solutions include a carbon tax for passengers, higher duties on airline fuel, or government subsidies that would incentivise less polluting forms of transport such as train travel over short-haul flights. But this is too big a problem to fall on the shoulders of just one group. It has to be a collaborative approach, and the industry is now starting to attack the problem from three different angles: avoid, reduce and offset.
Avoiding emissions
The carbon cost of travel doesn’t start when a plane’s wheels leave the tarmac. The logistics of loading up a jet with passengers, fuel and food also creates emissions, but they can be reduced with the help of new technologies. SATS, which manages logistics for more than 50 airlines across Asia, is working with the ride-sharing firm Grab to make its fleet of support vehicles more efficient. It’s using the company’s algorithm to minimise the number of movements vehicles have to make, cutting down on unnecessary journeys. In the past, staff would have had to return to the terminal between flights to check paperwork – now they receive the information remotely, on a wearable or handheld device. “We know the industry is going to be challenged if it doesn’t address these issues,” says Alex Hungate, CEO of SATS. “So we want to be part of the solution going forward, and I think people find that very motivating.”
New technology could help make your in-flight meal more climate friendly too. Digitalisation can allow passengers to order in advance to cut down on wastage, while the industry is also exploring the potential of plant-based or lab-grown alternatives to meat, and forms of packaging for cutlery, blankets and headphones that replace plastic with natural materials.
Reducing emissions
There’s also been a wave of interest in carbon-light alternatives to jet fuel. At the moment, sustainable aviation fuels are derived from waste cooking oils and sustainable oil crops, explains Melanie Lane, general manager at Shell Aviation, but work is ongoing to convert other kinds of waste into fuel that can be mixed with existing jet fuels in a blend that works with current infrastructure.
These are being used for some commercial flights at a small scale – United Airlines’ recent Flight for the Planet used a combination of 30 per cent sustainable biofuel, and 70 per cent traditional jet fuel. Sustainable aviation fuels are better for the environment not because they emit less, but because they recycle carbon from other industries.
Sustainable aviation fuels have come a long way in a short time, from their first tests in 2008. But, with sustainable aviation fuels accounting for just 0.01 per cent of the total fuel use, there’s still a long way to go. It’s something of a Catch-22 situation – it will take scale to make sustainable fuels cost comparable with current ones, but reaching that scale will require investment and collaboration.
“We need a trillion dollars to deliver this fuel to the aviation industry,” said Ned Harvey, managing director of the Rocky Mountain Institute, a non-profit organisation that conducts global energy research. “It cannot be the airline industry who shows up and pays for it – it has to be a market-based approach.”
Offsetting emissions
These solutions will take time to work their way through the industry, but one thing that airlines and passengers can do right now is offset their emissions. Offsetting – where investments are made in projects that pull greenhouse gases from the atmosphere – leans on the carbon capturing power of the natural world.
“Nature has the capacity to capture 11 billion tonnes of CO2 per year, at less than $100 per tonne,” says Van Bergen. But it’s not as simple as just buying credits, he says. You have to make sure that they are independently certified and high-quality, and that they’re not just pushing the carbon emissions somewhere else in the system. Shell plans to invest $300m over the next three years in natural emission reduction programmes across the globe, including ongoing pilot programmes in the Netherlands, Australia, Spain and Malaysia.
Better communication will also be key. Only half of airlines currently offer carbon capture as part of their ticket booking process, and only one or two per cent of those passengers actually take it up. Research commissioned by Shell with 4,000 members of the public across four European countries found that over half of respondents would be willing to pay a small amount to offset emissions when buying a plane ticket, but 60 per cent said they didn’t know enough about carbon offsetting to opt in.
Maria Rice, director of environmental policy, programs and sustainability at United Airlines, said her company was looking at giving offsetting a more prominent position in the booking flow. Often it sits at the end of a series of screens where passengers choose their sets, check-in luggage and in-flight extras and it’s all too easy to just skip past it.
“Nobody is saying that carbon credits are the solution by themselves,” says Van Bergen, and it will take progress on all three fronts – avoid, reduce and offset – to cut emissions as the number of journeys continues to rise. The challenge is not insurmountable, but it will require passengers, airlines, terminal operators and fuel providers to collaborate. “We cannot do it on our own,” says Lane.
--

title: The 18 Best Cyber Monday Laptop Deals Live Today
author: WIRED Insider
body:
With great strides in processing power, display technology, and battery life in the last few years, laptops have never been in better shape. Whether you want a compact companion to take your productivity up a notch, help you score glorious gaming victories, or just to curl up in bed with Netflix, there are deals to be had. These are the best Cyber Monday laptop deals we have uncovered so far on computers from the likes of Dell, Asus, and Lenovo.
We're into Black Friday and Cyber Week, so we've uncovered the top discounts. Check out the best Black Friday deals for 2022 here.
If you’re a Mac user looking for some more muscle than the M1 MacBook Air can provide, we suggest you take a look at its (slightly) bigger brother. The 2020 13.3-inch MacBook Pro also comes with the swaggering M1 at its heart, and has a slight edge over the Air in terms of power and battery life (a couple of hours extra of the latter). There’s the touchbar too, if that appeals to you, and a lovely screen and speaker setup.
What you get with the Huawei MateBook D 15 is a laptop with a slick design and more than decent performance to match. Yes, it takes more than a few design cues from Apple, but that's no bad thing, and we like the fine selection of ports and the hidden webcam in the keyboard. The downsides? Well, the battery life is disappointing but the included 65W USB-C charger can top you up to over 50 percent in just 30 minutes.
While you will find a laptop that looks just like this one selling for around £600 elsewhere, at Amazon you get a bump up from a 512GB SSD to a 1TB one. For £20 less. This is a great desktop-replacer for many people. It has a 15.6-inch Full HD screen and an Intel Core i5 processor. Acer’s Swift series laptops are a little snazzier in parts, but this one is still just about light enough to use as an ultraportable at 1.9kg.
You can find discounts that sound more dramatic than the “£100 off” of the Asus Zenbook UX425EA. But this laptop hits a sweet spot of design, performance and value. It has an aluminium shell and ultra-slim screen borders, and weighs just 1.2kg. Don’t be put off by the strange-looking touchpad. It can turn into a NUM pad, but it uses an LED light underneath. When you want it to look like a normal touchpad, it will.
Sporting a crisp 2K screen, 512GB of SSD storage, 8GB of RAM and an 11th Gen Core i5 processor, the MateBook 14 is more than capable of handling some heavier productivity tasks, despite its 1.49kg weight. There’s a decent 11 hours of battery life (with a 15-minute charge giving your 2.5 hours of standard use) and a fingerprint sensor for swift logins.
Who wouldn't like £250 off Samsung's super-thin, super-light AMOLED laptop? Yes, the featherweight design is svelte and sharp, but its that AMOLED display that draws attention. It’s a 1920 x 1080 141dpi 60Hz panel, so don't expect the sharpness of 4K screens, but the contrast and color accuracy on view are superb. Integrated Dolby Atmos AKG speakers deliver plenty of punch, no distortion and even passable bass. The clincher? Excellent battery life.
There’s nothing too fancy going on here: this is a decent budget model that’s ideal as a first laptop for kids, and with a hefty £50 off it’s even more affordable than usual. It’s powered by an Intel Celeron processor and 4GB of RAM, comes with 64GB of eMMC storage and runs on Windows 10 Home S, with a free upgrade to Windows 11 when it rolls out shortly.
If money is tight, you may be interested in one of our favourite budget laptops; the Acer Swift 1 is svelte and lightweight. It’s suitable for basic productivity tasks and boasts good speakers and a keyboard with decent travel, though the display is a bit bland. The processor is basic, as you’d expect in a laptop at this price. There’s 4 GB of RAM and a 128 GB SSD. But this laptop also comes with a year’s subscription to Microsoft 365 Personal, which is a nice bonus.
LG’s Gram range is obsessed with low weight. The LG gram 14Z90P weighs a gramme under a kilo, but still has inordinately long battery life and a powerful 11th Gen Intel Core i7 processor. You also get — unusual for the price — 16GB RAM. You don’t often see a performance laptop this light. Even the keyboard is well above average, and comfortable for long-form typing. The 14-inch Gram won’t necessarily seem as high-end as a MacBook Pro to your fingers, but this major saving is worth looking at for those after a laptop for roving portable use.
OK, so the cost of this laptop may make your jaw hit the floor. But this is a new model that sold for £670 more in the weeks before Cyber Monday. It is so expensive because this Razer Blade 17 has just about every upgrade you could ask for. You get the top-end 11th Gen Intel Core i9 CPU, an Nvidia RTX 3080 graphics card, 32GB RAM, a 1TB SSD and a 4K resolution 120Hz screen. It’s a monster of a gaming laptop, worth a glance even if you can in no way afford it.
We’ve all grown to appreciate the OLED revolution that started with smartphones and swept into our living rooms, but this superior display technology is still relatively rare in laptops. This Asus Vivobook combines a 15.6-inch OLED screen with an Intel i3-1115G4, 8GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage. Forget about gaming, but if you want something pleasant to work, browse the web, and watch the odd movie on, you could do a whole lot worse.
Easily the best-looking Windows laptop you can buy, this Surface Laptop 4 model sports a 15-inch touchscreen and an elegant design. There’s an AMD Ryzen 7 with Radeon Graphics inside, along with 8 GB of RAM, and 512 GB of storage. We like the keyboard and the large trackpad, and the speakers aren’t bad either, but the bezels are quite thick, and there’s no Thunderbolt port.
If you’re keen on a 2-in-1 design, this affordable convertible from Lenovo fits the bill. The keyboard attaches magnetically, there’s a 10.1-inch touchscreen, and it runs Google’s Chrome OS. Battery life is quite good at up to 10 hours, so this is a decent device for light work, web surfing, and movie watching. If you can make do with simply folding the screen back, the Lenovo IdeaPad Flex 3 is also on sale at £180 (£100 off).
Google Store, Argos, John Lewis
The best high-end Chromebook on the market, Google’s slick, minimalist design looks and feels a bit special and stands out from the crowd. It also has some grunt (for a Chromebook), and there’s a touchscreen display, a solid keyboard, and a responsive glass trackpad. Plenty of stamina in the battery department and seamless integration with Google’s apps round out a tempting device. Just be aware that Google’s UK hardware support is somewhat lacking. The 16GB of RAM model is also on sale at £799 (£150 off).
We were impressed by the build quality of the Triton 300 SE with its lightweight magnesium alloy case and a textured glass touchpad. And it’s no slouch under that stylish exterior with an 11th gen Core i7, an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, 16 GB of RAM, and a 1 TB SSD. It has a Full HD screen with a silky smooth 144 Hz refresh rate, and it should run most games you care to throw at it, though it can get hot and loud when you push it.
Deep discounts on Apple’s MacBook line are rare, and we haven’t seen any for Black Friday. The truth is that the 2020 MacBook Air has been available at this price for a while now, but we know some people will have their hearts set on an Apple computer. It has Apple’s powerful M1 chip inside with 8 GB of RAM and a 256 GB SSD. This compact MacBook has a 13-inch screen and plenty of stamina, but it’s relatively expensive for what you get.
If there’s a better compact laptop, we’d like to know about it. Dell’s 11th Gen XPS 13 is a slim beauty with a bright and vibrant 13.3-inch screen. It’s all business, with a Core i7, 8 GB of RAM, a 512 GB SSD, and support for Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.1. Extras like a fingerprint sensor in the power button and voice activation with Cortana may prove convenient. But, with space at a premium, ports are limited, and the trackpad is small.
Dell’s gaming brand is often accused of being overpriced, but this looks like the kind of laptop a space marine would own, and this kind of design comes at a premium. There’s no scrimping on the spec sheet here either with an 11th Gen Core i7, an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080, 16 GB of RAM, and a 1 TB SSD. The 15-inch display gives you the option to crank up the resolution to 1440p at 240 Hz or drop down to 1080p at 360 Hz, and there’s G-Sync support, too. Just don’t stray too far from a power socket.
This article was originally published by WIRED UK

title: Blind date: ‘We overstayed our welcome – the waiters were shaking the cutlery drawer really loudly’
author: Guardian Staff; Guardian staff reporter
body:
Alexandrea on Pardis
What were you hoping for?
 
A fun date and to hopefully meet the one!
First impressions?
 
Handsome and relaxed.
What did you talk about?
 
The sports we do. Books. Family. Friends. Our jobs. Travelling and travelling mishaps. Vermin infestations. Stocks and shares. ISAs.
Most awkward moment?
 
We both arrived at the restaurant on time but there was a big queue which resulted in me sitting at the table alone for about 10 minutes – I got a bit nervous.
Good table manners?
 
No faux pas so all good.
Best thing about Pardis?
 
He is very sincere. He asked lots of questions, seemed interested in what I was saying and was a great listener. I also loved how laid-back he was – he went with the flow when I proposed the tasting menu.
Would you introduce Pardis to your friends?
 
Of course – he’s interesting and really good company.
Describe Pardis in three words
 
Easygoing, kind, engaging.
What do you think Pardis made of you?
 
A ray of sunshine, akin to what everyone else thinks of me!
Did you go on somewhere?
 
No, but we did overstay our welcome at the restaurant, to the point where the waiters were shaking the cutlery drawer really loudly.
And … did you kiss?
 
A lady never tells … But no.
If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?
 
I would have loved it to be in Paris. Pardis in Paris!
Marks out of 10?
 
8.
Would you meet again?
 
Pardis is a lovely guy but I think we’re better suited as friends.
Pardis on Alexandrea
What were you hoping for?
 
The scene in About Time where the protagonist meets Rachel McAdams in that dark dining restaurant. (I appreciate that isn’t quite the same concept as a blind date.)
First impressions?
 
I was a few places behind her in the queue to get in the restaurant. I could only see the back of her head but thought: nice hair, good fashion sense.
What did you talk about?
 
There was a healthy amount of chat on the life cycle of a fly and the declining quality of mousetraps. We’ve both had minor pest issues recently – a perk of living in London.
Most awkward moment?
 
Probably mistaking her Irish accent for a Scottish one. Not my finest hour.
Good table manners?
 
Excellent, a picture of sophistication.
Best thing about Alexandrea?
 
Very down to earth, clearly adventurous and a great dinner party guest.
Would you introduce Alexandrea to your friends?
 
I wouldn’t put the poor girl through the trauma of meeting my rabble …
Describe Alexandrea in three words
 
Adventurous, kind, intelligent.
What do you think she made of you?
 
I think she enjoyed my chat. Either that or she’s great at acting entertained (or I’m completely oblivious).
Did you go on somewhere?
 
No, I was on early morning uncle duty the next day, so had to call it a night.
And … did you kiss?
 
No, a good wholesome hug.
If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?
  
I’d brush up on my accent recognition beforehand.
Marks out of 10?
 
8 (for a friendship connection, otherwise it would have been higher).
Would you meet again?
 
Sure, as friends I’d be happy to.
Alexandrea and Pardis ate at Mildreds, London W1. Fancy a blind date? Email blind.date@theguardian.com
