title: The first broken iPhone Duos are here
author: Jay Peters
body:
The iPhone Duo officially goes on sale today, but a few units already have broken screens. According to posts on Reddit about the affected units, the issue appears to be happening at a similar spot on all of them: Some kind of problem shows up on the inner screen along the hinge and a strange bright line (or lines) across the right side of the display.
The first broken iPhone Duos are here
Now that the first folding iPhone has launched, we’ll find out quickly what can go wrong.
Here’s how one user in Australia described what happened to their phone:
Had my iPhone Duo for about six hours and had probably opened it fewer than 20 times.
I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen.
As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.
There were no marks or damage on the inner screen’s surface or the external hinge to suggest anything had been caught or damaged.
The user said that the Apple Store replaced their phone with “a brand-new one on the spot.”
A post showing an image of another broken screen includes a video in a comment demonstrating yet another.
And a separate Reddit thread collected other pictures of affected Duos.
Apple didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

title: Innovating to Make Money More Inclusive
author: Branded Content By
body:
Recent years have brought significant innovation in financial services, with traditional banks rising to the challenge set by fintech and “Big Tech” players who transformed and enhanced the customer experience – often at better value. The pandemic has only accelerated the proliferation of solutions and driven their adoption. In theory, this is fantastic news. With a card for this and an app for that, you can pay anyone, anywhere, at pretty much anytime.
But there is such a thing as too much choice. It can be overwhelming. “When people have no choice, life is almost unbearable,” psychologist Barry Schwartz wrote in his book The Paradox of Choice. As the number of choices increases, initially we get autonomy and liberation. But, as that number keeps rising, we get overloaded and stressed. “Choice is great,” says Paul Stoddart, president of New Payment Platforms at Mastercard. “But creating an environment where you're bombarded with different providers of the same thing makes it very difficult to know which is the best one for you.”
But help is on its way. Open banking and more applied use of data could soon revolutionise choice by bypassing it altogether. It gives consumers and businesses the ability to securely share their bank account data with trusted financial service providers, including their neighbourhood bank to retailers, utility providers and fintechs, in exchange for more bespoke financial services that make intelligent decisions on your behalf. “It really changes the rules of the game,” says Stoddart.
Imagine being able to view all your accounts in one place and move money between them with a simple swipe or tap. Better than that, an AI assistant manages your money for you, helping you to avoid overdraft fees and maximise your savings and rewards. It frees up more of your time, does away with the headaches of manual tasks, and ultimately leaves you financially better off.
This type of invisible banking requires a lot of data, which in turn requires a trusted go-between, which is exactly what Mastercard does within this ecosystem. “We facilitate secure access to that information,” says Stoddart, “and then give control of it over to you.”
That “you” is everyone, not just fintech-savvy twenty-somethings or wealthy businesspeople. In fact, Mastercard is working hard to widen access to these kinds of services for those currently excluded from the system. That includes providing access to affordable credit for people who otherwise wouldn’t qualify, such as immigrants, students or anyone else without a long credit history.
For example, through open banking platform Finicity, now a Mastercard subsidiary, Rocket Mortgage is using data supplied from users about their spending, income and employment to help them get a loan to buy a home. “By aggregating that information together, we can help financial services companies make a decision around lending you money, or get you a better rate,” says Stoddart. “With this new data, we can present a more accurate view that shows that you are a lower credit risk than if they didn’t know anything about you.”
Digital banking has the potential to have an everlasting impact on anyone and everyone’s lives, no matter their starting point. But in order to do that, it needs to be accessible. According to Mastercard research, 85 per cent of people have tried at least one new payment type in the past year and 63 per cent said they’d tried one they wouldn’t have tried otherwise. But while the pandemic was a catalyst for adoption it also revealed a digital banking divide.
Mastercard has already brought 500 million financially excluded people into its digital economy and has committed to doubling that number by 2025 to include 50 million small and micro merchants with a direct focus on providing 25 million women entrepreneurs through multiple programmes around the world. One example is its Nobody in the Dark programme in the UK, which helps people build up their digital confidence so they can properly use the online tools at their disposal. Becky, a mother who couldn’t figure out how to turn on her children’s tablet to start with, ended up swapping out her weekly food parcels for digital vouchers so she could bulk shop online and save on travel costs. Becky’s story doesn’t boast the same type of innovation as open banking or AI-initiated payments, but the impact on her life is astounding. Another example is Strive UK, an initiative that will empower 650,000 British micro and small enterprises to thrive in the digital economy through tools and personalised support over the next three years and beyond.
Broadly, Mastercard is evolving its capabilities to put convenience, flexibility and control in the palm of anyone’s hand. One solution, Mastercard Send™, makes it possible to send money near instantly to more than one billion people from a banking app, a gig platform or a What’s App chat; its platforms connect 90 per cent of the world’s population to send and receive money at home and abroad using a bank account, card, digital wallet or cash. Mastercard has even begun supporting select cryptocurrencies on its network this year, to enable customers, merchants and businesses to pay and get paid in the way that suits them best.
Mastercard and its partners are innovating for trust and inclusion across the whole breadth of the banking system, and as we move into 2022 that has never been as important. As Stoddart says, “Whether people want to pay with cash, card or a digital currency, we’ve got to ensure that our bank and fintech partners can provide flexibility, security and control to people and organisations, whatever their level of financial literacy and however they choose to interact.”
For more information, visit mastercard.com/startwithpeople

title: Can a £5.8bn scheme help revive Grimsby and other town centres?
author: Sarah Butler
body:
“It is nice to see something happening for once,” says Jack Vincent, a Grimsby resident, as he considers a wave of change finally arriving in a town that had become a byword for deprivation.
In June, King Charles visited the Lincolnshire coastal town, celebrating the opening of a youth centre in a previously derelict Victorian warehouse building and a Care charity community drop-in centre in a vacant bank on the high street. Scaffolding also shrouds one end of the town’s shopping centre, part of which is being converted to house leisure facilities including a cinema and a food market.
“It is getting better and we have got the new cinema coming,” says Vincent, who is in town with his partner and two young children.
Linda Hooper, 75, who also lives locally, agrees: “They are generally making it nicer and there’s a good shopping centre.”
Once the world’s largest fishing port, Grimsby has been hit badly by the decline of its trawler fleet since the 1950s, and North East Lincolnshire council has spent the lion’s share of the £59m in government-backed regeneration funds awarded to it since 2021 trying to revamp the struggling town centre.
It is now beginning to spend a further £20m from the pride in place programme, the latest government attempt to support struggling communities. The scheme was launched under Keir Starmer as a revamp of previous Conservative plans, expanded to offer 284 deprived communities up to £2m a year for 10 years to help with regeneration.
On becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham made clear that reviving town centres would be one of his priorities and gave his backing to the £5.8bn national programme. It also fits within his wider devolution drive.
The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, says: “Our pride in place programme is a break from past approaches by putting local people in charge … no more ‘Whitehall knows best’. This is local people deciding what matters most to them.”
Residents in Grimsby feel the high street is the part of their town that has declined more than any other over the last decade, with household names such as Debenhams collapsing and shoplifting on the rise.
Henrietta Billings, the director of Save Britain’s Heritage, which campaigns for the preservation of historical buildings, says: “I think it is right the government is recognising that people are really fed up with seeing, at best, paint peeling off all the buildings … They see when no one cares about them and can feel let down.”
Despite hopes of further money for regeneration in John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October, and the announcement last month of another £210m to help turn boarded-up shops and other businesses into community spaces, the problem is bigger and more complex than just finding more funding.
Grimsby gives a glimpse into the challenges of how to adapt as more of us shop and bank online, amid years of central government cost-cutting and the decline of historical industries that once brought jobs and wages.
As in many other local authorities, the people of North East Lincolnshire registered their dissatisfaction with a big vote for Reform in the May elections, wresting minority control of the council. It is also a place that overwhelmingly supported Brexit, with the promise of a fishing revival, but which then lost processing jobs after the UK left the EU.
Despite its efforts at regeneration, many large commercial buildings, including a former Wilko and House of Fraser, and beautiful Victorian buildings such as the vast Victoria Mills and the Grimsby Ice Factory remain empty.
Local people say some empty office blocks and commercial buildings are vacant after being picked up for a song by out-of-town investors, who then realised redevelopment was more costly and complicated than they imagined.
The Covid pandemic and other hold-ups mean that, while three of Grimsby’s redevelopment projects funded by the predecessors to pride in place are complete, several more remain in progress.
As Spencer Hunt of the local council admits: “We still have issues.”
On a Friday in Grimsby, the Freshney Place shopping centre is busy with people popping into a revamped Marks & Spencer, a Primark and a good mix of other shops, while the nearby Abbeygate pedestrianised street is packed with independent boutiques and eateries.
However, the main high street is gap-toothed with vacant shops and has become a racetrack for local teenagers on bikes and scooters who join in lively banter with homeless people and daytime drinkers.
Hooper, Vincent and several other local people agree that something needs to be done to reduce what Hooper describes as “yobs going up and down the walkway”.
Some local teenagers agree that the town centre does not always feel very welcoming. “People need to feel more safe,” says Ewan Challender, 18, in town with Demi Sowerby, who says the shop where she works is frequently shoplifted.
Their scepticism about the redevelopment plans is fuelled by the struggles of previous efforts. The Riverhead building, which was built in the noughties and once home to a selection of bars, in September finally welcomed a new inflatable play park, after lying empty since 2024, while a revamped St James’ Square remains bordered by shuttered premises.
The effort to update town centres has been a long one. The rise of out-of-town retail parks and then internet shopping have been putting pressure on traditional retail-based high streets for decades.
In 2011, the David Cameron government commissioned the retail guru Mary Portas to come up with some solutions, leading to 10 pilot revamps. While a number of those towns – such as Margate, Stockport and Stockton – are now lauded as examples of regeneration, others such as Croydon and Wolverhampton continue to struggle.
A string of successors to the Portas scheme – including the town deals and the levelling up fund – have pumped almost £12bn into town centres in the past seven years, but so far failed to bring about widespread regeneration.
The towns fund wraps together the £2.3bn in the programmes money awarded to 101 places in 2019 with the future high street fund, under which 72 places shared awards worth £830m from 2020.
However, many recipients found that the pandemic and subsequent inflation, particularly on construction costs, as well as difficulties in securing sites or planning permission, forced them to scale back, pause or redraw plans.
A focus on investing in buildings and other infrastructure has also left projects stymied by a lack of resources for staff to run them. Continued weak high street spending has meanwhile led to businesses and entrepreneurs siphoning away cash once spent on improving stores towards selling online.
Almost £1.8m of town deals awards are only being released this year and next, according to a government evaluation report. At least £1bn of the £4.8bn levelling up fund launched in 2021 also remained “stuck in limbo” by 2024, according to the campaign group Power to Change.
The money from all these pride in place predecessors was incorporated into the local regeneration fund last year and the deadline for spending it was extended from March this year to March 2028 as many projects remained behind schedule.
Pride in place has tried to build on lessons from previous rounds of funding, which led to questionable decisions over allocation and funds going unspent. It has allocated funding based on published deprivation and community need data.
Its remit also stretches beyond doing up high streets, with the menu of automatically accepted spending options stretching to skills training for local people, modernising social housing and making space for nature. Communities can also seek approval for locally relevant alternatives.
Unlike many of the predecessor schemes, pride in place can also cover projects’ running costs. Local areas must also create neighbourhood boards, made up of residents, businesses and other members of the community alongside local authorities, to allocate the money.
In North East Lincolnshire, the council has brought in Our Future, a local group backed by Jason Stockwood, the entrepreneur behind Grimsby Town football club, to help catalyse community involvement in developing the town, backed by £850,000 to be handed out in grant funding to local projects to make the most of vacant buildings.
But Neela Parker Talwar, from the Centre for Cities , argues that “£20m is not so much money” and is unlikely to be able to fund major projects such as buying up large empty buildings for redevelopment.
She adds that communities might know their local problems better than central government, but the causes of high street vacancies may be beyond the reach of a local authority, things such as “access to jobs, transport, schools, things the local authority can have leverage over but only to an extent”.
“You can’t expect Blackburn to become Cambridge,” Talwar says.
Grimsby residents admit that perhaps its biggest hope for the future is not government-backed regeneration schemes but an improving local economy and entrepreneurship.
“For Grimsby the stars aligned when we stopped thinking about fishing and started thinking about wind. We stopped looking back and started looking forward,” says Mark Webb, who heads up the Grimsby 2025 group of local businesses aiming to invest in local regeneration. Local business niches include logistics, chemicals and food processing as well as renewables.
“We are a typical northern industrial town. We weren’t going anywhere, but now we are. People look at the town now and it is a bit of a mess, but it is a brilliant mess because someone is doing something behind those hoardings.”

title: LOOK BACK IN ANGER… AND HOPE
author: Mahnaz Rahman
tags: Your window to latest news, analysis and features from Pakistan, South Asia and the world.;newspaper
body:
INTRODUCTION
This story should have been written long ago. Much earlier. But, as always, life intervened. Now, here I am, at the age of 75, with a breast cancer diagnosis in hand, wondering whether time will grant me the luxury to finally tell my story. As Munir Niazi once wrote, “Hamesha dair kar deta hoon main [I am always too late].” I suppose that verse was written with people like me in mind.
When I say life got in the way, I mean it in every sense: my temperament, the weight of world affairs, years of activism and, now, the relentless demands of grandmotherhood. I often imagine my late husband, Ahfaz [journalist Ahfaz-ur-Rahman], smiling down from the heavens, amused: “So now you’re doing for the grandchildren all that you never managed to do for me or our kids.” And yet, knowing the perfectionist he was, I can just as easily imagine his disapproving frown: “You should be asserting yourself. Why are you putting up with their tantrums? You’re 75 for God’s sake. What’s wrong with you?”
Ahfaz was never pleased with my domestic efforts. My children, thankfully, are more generous. They tell me I may not have been the most structured or hands-on mother, but that my love was unwavering, that I cared for them in the best way I knew how. What I was lax in providing, they say, was tarbiyat, that essential Urdu term for life training and everyday discipline.
And they’re not wrong. What else could you expect from someone like me? I was raised under the wing of an overprotective, sheltering mother. Well into my university years, I still relied on her to buy my clothes. Me, the so-called independent leftist and feminist, was hopelessly ill-equipped for life’s practicalities.
The recently published memoirs by Mahnaz Rahman detail her life as a journalist, leftist activist and rights advocate, presenting an unvarnished account of its challenges, triumphs and setbacks, especially during Gen Ziaul Haq’s 11-year-long dictatorship. This was a time when Pakistan’s journalists faced censorship, arrests and brutal state reprisals. It is a story of youthful idealism, resistance and quiet determination. Eos presents, with permission, excerpts from Love, Life and the Left, published by Jumhoori Publications…
A walking paradox, I could live alone in a university hostel in Karachi in the sixties, embrace socialism and communism in my youth, defy my parents and marry for love… and yet, I couldn’t cook a decent meal or manage a household without chaos. As my mother often said, I was sifar bata sifar (zero upon zero) in practical life.
That same impracticality, of course, followed me into marriage. Despite being a revolutionary and a man of rare integrity, Ahfaz had certain traditional expectations of me at home; expectations I simply could not meet. I remember telling him once, quite sincerely, “Apart from your temper and your traditional expectations from me, you are like a saint.” But true to his sensitive nature, he didn’t take it as a compliment. He sulked. He grumbled. He took offence. And there I was thinking I was praising him. Such was our chemistry: spiced with friction, layered with love.
Today, ironically, I perform acts of service for my grandchildren with a kind of reverence that I never afforded my husband or even my children. They’ve succeeded in enlisting me into their army, one where I march to their tunes, attend to their smallest whims, and revolve my world around their joy and comfort. It is for them too, partly, that I have delayed writing this memoir for so long. Only now, when cancer has knocked on the door, have I finally sat down to write. Better late than never, they say. I hope that sentiment holds true for both of us, dear reader.
Let me be clear: this is not an act of self-congratulation. If I were a writer of books for the sake of books, I could have published volumes drawn from the thousands of columns and articles I’ve written. But this is something else. This is an attempt, perhaps my only real attempt, to make peace with the whirlwind of a life I’ve lived. A life of relentless movement, sporadic reflection, and very little calm contemplation. This book is my bid to reflect, not in guilt, but in peace. I won’t sugarcoat anything. You will find, in these pages, my story warts and all.
This memoir is also, in part, for the young activists and leftists of today. I hope you’ll learn from our generation’s missteps, but also from our moments of grace, our acts of resistance, our quiet strength. Yes, I have inverted the cliché. In these dark times, you deserve to hear not only what we did wrong but also what we did right. And if ever you feel disillusioned, remember what our beloved Rosa Luxemburg once said: “You lose, you lose, you lose, you lose, and then you win.”
BEFORE ZIA, THERE WAS BHUTTO
It’s easy to forget now, drowned in the inky shadow cast by Gen Ziaul Haq’s dictatorship [1977-1988], that the seeds of oppression, and thus resistance, were sown earlier, under the regime of none other than Zulfikar Ali Bhutto.
Though Bhutto inspired a generation with his populist slogans, his government did not shy away from cracking down on a free press. In the foreword to Ahfaz’s Freedom of the Press: The War on Words (1977–1978), [journalist] Wahab Siddiqui recalls how the Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists (PFUJ), buoyed by the clear promises of the [Pakistan] Peoples Party [PPP] upon its rise to power on December 20, 1971, held high hopes, only to see them quickly shattered.
Within just two months, the government banned three publications: the Lahore-based fortnightlies Punjab Punch and Zindah, and the monthly Urdu Digest, all under martial law orders. Their editors were not only imprisoned but also barred from editing any publication for 10 years, without even the chance to face trial under normal legal procedures. Notably, even though Zindah and Urdu Digest had previously attacked the PFUJ with serious accusations, the union still protested the ban and the editors’ arrests. The PFUJ demanded their release and the lifting of the bans or, at the very least, that they be tried under the regular legal system.
The Bhutto regime used economic pressure to suppress dissenting media, withdrawing government advertisements and cutting off newsprint to critical publications such as Hurriyet, Nawa-i-Waqt and Jasarat. These tactics intensified, culminating in the closure of several newspapers under emergency laws in 1973. By 1974, the dismissal of 18 workers at Musawaat (Lahore) triggered a significant resistance movement led by APNEC [All-Pakistan Newspaper Employees Confederation] and the PFUJ.
It is important to note that the above is not intended to draw a false equivalency between the monstrous dictatorship of Zia and Z.A. Bhutto. For all his flaws (and there were many), Bhutto was a democratically elected leader with a visionary agenda and a deep connection to the people, qualities that set him entirely apart from Zia. Whatever criticisms one may have of Bhutto, he is in no way, shape or form comparable to a brutal autocrat like Zia.
Rather, the intention of the preceding paragraphs was twofold: first, to underscore that the trend of press suppression, entrenched during [Gen] Ayub Khan’s rule, had only intensified during Bhutto’s tenure in the 1970s; and second, to highlight that the PFUJ had already begun to resist such repression.
In that sense, the confrontations with Bhutto’s government served as critical preparation for the graver battles the PFUJ would face during Zia’s brutal regime.
‘ZULMAT KO ZIA KYA LIKHNA’ [WHY WRITE DARKNESS AS LIGHT]
Then came July 5, 1977, a date burned into our national memory like a scar. Gen Zia overthrew a democratically elected government and unfurled a regime so repressive, so suffocating, it nearly crushed the country’s spirit.
Almost immediately, Zia issued a secret memo to his martial law administrators warning them: “Beware of the left. Beware of a united front of journalists, workers, and students.” And yet, ironically, and beautifully, it was precisely that alliance, with farmers joining in, that would coalesce just months later.
The first blow was personal. Zia’s regime terminated PFUJ president and Pakistan Times Karachi Bureau Chief, Minhaj Barna. Barna was my friend Rukshana’s uncle (and the brother of [leftist politician] Mairaj Muhammad Khan). He was also Ahfaz’s guru in trade unionism, someone Ahfaz respected and loved above anyone else in the journalist fraternity.
The allegation against Barna sahib was hilarious in that he was charged with writing articles for Al-Fatah, whose editorial policy was deemed contradictory to the dictates of the [state-owned] National Press Trust [NPT]. Al-Fatah was further deemed guilty of promoting ethnic nationalism (sound familiar? Nothing in the ruling elites’ attitude has changed!).
On the 23rd of December, 1977, the PFUJ roared in response. The national action committee of PFUJ and APNEC issued a fiery ultimatum: reinstate Barna or face a national uprising. Under growing pressure, Zia’s government relented, for then. But the beast was only licking its wounds.
THE SILENCING OF MUSAWAAT
[The PPP-owned] Musawaat, my former, and Ahfaz’s [then] current, paper became the martial law regime’s next victim. It never had a huge circulation but that had changed in the wake of Bhutto’s incarceration, wherein Musawaat’s circulation had now soared. That alone made it dangerous in Zia’s eyes.
The regime seized the Sheikh Sultan Al Nahyan Trust, the trust that owned Musawaat’s printing press, and issued a decree: no printing without clearing massive dues and obtaining a no-objection certificate. Every other [printing] press, afraid of Zia’s wrath, refused to touch Musawaat. And so, in a single swoop, two hundred journalists and press workers found themselves without a job, including Ahfaz.
Every morning, journalists and workers would gather in the paper’s Karachi office, clutching hope like fools, only to return, empty-handed by evening. Though writing for another newspaper at that time, on a couple of occasions I accompanied Ahfaz to Musawaat. I still remember those tired faces. And among them was the editor, the legendary writer Ibrahim Jalees, who ran from ministry to ministry trying to revive the paper. However, this was all to no avail, as the government had no intention of allowing Musawaat to publish again.
One day, while sitting in that broken-down office, Jalees suffered a heart attack and was gone by morning. A giant felled not by illness but by the quiet violence of censorship and despair.
‘MS BHUTTO, IS THIS A NEWSPAPER OFFICE OR A WAREHOUSE?’
In honour of Jalees sahib, the workers organised a memorial at the office, an office, as I mentioned earlier, so run-down and dusty, it barely looked like a workplace. Broken furniture, leaking roofs, creaking floorboards. Still, the city’s literary and journalistic luminaries came to pay tribute. I wasn’t personally present at this memorial, but it turned out to be a significant one. What follows was recounted to me by several journalist friends.
Shabbar Azmi was the president of the Musawaat Employees Association while Ahfaz was, at that time, the general secretary of the Karachi Union of Journalists (KUJ). As the event was going on, a loud commotion was heard. The attendees were greeted with the unannounced arrival of [Z.A. Bhutto’s wife] Nusrat Bhutto and [daughter] Benazir. My former office’s infamous staircase creaked under the weight of history as they climbed up. Everyone was surprised, because it was the first time any prominent PPP leader had visited the Musawaat office since the crackdown began.
Nusrat Bhutto looked visibly dejected due to what her husband was enduring at that time. When she saw the office, she seemed gobsmacked by its pathetic condition. There weren’t any proper, fully functional chairs available to offer them. Some colleagues managed to unearth two chairs which were in a relatively better condition, so that they could eventually sit down. After Shabbar gave his introductory remarks, he asked Ahfaz to come and speak.
However, Ahfaz said that he would speak from the audience, where everyone turned to look at him. As I’ve mentioned before, Ahfaz was, at that time and indeed throughout his life, the embodiment of the proverbial “angry young man.” Apart from lambasting the Zia dictatorship, he took the opportunity to also lambast the PPP leadership for their apathy. He turned to Nusrat Bhutto and said, “See for yourself, is this an office or an abandoned warehouse? The roof leaks, the floor creaks, the furniture is broken!”
Nusrat Bhutto listened to his remarks and later got up to give her own speech. During her speech, she criticised the Zia regime for its oppression. Ahfaz, still angry, interrupted: “The Bhutto regime was also very oppressive.” Ms Bhutto was stunned for a few moments. She continued her speech. The event proved to be an important milestone in the movement. Later, we discovered that Nusrat Bhutto had been quite impressed by Ahfaz’s honesty.
Three days later, Musawaat’s chief photographer Altaf Rana came running to Ahfaz: “Nusrat Bhutto wants to meet you.” Ahfaz was incredulous: “She doesn’t even know my name.” But she did. She had asked to meet “the young man with bitter words.” That was Ahfaz; raw, blunt, burning with honesty.
And that was the movement: willing to speak truth even when it burnt bridges, even when it cut through allies. Because what we were fighting was bigger than party, ideology or reputation. We were fighting a regime built on fear and silence. And we chose to speak.
THE CHEQUE FOR 180,000 RUPEES
When Ahfaz arrived at the Bhutto residence, the air was thick with tension. Waiting there were Musawaat’s top administrative officers: Chief Editor Badruddin, Manager Noor Muhammad and Chief Accountant Hashim. But it was Ahfaz whom Begum Nusrat Bhutto was waiting for.
She welcomed him warmly and asked directly: “What do you think we should do?” Ahfaz replied: “Your senior party leaders would know better than me.” But Nusrat Bhutto insisted. “No, I want your opinion.”
With characteristic clarity, he laid it out: “The government claims it shut down Musawaat over unpaid dues. If we pay those dues, we remove their pretext. And we expose their real motives for what they are.” She sighed deeply. Not because she disagreed, but because she was surrounded by voices urging her not to waste the money. “They all say it will be for nothing,” she admitted. “That Zia is just using this as an excuse.” “Yes,” Ahfaz said, “but let’s take away that excuse.”
Ahfaz’s insistence on paying the dues stemmed from a strategic reason: many members within the PFUJ were anti-PPP and were arguing that the closure of Musawaat was not an attack on press freedom but merely a legal issue arising from non-payment. By ensuring the payment of dues, Ahfaz aimed to strip those opportunistic elements within the PFUJ of that excuse, leaving them no place to hide behind procedural justifications.
At that, Nusrat Bhutto called for a cheque that had evidently already been prepared. She signed it, one lakh and eighty thousand rupees, and extended it toward Ahfaz. “These people are telling me not to give this,” she said, “but I want you to take it. Do what needs to be done.” Ahfaz, stunned, pushed the cheque back. “I’m just a magazine editor. It should go to the administration.” She refused. “I want to give it to you.”
Eventually, they struck a compromise: she would hand it to the officers, but only if Ahfaz went with them. Together, they marched off to the Press Trust office to submit the cheque. The Press Trust took the cheque, but the printing ban on Musawaat remained. The deception was plain. As Ahfaz had predicted, this would be the final straw.
Now, the moral high ground was no longer up for debate. The PFUJ and APNEC had been handed the justification they needed to escalate the struggle. The state had lied. Musawaat had paid. And still, the voice of dissent was silenced. As mentioned at the beginning of this chapter, the PFUJ was primed for action and this latest act by the brutal martial law administration served as the last straw. Barna sahib, as the president of PFUJ and APNEC chairperson, took immediate notice of this deception by the government.
In December 1977, PFUJ started a full-fledged movement against the closure of Musawaat. However, unlike its earlier fights against Bhutto, this was going to be a tougher fight, with the martial law administration ruled by army boots.
There was no political support that could be found, save for the PPP and some small leftist groups. The rest of the political parties either joined the government or were, at the very least, supportive of Zia’s regime. Even senior leaders such as Wali Khan supported Zia insofar as he (Wali Khan) supported the slogan of “Accountability before elections”, basically ratifying Zia’s stance.
LT GEN MUJIBUR RAHMAN AND JAMAAT-I-ISLAMI’S UGLY ROLE
In this movement, Minhaj Barna led the charge, supported by a formidable core team: Nisar Usmani, Hafeez Raqib and Ahfaz. The PFUJ’s plan was audacious. Journalists from across Pakistan would travel to Lahore and Karachi in coordinated waves to voluntarily court arrest, a nonviolent strategy that would keep the flame of protest alive and the jails full.
The movement gained momentum and journalists from all over the country came to Karachi to court arrest in batches. From April 30-May 30, 1978, more than 120 journalists who came from various cities to court arrest in Lahore were arrested and sent to different jails of the Punjab province. Ahfaz was one of these journalists.
Then, in July 1978, journalists from all corners came to Karachi for courting arrest and were sent to different jails of the Sindh province. After going to jail in Punjab, Ahfaz was released and barred from entering Punjab. He returned underground in Karachi, helping coordinate the next round of protests. Now joined by workers, students, peasants and members of the Hari Committee, the movement grew teeth.
Zia’s regime struck back. His information secretary, Lt Gen Mujibur Rahman, a master of psychological warfare, unleashed a campaign of vilification and infiltration. The Jamaat-i-Islami, always ready to act as the establishment’s attack dog, called the PFUJ “seditious”, “communist” and “traitorous.” They even turned comrades against each other.
I still remember one particular day very well. Ahfaz had to go to Lahore in connection with the movement. I came to see him off at the house-gate. A white-bearded gentleman had come to pick him up. He was a calligrapher and, if I remember correctly, his name was Naseemul Haq Usmani. Both left Karachi together but did not return together. Their paths diverged. Why? Zia’s government had succeeded in infiltrating the ranks of the PFUJ and it turns out the calligrapher had sold out. But this was just the start.
A few days later, [sports journalist] Rashid Ahmed Siddiqui, in cahoots with the martial law administration, formed a separate PFUJ! About this traitorous act by those shameless journalists Ahfaz wrote in his book: “Two deeply shameful and reprehensible incidents occurred during this movement. On May 13, 1978, three journalists were publicly flogged on the orders of a military court, an act so disgraceful that it drew strong condemnation from journalists and democratic voices across the world. Just five days later, a group of four journalists arrived in Islamabad. They were welcomed at the airport by senior officials from the Information Department, and both national television and radio broadcast the news of the ‘arrival of PFUJ and APNEC leaders in Islamabad.’
“On the very same day, Zia’s information secretary, Gen Mujibur Rahman, met with these turncoats. In this meeting, all parties agreed that PFUJ and APNEC were ‘subversive’ organisations, a label that was not new. (Zia had once publicly declared that he would hang Minhaj Barna and his next seven generations.) The result of this meeting was a treacherous plan to form a puppet union, later known as the Rashid Siddiqui Group.
“These traitors struck the deal in exchange for promises of power and money. Rashid Siddiqui, an otherwise ordinary reporter, was later elevated to the top position at Daily Mashriq and NPT. The other three collaborators were similarly showered with lavish rewards. They certainly received their material prizes from Zia, but history, too, gave them a reward of its own, branding them forever as immoral cowards.”
Gen Mujibur Rahman may have been a master of psychological warfare, but he failed to break the spirit of Minhaj Barna and his associates. The PFUJ and APNEC executive committees ensured a steady stream of activists stepping forward to court arrest, an unrelenting pressure that proved nerve-wracking for the military junta. The Workers’ Coordination Committee also announced its participation in the movement. In addition, the Hari Committee and several student organisations joined the struggle.
Nisar Usmani, Hafeez Raqib and Ahfaz-ur-Rehman went underground to organise the court arrest campaign. The three constantly changed their hideouts, sometimes staying at [architect] Arif Hasan’s house, at other times at [then university teacher] Taj Haider’s place, or occasionally at the home of [journalist] Ghazi Salahuddin’s father. Shamim Alam and Altaf Siddiqui handled the duties of communication and coordination. As Ahfaz mentions in his book, [journalist] Irshad Rao and Wahab Siddiqui also played key roles in organising batches of potential arrestees.
The Karachi police were desperately searching for Ahfaz. They swore they’d catch Ahfaz. “Once we get our hands on him,” they sneered, “we’ll beat him senseless.” During this time, while Ahfaz was in hiding, I would occasionally go to meet him in secret, often taking little Fayfay [daughter] along with me. I remember, one day, Ahfaz smiled shyly and said to me, “Hafeez Raqib says Mahnaz will get us all arrested with these rendezvous.”
Once, Ahfaz was hiding at Taj Haider’s house and Fayfay and I went to see him. Taj Haider, who later joined electoral politics and became a senator, was Ahfaz’s close friend. That day, he took Ahfaz and me in his car all the way to ‘Bund Murad’, a secluded spot by the Hub River. At that time, this remote area outside the city was rarely visited, even by picnic-goers. Perhaps he simply wanted to give Ahfaz a break from the constant mental stress he was under. The two of them thoroughly enjoyed splashing about in the water while I sat on the bank with my feet dipped in the cool river.
On the drive back, I couldn’t shake the thought: what if the police stopped us and discovered that the very man they were frantically searching for was right there, sitting in Taj Haider’s car? They wouldn’t have spared Taj either. And yet, that was the kind of bravery and unwavering commitment our friends showed without hesitation.
IF INDIRA GANDHI HAD FACED PFUJ
Despite all this, despite betrayal and oppression, the movement held strong. On October 10, 1978, the struggle reached its end. More than 400 people had been jailed, including workers, peasants, students, journalists. The final blow was delivered by the moral force of hunger strikes.
When Minhaj Barna began his hunger strike in Sukkur Jail, it sparked a chain reaction across the prisons of Sindh. The state’s iron fist trembled. The newspapers may have blacked it out, but the nation heard the roar of defiance. The government backed down. The prisoners were released. And Musawaat, silenced for so long, returned to print.
This was a landmark movement and a historic victory, one so significant that even our neighbours took notice. India Today, in a powerful editorial, observed that had India possessed a principled and formidable organisation like the PFUJ during its own political crisis, Indira Gandhi would never have succeeded in imposing the Emergency in the country!

title: WIRED Brand Lab | The Omnichannel Future of Digital Sales
author: Branded Content By
body:
Sales teams face a new challenge when it comes to reaching customers: finding the right way to connect.
This is especially true in the business-to-business (B2B) world. Until just a few years ago, sales efforts relied on person-to-person interactions. But the online transition came fast—and it was permanent. According to a recent report, 33 percent of B2B buyers now prefer to do business seller-free. By 2025, 80 percent of B2B transactions will occur through digital channels.
For sales teams, this transition can be difficult to navigate.
To manage the shift to remote sales during the pandemic, many B2B teams adopted a hybrid approach, connecting with clients and prospects through a mix of marketing channels—email, text, mobile apps, in-person communications, and more. According to an industry study of 2,500 B2B organizations, more than 90 percent of enterprise companies plan to continue reaching customers this way for a simple reason: it works. Customers “want the right mix of in-person interactions, remote contact via phone or video, and e-commerce self-service across the purchasing journey,” the report states. “Because of its omnichannel nature, it enables broader and deeper real-time customer engagement.”
The new challenge? Streamlining the process.
In the rush to keep up with buyers moving online, many companies had seemingly unlimited budgets to scale their sales teams, test new tools, and use SaaS platforms to manage data and identify customers. Now, however, funding is tight because of economic uncertainty, and sales teams are forced to adopt a new byword to tackle an ever more complex world: simplify.
“Having the right data and tools, as opposed to a lot of tools, is key,” says James Casola, vice president of sales and marketing solutions for Dun & Bradstreet. “Simplifying the sales process with an end-to-end, data-driven solution that can serve multiple markets is the direction companies are headed.”
The Great Simplification
For a few years, investment in sales departments appeared to have no end in sight.
During COVID-19, many companies seemed to transition to digital B2B sales overnight, expanding teams, tech stacks, and tools to connect with customers in new ways. “I call this the great complication,” Casola says. “Companies tried anything they could to remain competitive in a fast-moving environment.”
Investment in sales tech generated a lot of value. Digital sales and clients’ buying journeys produced vast amounts of data, and companies enriched their knowledge of customers.
Yet all that data presented a new problem to solve: organizing and deploying it effectively.
“Many companies became overwhelmed,” says Casola. “Now they’re focusing on finding the right tools to maximize the data they already have in house.” Often, businesses aren’t making full use of their data. A cybersecurity company, for instance, approached Dun & Bradstreet because it assumed that the largest share of its customers was with Fortune 500 companies—their most expansive and lucrative accounts. Yet when Dun & Bradstreet analyzed the company’s customer data and ran it against its own proprietary database, a surprising discovery was made. Twenty percent of the company’s clients were in education, while another 25 percent came from businesses with 150 employees or less.
“If that company had targeted businesses that weren't its primary customer types, that would have been an absolute failure,” Casola says.
Narrowing a customer type can be achieved efficiently and quickly with the right data. Casola, for instance, had four clients that insisted on doing businesses with companies using a specific CRM software. Vetting that information against its data, Dun & Bradstreet shrank the target market by 80 percent, then applied additional metrics to arrive at an exact buyer type that offered a better chance of a sale. “At that point, we lock arms with the CMO and apply our assets to a much smaller target and drive traffic,” he says.
The key to winnowing the target market efficiently was to pair the company’s first-party data with third-party data that created deeper, richer sets of information—then it presented everything in a single, easy-to-use platform. At that point, the company could come up with a game plan for contacting the right person at the right time with the right message.
“In today’s environment, leadership teams don’t want their salespeople going wide anymore,” Casola says. “You have to be targeted.”
Simplifying the Customer Experience, Too
Increasingly, speed and convenience for customers is paramount.
Take for instance a company offering an online summary of its product. If a prospective customer wants to access that to learn more, but has to enter a lot of data to do so, the sale could be derailed. “Nobody wants the great inquisition,” Casola says.
The trick is to find the right balance between convenience and getting enough information to create amore robust set of robust first-party data. Dun & Bradstreet offers a solution that pre-populates the online forms, making it easy to quickly click through to the desired content. Then, with that basic information, Dun & Bradstreet can compare a potential buyer’s profile with its own data sets to fill in additional details. Since many purchases are made by buying groups, not individuals, that comprehensive picture helps sales teams create a hybrid strategy that effectively reaches all the desired groups of customers.
“You might have 5,000 customers who’ve visited your site, but all you have is their company name, address, one contact, and an email address,” Casola says. “You need to know where the buyers are coming from, their industry, and how big they are. That’s where we come in. We can fill in the holes with about 2,700 data elements and scores, and this information helps you find the businesses that are more likely to be your desired customers.”
It’s also important for sales and marketing teams to have a complete, coordinated view of the data they’re looking at. If, say, a prospective customer has read a summary, has already spoken with someone in the company, and is then contacted by a salesperson unaware of that history, the result may be frustration.
“Inbound traffic is no longer one-size-fits-all,” Casola says. “Prospective customers should be able to talk with someone who can address their specific needs quickly, without additional screening. The future is about integration and simplification.”
Make B2B Feel More Like B2C
Given all the focus on data, it can be easy to forget a basic truth: sales is still about people connecting with people.
As B2B buyers increasingly do their purchasing online—and as data becomes more important to thriving in this environment—it becomes important to target them as individuals. In this way, the B2B and B2C worlds are merging, with many of the same tactics useful for both, whether customers are buying for themselves or for their company.
“One of the biggest transitions in data is the ability to stitch together business and personal information,” Casola says. “There’s no reason why your personal interests can’t bleed over into your business interests and vice versa, and the sophistication of what can be done here is just exploding.”
For years, for instance, a leading bank in the United States kept the data of its business and retail customers separate. But by comparing its data sets with those of a third party like Dun & Bradstreet—and discovering where B2B and B2C customers overlap—the bank was better able to market to both.
In the end, the true power of data is the ability to enhance relationships. What does that look like after all the back-end research about a customer has been done? Sometimes all it takes is a simple text to stand out.
“We’ve made a huge investment in cell phone numbers, because that’s where people want to interact,” Casola says. “For every text you get per day in B2B, you might get 20 emails.”
Overall, the power of the hybrid approach—one built on proper data—is the ability to reach customers in the way they prefer. “Again, the future is the great simplification,” Casola says, “using data to make our lives—and sales—easier.”
This story was produced by WIRED Brand Lab for Dun & Bradstreet.

title: When Aboriginal people appeared in a 1950 film they were asked to invent dialogue. Now a spotlight is shining on the tale they told
author: Douglas Smith
tags: Indigenous Australians,Australian film,Film,Australia news,South Australia,Rural and regional Australia,Culture,Frontier wars
body:
The first time Vonda Last watched Bitter Springs, she recognised her grandfather. The black-and-white Australian classic drew headlines at the time for being the first English film made in South Australia, starring the likes of Tommy Trinder, Chips Rafferty and Charles “Bud” Tingwell. But for the people of Ooldea in the central desert, it is notable for a different reason: it also stars 120 Anangu people, speaking in language.
Last’s grandfather, Thumu Pluto Hicks, was among those who travelled for two days in a train carriage from his remote community to the railway town of Quorn in the Flinders Rangers to appear in the film.
He died when Last was seven but she recognised him “straight away”.
“I was very proud,” the Ngaantjatjara woman says. “He was a wati [initiated man], and all of the men would’ve been senior men in that film, who were representing their strength and identity as Aboriginal men.”
The film tells the story of Wally King, played by Rafferty, who moves 600 miles into the outback to settle land he has leased from the government. On the journey, white settlers warn him about the “Abos, blacks – hundreds of them” he would most likely encounter.
It is regarded as one of the first mainstream stories to challenge the narrative of the Australian frontier and the right of settlers to take Aboriginal land.
The Anangu actors weren’t given a script. They were cast in the roles of two fictitious tribes and just told to talk.
A joint project by linguists and First Nations language speakers to unpick the older dialect and translate what they said has now revealed a second, deeper story. The Anangu actors weren’t just saying meaningless words or sentences, which is what the film crew thought at the time – they were improvising this historical dialogue and giving a true depiction of what life was like when white settlers invaded their land and displaced them.
The translation project aims to shine a light on a forgotten piece of history and bring recognition to the Anangu actors who journeyed by train from remote parts of north-west SA, including from communities near the Maralinga lands. Some also came from remote parts of Western Australia
“Its powerful to hear that language because that’s the first language spoken in country,” Last says. “I said to another aunty, I said, ‘Can you understand that language?’ – because I sent her a link to that film.
“She reckon it’s language they spoke at Ooldea, back down Tjuntjuntjara. You can hear that it’s a different dialect to Pitjantjatjara. I don’t know if it’s an old language that people haven’t spoken for a while.”
‘Bitter Springs time’
A social anthropologist and honorary associate professor at the Australian National University, Dr Maggie Brady, has been working with people from the remote Aboriginal communities of Yalata, Oak Valley, Maralinga and the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara lands for the past five decades. While working to support the 1984 royal commission into the British nuclear tests at Maralinga, she heard locals speak of the years immediately proceeding the tests, which began in 1952, as “Bitter Springs time”.
Later, she would travel to Quorn to ask the non-Indigenous locals what they remembered of the production. She was shown photo albums featuring the film production and crew on set, including many pictures of the Anangu, and took a reel-to-reel copy of the movie to Yalata to play for the community.
“I guess I just realised that the film is probably a big part of their history,” she says, adding: “I got permission from the Quorn Historical Society to make copies and I made them up into photobooks and took them back to Maralinga and Oak Valley.
“I thought maybe we can identify some people in these photographs and, to my shock, I found that people were able to recognise their parents and grandparents in these images, even though, when those pictures were taken, their grandparents were just children.”
The production was scheduled to take 10 weeks but was delayed by bad weather. The white stars of the film stayed in Quorn’s Transcontinental hotel while the Anangu were housed in a campsite near the filming locations.
An Aboriginal language expert at Adelaide University, Associate Prof Sam Osborne, who speaks fluent Pitjantjatjara, is working with the Iwiri Aboriginal Corporation in Port Adelaide, alongside Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara interpreters, to translate and subtitle the film. It’s a complex process, involving some now unspoken dialects.
The primary question about the Anangu actors’ involvement before the translation project began, Osborne says, was whether they were just “verbalising, or vocalising and saying ‘blah, blah, blah, blah’” or whether they were improvising and taking part in the story’s development.
“What we discovered is that Anangu were improvising in really clever and thoughtful ways throughout the film,” he says. “It showed that a very creative space was opened up for meaning and understanding for the times …
“In coming together and meeting each other, there’s a series of interactions like seeing yourself in a mirror, striking a match, there’s a scene where the guy shows his rifle and what it can do.
“Then the Anangu goes, ‘Yeah, well it can’t shoot over a tree or around a rock’… and he sort of shows that you can sort of spear around a corner, but his bullets can’t do that.
“Theres a creativity and a genius to what the Anangu actors performed.”
In one scene, when the two fictitious tribes of Mangarayi and Yangman are confronted by the white settlers, a senior man holds his spear and yells “ma-pitija”, telling the white men to “go away”.
Watching translated extracts of the film, knowing that the director, film producers and white actors did not understand the whole of what they were making, was to this reporter – an Aboriginal man who grew up on the same country where many of the Anangu actors were from and can understand much of the language – a surreal experience. There is a depth to the story that is inaccessible to most viewers.
Osborne says the translation project gives a “rare insight into what [Anangu] people were thinking about and how they were contributing to that bigger story”.
Redress through rescreening
In 2024, while back in Quorn conducting more research about the film, Brady was introduced to Cindi Drennan, the founder and director of Illuminart, a company that projects art on to landmarks.
Drennan has since joined the project and effort to see the film translated in full, subtitled and shown at future Australian film festivals. In May, Illuminart produced and showcased a 30-minute documentary about the filming and production of Bitter Springs, and projected it on to grain silos in Quorn.
“When the film was played in Adelaide and it opened, there was a big hoo-ha fanfare but no Aboriginal actors were invited,” Drennan says, adding: “There was all this fanfare about the white actors in it but there was no recognition for the Aboriginal actors. They were just kind of like, black extras, even though they spent far more time speaking on screen I reckon then the white actors do.”
Together, Drennan and Brady are dreaming of a second chance at the film’s premiere, this time with the contribution of Anangu actors recognised.
“Maggie, she keeps coming back to, ‘We want to play this in Adelaide and we want to invite as many people as we can to that screening,’” Drennan says. “I think she justifiably feels like that would be, kind of a redress, or reparation for a lack of recognition over many years and I agree with her.”

title: Bachat Bazaar provides much-needed relief
author: Recorder Report
tags: Municipal Corporation Hyderabad;Aftab Soomro;Research and Development Foundation;Muhammad Naeem Sheikh;Muhammad Fahad Mian;Sikandar Ali Rajput;Irfan Arbiani;RDF;Zain ul Abideen Memon;Hyderabad Chamber of Small Traders & Small Industry;Bachat Bazaars;HCSTSI;government of Sindh;Municipal Corporation Hyderabad,Aftab Soomro,Research and Development Foundation,Muhammad Naeem Sheikh,Muhammad Fahad Mian,Sikandar Ali Rajput,Irfan Arbiani,RDF,Zain ul Abideen Memon,Hyderabad Chamber of Small Traders & Small Industry,Bachat Bazaars,HCSTSI,government of Sindh
body:
HYDERABAD: Senior Vice President Muhammad Fahad Mian and Vice President Irfan Arbiani of the Hyderabad Chamber of Small Traders & Small Industry (HCSTSI), along with a delegation, attended the Bachat Bazaar organized by the Research and Development Foundation (RDF) at the New Sabzi Mandi, Hyderabad.
They inaugurated the bazaar alongside the chief guest, Deputy Commissioner of Hyderabad, Zain-ul-Abideen Memon.
The initiative was also supported by HCSTSI and the Municipal Corporation Hyderabad. The delegation included Executive Committee Members Sikandar Ali Rajput, Muhammad Naeem Sheikh, and others.
Addressing the inaugural ceremony, Senior Vice President Muhammad Fahad Mian commended RDF Hyderabad Project Manager Aftab Soomro for his efforts towards public welfare. He said that Bachat Bazaars offering essential commodities at affordable prices provide much-needed relief to the public amid rising inflation.
Making essential items such as flour, pulses, sugar, rice, cooking oil, vegetables, fruits, clothing, and other household necessities available at reduced prices is a commendable step towards easing the financial burden on citizens.
He urged the Government of Sindh to allocate suitable land for the establishment of a permanent Bachat Bazaar in Hyderabad and promote such initiatives on a sustainable basis to provide lasting relief to the public from the impact of inflation.
Speaking on the occasion, Deputy Commissioner Hyderabad Zain-ul-Abideen Memon appreciated RDF, HCSTSI, and the Municipal Corporation Hyderabad for their collaborative efforts in facilitating the public.
He emphasized the importance of initiatives that make essential commodities available at affordable prices, particularly during periods of inflation, and highlighted the need for effective coordination among public institutions and relevant stakeholders to promote public welfare and provide relief to citizens.
RDF Project Manager Aftab Soomro stated that the Bachat Bazaar featured stalls offering food items, vegetables, fruits, traditional cuisine, clothing, and other household goods. Expressing satisfaction over the keen interest shown by citizens, he thanked the participating organizations and all stakeholders for their cooperation and support in making the initiative possible.

title: Word Problems About Dealing with a Friend’s Weird Boyfriend
author: Jennifer Kim
body:
1. Jessica will be hosting a small get-together at her house on Friday. If she invites 9 friends, how many people, including Jessica, will be in attendance?
A) 8
B) 9
C) 10
2. Jessica’s friend Elizabeth calls to ask if she can bring her boyfriend, Tim, to the small get-together. Suddenly, Jessica’s voice gets all high and weird, and she starts talking about how, if Tim comes, she’s worried that there won’t be enough hot dogs for everyone. If Tim comes, how many people will be in attendance?
A) 10
B) 11
C) 12
3. Elizabeth says that it’s fine—that she and Tim can just bring extra hot dogs, and buns, if needed. But Jessica insists that Elizabeth doesn’t know the specific brand of hot dogs and buns she’s already acquired, which means that if, for instance, Elizabeth brought Hawaiian buns and chicken sausages, there would be an inconsistency. Elizabeth says she knows that Jessica doesn’t like Tim. How long is the silence that follows?
A) 10 seconds
B) 30 seconds
C) 60 seconds
4. Jessica carefully clarifies that it’s not that she doesn’t like Tim, it’s just that she has some reservations. Elizabeth asks her to elaborate, so Jessica brings up that time Tim showed up to her birthday party, which was at a bar, like, in public, and started cutting his nails even after repeatedly being asked by the staff to stop. How many times was Tim asked to stop cutting his nails?
A) 2
B) 3
C) 5
5. Elizabeth gets defensive and tells Jessica that public nail-cutting is actually normal where Tim’s from. Jessica tries to confirm that Tim is from Connecticut, which Elizabeth ignores, because he is. Elizabeth expresses hurt that Jessica would judge Tim based on just one quirk. Jessica replies that it’s not just one quirk. How many quirks does Tim have?
A) 2
B) 4
C) 16
6. Jessica recounts the time they were all on that hike and Tim ate Jessica’s protein bar but kept blaming it on Elizabeth. Also the time they were at a bookstore and Tim kept saying that he’d read a bunch of books when it was clear he hadn’t, and then, when they’d try to test his knowledge about a particular book, suddenly he’d get “too sleepy” to respond. And, finally, the time they went to the boardwalk and Tim got into a verbal altercation with a child. How old was the child with whom Tim got into a verbal altercation?
A) 4
B) 5
C) 8
7. Elizabeth breaks down in tears and admits that, O.K., sure, Tim isn’t perfect, but then reminds Jessica that she doesn’t know what it’s like out there. Jessica is lucky that she met Chuck in college and doesn’t have to date right now, because it’s really bad. Elizabeth reiterates that it’s so, so, so, so bad to the point where she could tell Jessica some fucked-up stories, but she won’t do that to her. How many years has Elizabeth been single?
A) 4
B) 6
C) 9
8. Jessica didn’t realize how hard it’s been for Elizabeth and she’s happy that her friend found someone that she, at least, likes. Jessica mentions one good quality about Tim which is that he has a nice smile. This makes Elizabeth feel better and she asks Jessica to name other good qualities of Tim’s. How many good qualities is Jessica able to come up with?
A) 1
B) 1
C) 1
9. After trying for sort of a long while, Jessica ultimately reminds Elizabeth that it’s not about the quantity of good qualities someone has but the quality of those qualities. Elizabeth is confused and asks if this means that she can bring Tim to the small get-together. Jessica says yes. How many people will be attending Jessica’s gathering now?
A) 10
B) 11, because of fucking Tim
C) 13
10. Elizabeth asks if she and Tim should still bring some extra hot dogs and buns for the party. Jessica says no, that she went nuts at the store and bought 65 hot dogs and buns for the party, and that the whole hot-dog thing was just an excuse to uninvite Tim. If each attendee eats an equal number of hot dogs, how many hot dogs will each person eat?
A) 6
B) 7
C) 5.9
♦

title: How can the UK successfully create digital identities?
author: Branded Content By
body:
Society is becoming ever more digitised as citizens connect to the internet through an increasing array of apps, websites and devices. Even before the coronavirus pandemic, which has accelerated this trend, 96 per cent of UK households were connected to the internet – up from 93 per cent the year before. Through our online interactions, the vast majority of us are building up a digital footprint – a unique and complicated map of data trails, passwords and profiles that could, in theory, come together to comprehensively chart our lives as digital citizens.
However, for better or for worse, in the UK, these data sets remain largely disparate. Even within the public services sphere, systems remain unconnected, and rich and inclusive online profiles that connect all of our activities across our online lives do not exist. The reason for this is simple – we lack a unique digital identifier, something that could be used to connect our online activities to us as a verified individual.
While many might recoil at such an idea, digital identifiers, when deployed consensually and in a way that clearly delivers benefits to the user, are a much more palatable concept. As Doug Brown, Capita Consulting’s chief data scientist and head of data and AI guild explains, “this is all about the value exchange of accessing services as a result of providing data.” Across public service provision in particular, having a digital identity that improves access and saves time could offer significant benefits to the population.
Several governments, such as those in Estonia and Sweden, have already embarked upon a mass rollout of digital identity systems, enabling the public to access services with reduced friction. However, as Greg Williams, WIRED’s deputy global editorial director, summarises, “in the UK, we are still relying on physical documents for everything from getting a mortgage to proving our identity.”
The UK’s digital identity debate is not new. But according to Taavi Kotka, Estonia’s first government CIO and a cornerstone of Estonia’s successful e-residency rollout, after years of inaction, the UK risks being left behind in the wake of other nations’ digital successes.
To explore this topic further, in partnership with Capita, WIRED brought together a group of leading experts from the London School of Economics, Goldsmiths, University of London, the Golden Valley Development and Estonia’s first ever CIO to discuss pros, cons, and the potential path ahead.
Any UK citizen who has changed their name will have endured a heavy administrative burden associated with updating multiple organisations. Identity documents must be scanned, signed, witnessed and shared several times over. Imagine a world in which critical services – banks, GPs, dentists, HMRC, pension providers, the DVLA, to name but a few – can all be updated through one set of actions.
Having a unique digital identity could present an easy, convenient solution to a public services sphere that is, at present, unnecessarily complex. It could also link to trusted private sector institutions such as banks and private healthcare providers to further reduce friction.
But, for citizens, it’s not just about reducing admin. Having a single unique identifier connecting their data has a multitude of benefits. As Capita Consulting’s Brown explains, “digital identity could be the door to providing citizens with seamless access to healthcare and education, as well as other government programmes.” For example, using a patient’s unique digital identity, healthcare providers can instantly know their past medical history, helping to inform treatment decisions.
Governments also stand to benefit from digitised public services provision, verified digital identities and unique citizen identifiers. As highlighted by Capita in its most recent Pulse survey, over 85 per cent of respondents believed that the informed use of data will be important for driving decision making following on from the pandemic. With the influx of good, representative data, any decisions made are better informed. Policies can become more relevant and useful to the populace. Even fraud can be reduced as systems can instantly prove if a user is legitimate or not. Additionally, the longer term economic savings associated with fewer, more efficient systems could be immense.
As many countries have shown, there are clear benefits of digitising and connecting public services, and giving citizens a unique identifier to access these. Canada, Sweden, India, Estonia and China have rolled out digital identification schemes, and have seen the benefits. As Kotka states, “for the countries who have implemented unique identifiers, the results are great. In Estonia, the public trusts the government more and feels more empowered, as they know exactly how and where their data is being used.”
In terms of realising the vision of having better, more joined-up digital services, accessed through a unique user identity, Kotka presents a relatively simplistic path ahead. The first step is finding a universally accessible, indisputable way to prove an individual’s identity. This might be achieved through a predominantly private-sector based stance, following a scheme such as the Swedish bankID model which utilised the existence of a citizen’s bank account along with a national registration number. Alternatively, it might be wholly government led, such as in Estonia’s e-residency scheme. The second step is to use this identity to connect data-sets and services in a joined-up way. So, if the steps are so clear, and the opportunities so sizable, then why hasn’t the UK government taken them?
While it is clear that opportunities exist, this is a multi-faceted debate, with several factors impeding the move from talk to action.
According to Kotka, for the government at least, it’s all about the incentives. Those countries that have rolled out successful digital identity schemes had a clear incentive to do so. For India, it was tackling corruption; for Estonia, it was the need to elevate the country’s status as a leading digital economy to help it access global talent. Although incentives such as longer-term economic savings and improved citizen experiences are clear, for the UK, the short-term benefits are unlikely to outweigh the upheaval, time and expense of rolling out joined-up, digitised services with unique identifiers to enable easy access.
The challenge here is also one of systems and strategies. The UK has a large number of unconnected ways to prove identity; from passports, to driving licences, to the Verify system – the list is ongoing. According to Dr Edgar Whitley, associate professor in Information Systems at LSE, “government departments are all claiming to sing from the same song sheet, but are all doing it slightly differently”. The UK government has a National Data Strategy but, as Brown points out, this is unlikely to address necessary transformations.
A further barrier to progress is public mistrust around the government’s approach to data and identity. Individuals worry about how their data could be used against them and are wary about trusting the government with any further information than necessary. It is likely that the actions of Big Tech companies and other bad actors over the course of the past ten years have indelibly changed public trust in government data sharing. This is compounded by the UK’s track record in the space of National Identity. As Lisa Talia Moretti, Goldsmith’s associate lecturer in management studies, phrases it, “the UK has a long and chequered history with identity cards.” The then government’s attempt at a National Identity scheme in 2002 was perceived by many as an infringement upon civil liberties, and memories of this will potentially taint user attitudes to any schemes that might follow.
While the public’s attitudes towards data collection and usage are shifting, concerns around data usage and consent remain. According to Moretti, “there has been a huge sea change in how people understand data and the value of their own data. As awareness about safety and security online grows, many prefer to opt out of sharing their data. But for those that do share, they want to know that it will be protected and secured.”
Finally, we must not overlook the fundamental flaw with digital services and digital identity schemes – by their very nature, they are unavailable to the digitally excluded. This important minority is then left out of data sets, which leads to inaccurate assumptions, skewed data and unhelpful policies. Representative data is vital to increasing understanding and rolling out nuanced schemes that are valuable for users and governments alike. Any future initiatives need to be designed in a way that ensures the benefits are for all and, critically, serve to reduce, and not widen, the existing digital divide.
What cannot be done is a copy-and-paste effort based on the successes of other countries. What follows next has to be tailored to the unique context, demographics and public attitudes of the UK. If we are to deliver better solutions for all, then there are several things which need to be done differently:
Put citizens at the heart of the initiatives
Before rolling out new initiatives, understanding public attitudes and needs is vital. There is a line between convenience and intrusion, and it is important to understand where that line exists for the public. This means listening to, and actively involving, communities across the UK. As Reid Derby, innovation lead at the Golden Valley Development, explains, “there are a whole set of assumptions that we need to test. We need to figure out how we can put the citizen at the heart of this.” Moretti supports this, suggesting we flip the question on its head, “perhaps rather than just asking people what they want, we should also explore the value that we are trying to create for individuals in society”.
Build trust in data-sharing through total transparency and dynamic consent
In-building trust is vital to the success of any scheme. Privacy should be a cornerstone of the strategy, so individuals can trust that any and all data is collected securely. As Whitley phrases it, “we’re not objecting to data sharing – we just need the system to do it transparently and with full openness.” Individuals should also be able to access systems, consent to their data being collected, agree what it can be used for and change their mind whenever they want. Critically, they should be able to see exactly where and when their data is being used. This rebalance of power would place the emphasis on the user, not the system. According to Kotka, a key success factor in Estonia was “showing the benefits of such a system early, so that society buys into it”. This helped citizens to want similar experiences which, in turn, helped drive further adoption.
Ensure skills, systems and legislation support success
The right systems, skills and legislation must be established by governments before they initiate any changes. Legislation has to support easy, safe, relevant and secure data sharing between service areas. Systems must be dynamic, offering clear user benefits and easy access. The skillsets of those involved in developing the solutions must cover the technical build and human-centred design thinking critical to developing solutions that are truly fit for purpose.
Educate citizens around the opportunities
As Derby points out, “improving digital literacy will ensure that a wider cross-section of individuals can engage with, and play a part in, shaping the systems that they utilise regularly, while delivering wider benefits for both the public and the economy.”
Furthermore, helping citizens to understand the value exchange in sharing their data, and why their data holds value, will help encourage uptake of digital services. A cornerstone of bridging the gap should be the drive for inclusivity and ensuring that members of marginalised communities are not left behind.
Reframe our thinking – it doesn’t have to be all or nothing
Ultimately, a reset needs to happen regarding the way that digital service provision is thought about. It’s not a matter of all or nothing. More public services can become digitised without the need for unique digital identifiers, fully joined-up public service provision or links to commercial data sets. It may be that a scaling-up approach, which gradually builds services (and trust) is the way ahead.
In fact, the UK may already have a viable start-point from which to scale up. The NHS app, developed during the Covid-19 crisis, which already has over 4.8 million users, could perhaps be used as a model to build trust around a whole range of digital service public provisioning. With public trust in this app seemingly high, it is not so hard to imagine expanding its functionality to see it act as an interface between healthcare practitioners and patients.
There is a clear argument for starting with the end in mind. That means having a shared view of outcomes that the UK is trying to achieve. It will involve answering questions such as which services would benefit from greater digitisation? Is the goal to connect new services to existing ones? Should individuals have unique identifiers that enable them to access these services with ease?
Of course, it’s not just about where the journey is heading, it’s also about how we will get there. As Whitley states, “do it right – as there are lots and lots of ways to do it wrong.” There needs to be clarity on what the path to success looks like, and the metrics by which success will be measured. It also needs to work to include the public throughout, which includes addressing who has the skills and knowledge to make the system happen. Critically, the question of who is going to fund the scheme also needs to be addressed.
To answer these questions in a meaningful way, different perspectives and voices need to be heard – including those that have little access to the digital world. Whatever the answers, collaboration between multi-disciplined groups will be vital to delivering desired outcomes. As Brown envisions, “we need to get started - we get a team of people, with different perspectives and different views, that want to get something practical in place.” This will mean looking beyond the usual suspects and finding those with the right insights and skills to deliver the vision. For Derby, it’s that “we’ve got to be more honest and open about how we work on this together, because we are all in it together.”
But perhaps, most importantly, if the UK is serious about pushing forward in this space, it’s time to do as Kotka suggests and “stop talking and act”. This debate is not a new one, and as more and more countries roll out connected digital services and digital identification schemes, the UK risks being at the back of the pack.
For more information on Capita's Pulse surveys, head to https://www.capita.com/c/great-opportunity-yougov-report
For more information on WIRED Consulting, head to https://consulting.wired.co.uk/
