title: Copper prices rebound
author: Reuters
tags: Hansen;International Nickel Study Group;COPENHAGEN;Saxo Bank;Ole Hansen;Shanghai Futures Exchange;London Metal Exchange;United States;Hansen,International Nickel Study Group,COPENHAGEN,Saxo Bank,Ole Hansen,Shanghai Futures Exchange,London Metal Exchange,United States
body:
LONDON: Copper prices bounced on Friday after a sharp decline in the previous session as stock markets stabilised and the build-up of inventories slowed.
Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange gained 1 percent to USD14,217 a metric ton by 1430 GMT, having slid 1.9 percent to a five-week low in the previous session.
Metals markets were supported as a rout in global tech shares eased after concerns over the enormous funding needs of AI had hammered Wall Street.
“Today we’ve got the Nasdaq futures bouncing after that selloff yesterday and that’s probably why we’re seeing some metals investors getting back in,” said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank in Copenhagen.
Investors were still nervous and there was the risk of further losses in copper, especially if prices broke below the September low of USD13,925, he said. Worries about excess inventories abated after daily data showed on Friday that LME copper stocks rose by 800 metric tons, having jumped by a fifth over the past week to 273,750 tons.
In China, inventories in warehouses registered with the Shanghai Futures Exchange tumbled by 26.5 percent, weekly data showed on Friday. Investors were still concerned about the overhang of stocks in the United States, which has attracted huge flows of copper due to speculation about the government imposing tariffs, Hansen said. “That massive pile of copper in the US is clearly weighing on prices given the risk of re-exporting that copper into the rest of the market,” Hansen said.
Nickel was the worst performer on the LME, giving up 2.1 percent at USD15,780 a ton as traders awaited clearer signals from Chinese companies considering coordinated output cuts at their Indonesian operations.
The International Nickel Study Group last week forecast a small global surplus this year, reversing an earlier deficit forecast. Among other metals, LME aluminium gained 0.6 percent to USD3,028 a ton, zinc advanced 1.6 percent to USD3,731, lead added 0.5 percent to USD1,907 and tin rose 0.7 percent to USD50,445.

title: Let’s go nuts in the garden – and the cobnut is a great place to start
author: Claire Ratinon
tags: Gardening advice,Gardens,Life and style,Nuts and seeds,Food
body:
When I think of the crops I’m eager to grow, my mind rarely goes to nuts. But when I spotted the last of the season’s cobnuts at the greengrocer’s, it occurred to me that this could be one to consider. The nuts that come from the hazel – a tree that grows in many a woodland and also my front garden – have been foraged for millennia and cultivated versions have existed since Roman times.
It’s the cultivated varieties you want to plant for a decent crop of cobnuts, as wild hazel produces smaller yields. This is a tree that prefers mild conditions, hence their connection to Kent, where they were grown abundantly during the Victorian era (one of the most popular varieties is called the Kentish cob.) They prefer a sunny spot, in free-draining earth – a challenge for me with my clay soil – in a sheltered position where they’ll be protected from frosts that would affect pollination.
As cobnut trees are monoecious – meaning that the pollen-bearing catkins and the fruit-bearing flowers grow separately but on the same tree – pollination is a key consideration. Some cultivars will not self-pollinate and so rely on the presence of another tree (as well as the wind) for successful pollination. Fortunately, wild hazel can pollinate most cultivars, so if you have some in your garden, as I do, you may well be fine.
As with most trees, the best time to plant them is when they are dormant, so from November through to late winter works for cobnuts, which are generally sold as one- to two-year-old trees. While it is possible to get a crop of nuts from an unpruned tree, making the effort to prune should result in larger, better quality nuts. Aim for an open structured tree with about 10 leaders growing outwards. Once established, prune to prevent overcrowding in winter. If you do this after the catkins have arrived, this can help distribute pollen for better pollination. Additionally, brutting is a traditional pruning technique that encourages heavier cropping and involves bending that season’s side shoots in late summer, but leaving the broken section still attached.
Cobnuts are ready to harvest from August if you like the taste of them when fresh, before they start to ripen. In any case, this might be your only opportunity if you share your garden with squirrels. Green cobnuts have a delicate nutty flavour and a juicy texture, but for those who prefer the more typical nut experience, wait until the husks start to turn yellow a month or so later. Cracking, shelling and then lightly roasting your cobnuts serves to enhance their nutty flavour.

title: Susanna Clarke discusses her book 'The Bishop of Durham Attempts to Surrender the City'
author: Scott Simon
body:
Susanna Clarke discusses her book 'The Bishop of Durham Attempts to Surrender the City'
NPR's Scott Simon speaks with Susanna Clarke about, "The Bishop of Durham Attempts to Surrender the City," an illustrated story set in the world of her earlier novel, "Jonathan Strange & Mr. Norrell."
SCOTT SIMON, HOST:
The town of Durham in northern England, 1110 AD, prepares for a siege from encircling forces. But then people notice something unexpected.
SUSANNA CLARKE: (Reading) A thick mist covered the country. This was not so very surprising. It was winter. Yet the people of Durham felt some apprehension as to what would happen next. Looking out, they thought they saw shadowy figures in the mist. These did not appear to be fairies or men - the shape was wrong. Some people said the figures were slowly approaching. Others thought they were not moving at all. By the next day, two things were clear - the figures were indeed moving, and they were huge.
(Reading) When at last they emerged out of the mist, the citizens saw that they were not giants or ogres, as they had feared, but trees - the ordinary trees of England. One by one, they crossed the fields and meadows and assembled to form a dense wood. Within a few days, it surrounded the town.
SIMON: Susanna Clarke reading from her new illustrated short story, "The Bishop Of Durham Attempts To Surrender The City." The bestselling novelist, author of the Hugo Award-winning "Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell," joins us now from London. Thanks so much for being with us.
CLARKE: You're very welcome. It's a pleasure to be here.
SIMON: There's a fairy host sweeping across the countryside. What do we know of - I don't know if I say him or them or whatever.
CLARKE: Them. The story expands on a part of "Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell" which appears in the book about two-thirds of the way through, when I finally give the kind of foundational history of that world, which is a world in which a young king suddenly appears at the head of an army - a fairy host - and takes over, basically, the north of England and establishes a kingdom there. He's not himself a fairy but a child that was stolen away. As a teenager, he returns in this rather alarming way.
SIMON: And tell us about the bishop of Durham.
CLARKE: Ranulf Flambard. Yes. He was an actual bishop. He has a Wikipedia page and everything. All of this takes place shortly after the Norman Conquest, when the Normans came from France and took over England. Ranulf is a Norman. The Normans were very, very good at administration, at building castles, dominating the country, getting communications going. And Ranulf - primarily, he's a politician and an administrator. So what he sees when the fairy host appears is almost an opportunity. He wants to kind of stabilize the country. But he also wants to make his own position a little better, which he thinks he can do by sort of muscling in on the court of the new king.
SIMON: It's hard not to think of the Bayeux Tapestry, which is now on display in England.
CLARKE: Yes. I didn't know when I wrote the story that that was going to happen, I have to say. But when it was suggested to me that we should have illustrations, that was very much the sort of thing that I was thinking of - little quaint illustrations that kind of gave you a bit of a sort of way into this medieval world.
SIMON: The illustrations are by Victoria Sawdon. Did you go back and forth, or did she just take the tale and begin to draw?
CLARKE: We did have some back-and-forth. The Norman castles immediately after the conquest had to be put up very, very quickly, so they were made in wood. But English people can't quite imagine that because now we see castles dotted round the landscape, and they're all gray stone. So the illustrator, quite understandably, kept drawing stone castles, and I kept having to say, no, no, no. They're wood. They're wood.
SIMON: You also write a little bit in this book about your life as a writer and say you were never good at putting away childish things.
CLARKE: That's certainly true. I tried. I did try to write a sort of grown-up novel and realized I really couldn't. It didn't work. I gave up. But within about a month, I'd returned. And something about that giving up allowed the fantasy to flow in. I began to feel that I wanted to write something about the English landscape, really, and how I felt about it. And out of that came the idea for "Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell," this story of two magicians in the 19th century but which had another story behind it, which was the medieval story - a sort of story showing through.
SIMON: Do you think we might all benefit now by seeing the world alive as a child does?
CLARKE: Absolutely. The natural world is in trouble. North America, more than here, is suffering from storms and hurricanes. Worldwide, we're suffering with species becoming extinct. Nature is in trouble, and I think we have to start seeing the natural world as having a dignity and an importance of its own. Fiction, possibly particularly fantasy fiction, can give a voice because the natural world used to have a voice - naiads and dryads in Greek mythology. The spirits spoke for the trees and the rivers. And I think the descendants of those naiads and dryads and spirits tend to show up more in fantasy fiction.
SIMON: How many different worlds are in your mind as you go through the day?
CLARKE: Probably two. This one - the world of "Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell," and the one I have to live in. But they do fade in and out of each other quite a lot.
SIMON: (Laughter) Do you find yourself seeing the world differently because you see it differently in what you write?
CLARKE: I think that what I write flows naturally out of the way I see the world. The older I get, the more I return to how I saw the world, if not as a young child, then certainly as an older child and a teenager and a young person. I've been on a train journey and just looking out at a rather misty, gray English day, but a day where the autumnal trees are absolutely glowing gold and just creating this wonderful glow. That's very important to me, and I think no longer do I see it as merely scenery. I see it as something terribly important that we need to connect to.
SIMON: Susanna Clarke. Her new short story is "The Bishop Of Durham Attempts To Surrender The City." It is illustrated by Victoria Sawdon. Thank you so much for being with us.
CLARKE: Thank you. It's been wonderful.

title: Obama tears into Trump over corruption, Iran war and 'tacky' White House makeover
author: Reuters
body:
Published October 25, 2026
US President Donald Trump has been telling voters to view the midterm elections as if he were on the ballot, and on Saturday one of his Democratic predecessors did just that.
Ten days out from the elections that will determine control of the closely divided Congress, Barack Obama took to the campaign trail to accuse the Republican president of corruption, deride his strategy for Iran and skewer the gilded aesthetic he has applied to White House renovations.
Obama stumped for Democratic candidates at rallies in Cleveland and Detroit, lampooning the Trump administration.
Campaigning in Michigan for US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Obama framed the November 3 vote as a "circuit breaker" to "at least rein in some of the foolishness" of Trump's presidency.
"We got to flip that circuit breaker, bring some accountability to this government," Obama said.
Obama, president from 2009 until Trump began his first term in 2017, remains one of the most popular figures among Democrats. They hope that bringing him into the race can fire up their supporters for a tight US Senate race in which El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, a former US representative.
The former president obliged the Michigan crowd by playing to Democrats' frequently repeated criticisms of Trump and of Republicans' willingness to go along with him.
"We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting, on your dime, like this," Obama said. "Never seen a president so intent on selling favours like this ... Now the party seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government."
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll in August found that 63% of Americans think the president and his family have inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency since he returned to the White House last year and that 69% believe his policy decisions are influenced by his private business dealings.
Obama also ridiculed the administration's claims of victory against Iran. He argued that the war has given Iran more economic leverage because its threats to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have unsettled oil exporters.
"Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to get to the world," Obama said.
The former president also accused the Trump administration of emphasising unimportant matters, sarcastically calling Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth someone "laser-focused on important matters like the jawline and testosterone levels of our troops" and ridiculing White House renovations as tacky.
"He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Obama said.

title: Driving Inclusivity: The hybrid branch of the future
author: Branded Content By
body:
After months of elbow taps and fist bumps, we’ve finally welcomed handshakes and hugs back into our social lives. When it comes to our financial lives, however, it seems as though we’re not reverting to old habits—the shift to digital and contactless is here to stay, with over two-thirds of those surveyed in Mastercard’s New Payment’s Index planning to use cash less often in future.
Still, as Gregor Dobbie, CEO of payment infrastructure, application and service provider, Vocalink, a Mastercard company, points out, cash remains an important method of payment. “There’s been a lot of talk about how cash use has declined as a result of Covid,” he explains. “But I’m equally as focused on the number of people who prefer cash and have already begun to move back to it.”
While the pandemic has helped convert millions of people worldwide to the benefits of the digital economy, the experience hasn’t always been a smooth one. Despite the rise of digital payments and technology—such as mobile wallets—Mastercard’s research shows that 30 per cent of UK consumers remain uncertain about using it.
“The number of choices that you can make now about where and how you transact must be terrifying for people who have not been educated in the area of digital payments,” Dobbie says, “Many of us had phone calls in the pandemic from elderly relatives asking for assistance with technology.”
Beyond difficulty in making purchases, the older generations may be particularly at risk of being cut off from access to financial services as branches close, with only 42 percent of over-65s using a banking app, according to Mastercard’s research.
This digital divide also disproportionally impacts those in poverty. Around half of UK residents with an income below £11,500 lack essential digital skills, compared to just over ten per cent of those with an income above £25,000. For many, questions about the security of digital methods remain a barrier to making the switch, with 39 per cent of UK consumers surveyed by Mastercard citing this as an area of concern.
That’s why Mastercard has partnered with the Nobody in the Dark foundation to offer one-to-one support, online resources and access to digital devices to help those who are most at risk of digital financial exclusion.
“If people don’t trust digital, then the most important element is education, which right now is truly lacking,” Dobbie says.
While education is an important piece of the puzzle, as Dobbie emphasises, the aim is never to force people into digital banking. It’s important to remember that the transition can be difficult and that some have reasons to prefer cash—such as the ability to easily control spending in line with a constrained budget. Digital banking will need to continue to improve to meet these needs, and where it cannot, it’s vital to ensure that people can still manage their finances in whatever way works best for them.
That means it’s crucial to retain access to cash and banking services for people who prefer to speak face-to-face. Yet over the past six years, more than 4,000 bank and building societies branches in the UK have closed down, as financial institutions find it’s no longer viable to maintain as many premises as they used to.
“Small business owners often select their banking provider based on branch location,” Dobbie says. “When branches get closed down, their nearest branch can go from a mile away to 20 miles away. That’s a lot more time—and often money—to deposit your salary.”
For many, the Post Office has provided a lifeline. Just shy of 100 percent of the UK’s population lives within 3 miles of one of its 11,500 branches, which allow business and personal customers from 26 banks to withdraw and deposit cash via the Vocalink-powered Everyday Banking services and its 1,400-strong ATM network.
“There’s now a move towards legislation ensuring that people have free access to cash within a certain distance of their home,” Dobbie explains. “That’s where the Post Office will be critical, because it has an expansive distribution network across the UK, it's very much a trusted community hub brand. If you look at where ATMs recovered volume quickest following Covid, you’ll see it’s in the Post Offices serving the more vulnerable sectors of society.”
As Dobbie points out, ensuring people can move their money around is only half of a bank’s job.
“Branches have been traditionally doing two things,” he says. “There’s offering the ability to transact, whether that’s depositing cheques or withdrawing cash, and then there’s the ability to get advice, whether that’s on the best mortgage product or guidance about how to avoid getting into an overdraft.”
By connecting the operations of multiple institutions together, the Post Office is allowing different banks to operate their advice and sales services out of a shared hub. Two Post Offices in the UK have already trialled this “banking hub” model, with plans for a rollout across the UK.
Digitalisation does not spell the end of in-person banking, but rather the opportunity to improve it, such as through the introduction of biometric security for automatic identity verification when a customer enters a branch, automated cheque-clearing, or AI-assisted instant credit checks. The future branch will combine the ease and efficiency of digital technologies with the interpersonal skills of branch representatives, whose time can now be dedicated to helping those who need a more human touch.
“It’s very important that the customer has access to all services, whether they’re using physical or digital,” says Dobbie. “Our view is that no one should be forced to transact in a way they're not comfortable with, and our job is to ensure they have that choice, and no one is left behind.”

title: European student protests take aim at Serbia's elections
author: Hannah Bloch
body:
European student protests take aim at Serbia's elections
European student protests take aim at Serbia’s elections
Students have been protesting across Europe. In Serbia, they've selected candidates to run for parliament in Sunday's elections. And they're aiming to end 14 years of government by the populist leader Aleksandar Vucic.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST:
Students across Europe have been taking to the streets in protest. In Serbia, they're taking their movement to the ballot box, with a list of candidates ranging from academics and economists to athletes and engineers who are running in Sunday's parliamentary elections. They hope to end 14 years of rule by a populist leader in the Serbian Progressive Party. Guy De Launey reports from Serbia's capital, Belgrade.
GUY DE LAUNEY, BYLINE: Tens of thousands of people are gathering here at Slavija Square in the center of Serbia's capital, Belgrade. They're turning out for the final pre-election rally of the Student List. That's the opposition movement, which emerged from the long-running student-led protests. Now it's posing the most serious challenge to Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vucic, since his Progressive Party took power in 2012.
MIHAIL DUDAS: I want people to be free - to be free to say whatever they want, to be free to talk about the political situation, to talk about the solutions.
LAUNEY: Mihail Dudas represented Serbia in the decathlon at two Olympic Games. Now he's among the people running for parliament on the Student List.
DUDAS: I am very honored to be selected to be in 250 very, very smart, good, powerful people who are ready to basically change the direction in - for Serbia in the right direction.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
LAUNEY: Around 150,000 people attended the Student List rally this week, marking the culmination of a protest movement that started two years ago. That's when a concrete canopy collapsed at the recently renovated railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second-largest city. Sixteen people died, and the disaster sparked student-led protests accusing Aleksandar Vucic of presiding over endemic corruption. He'd made infrastructure improvements a key part of his image as the strong leader steering Serbia into the future. So the station disaster has been hard for him to shake off.
MAGDA ANASTASIJEVIC: The government expected the protests to die down after the initial spark.
LAUNEY: Magda Anastasijevic is the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor ACLED.
ANASTASIJEVIC: Vucic has survived this in the past. He was always find a - able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
LAUNEY: In the home of the student protest movement, the pre-election atmosphere seems calm.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
LAUNEY: The young people studying here in Novi Sad have been collaborating with colleagues around the country to choose the candidates for the Student List. They didn't put themselves forward. They deliberately selected candidates with no background in politics.
VUK STOJIC: We are offering something new, something different.
LAUNEY: Vuk Stojic is a law student at Novi Sad University. He's one of the activists who've been involved in selecting the candidates for the parliamentary elections.
STOJIC: This is not only a student movement. It's a movement of all the free-thinking people in Serbia. And that's what gave us strength.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED RALLYGOERS: (Chanting in Serbian).
LAUNEY: At pre-election rallies, Aleksandar Vucic has brushed off his critics' accusations of autocratic tendencies. He resigned as president last month because he couldn't serve a third term, and he's now hoping to stay in power as prime minister.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED RALLYGOERS: (Chanting in Serbian).
LAUNEY: International monitors of previous elections have noted that Vucic's dominates the media and uses state resources for its own benefit. Many Serbians have been willing to overlook that as long as they accepted Vucic's carefully curated image as the protector of Serbia's interests. The Novi Sad disaster has undoubtedly damaged that, but Vucic remains defiant.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
ALEXSANDAR VUCIC: (Speaking Serbian).
LAUNEY: "We're going out there to win," he tells the crowd at this rally in Novi Sad. "We're going out there to defeat them, and we're going to deliver our biggest landslide victory yet."
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
LAUNEY: The Student List and the tens of thousands backing it beg to differ. For the first time in 14 years, Serbia's election looks uncertain.
For NPR News, I'm Guy De Launey in Belgrade, Serbia.

title: The Future of Digital Assistants Is Queer
author: Salomé Gómez-Upegui
body:
This November, the Smithsonian’s FUTURES festival, featuring innovations that are set to change the world, will include a familiar face. Or, rather, voice: Q, introduced in 2019 as the first “genderless AI voice,” is a human voice for use in digital assistants specifically created to be gender-ambiguous.
“Q was designed to start a conversation around why we gender technology when technology has no gender to begin with,” says Ryan Sherman, one of Q’s co-creators. To design the voice, a team of linguists, sound engineers, and creatives collaborated with nonbinary individuals and sampled different voices to land on a sound range they felt had the potential to disrupt the status quo and represent nonbinary people in the world of AI.
When Q was announced several years ago, it was hailed as “the genderless digital voice the world needs right now,” and an acknowledgment of the harm of feminizing assistants, which perpetuates misogynistic stereotypes of women as submissive and obedient. It won praise from a United Nations report on gender divides in digital skills. The same report warned that “nearly all of these assistants have been feminized—in name, in voice, in patterns of speech and in personality.” The title of the report—“I’d blush if I could”—was the answer Siri originally provided to users who called it a bitch. (Nowadays, Siri simply replies, “I won’t respond to that.”) In another sign of progress, earlier this year Apple eliminated the default “female” voice for Siri, now including the option for a male voice and allowing US users to choose from a set of voices referred to as voices 1, 2, and 3. Similarly, Google Assistant and Cortana currently let users select a male voice, further proving that companies do respond to public pushback about their products.
Yet uprooting the feminization of digital assistants will take more than just adding a male voice option to the roster. And even the idea of a “genderless AI” voice that registers somewhere between what would be traditionally considered masculine and feminine pitch ranges reveals some of the misconceptions we still confront when thinking about ways to avoid reinforcing stereotypes. In particular, Q might strengthen the outdated belief that nonbinary individuals are neither men nor women, but something in the middle of the binary, rather than outside of it. Instead of striving for “neutrality,” we must reimagine the future of the relationship between digital assistants and gender altogether.
One path forward comes from Yolande Strengers, associate professor of human-centered computing at Monash University and coauthor, with Jenny Kennedy, of The Smart Wife: Why Siri and Alexa Need a Feminist Reboot. They don’t think the solution is to remove gender from the equation altogether, because “this oversimplifies the ways in which these devices treat gender, which are not only gendered by voice, but by the types of things that they say, their personalities, their form, and their purpose,” Strengers says. Instead, they propose queering the smart wife so that digital assistants may exist in defiance of gender stereotypes.
Queering the smart wife could mean, in its simplest form, affording digital assistants different personalities that more accurately represent the many versions of femininity that exist around the world, as opposed to the pleasing, subservient personality that many companies have chosen to adopt.
Q would be a fair case of what queering these devices could look like, Strengers adds, “but that can’t be the only solution.” Another option could be bringing in masculinity in different ways. One example might be Pepper, a humanoid robot developed by Softbank Robotics that is often ascribed he/him pronouns, and is able to recognize faces and basic human emotions. Or Jibo, another robot, introduced back in 2017, that also used masculine pronouns and was marketed as a social robot for the home, though it has since been given a second life as a device focused on health care and education. Given the “gentle and effeminate” masculinity performed by Pepper and Jibo—for instance, the first responds to questions in a polite manner and frequently offers flirtatious looks, and the latter often swiveled whimsically and approached users with an endearing demeanor—Strengers and Kennedy see them as positive steps in the right direction.
Queering digital assistants could also result in creating bot personalities to replace humanized notions of technology. When Eno, the Capital One baking robot launched in 2019, is asked about its gender, it will playfully reply: “I’m binary. I don’t mean I’m both, I mean I’m actually just ones and zeroes. Think of me as a bot.”
Similarly, Kai, an online banking chatbot developed by Kasisto—an organization that builds AI software for online banking—abandons human characteristics altogether. Jacqueline Feldman, the Massachusetts-based writer and UX designer who created Kai, explained that the bot “was designed to be genderless.” Not by assuming a nonbinary identity, as Q does, but rather by assuming a robot-specific identity and using “it” pronouns. “From my perspective as a designer, a bot could be beautifully designed and charming in new ways that are specific to the bot, without it pretending to be human,” she says.
When asked if it was a real person, Kai would say, “A bot is a bot is a bot. Next question, please,” clearly signaling to users that it wasn’t human nor pretending to be. And if asked about gender, it would answer, “As a bot, I’m not a human. But I learn. That’s machine learning.”
A bot identity doesn't mean Kai takes abuse. A few years ago, Feldman also talked about deliberately designing Kai with an ability to deflect and shut down harassment. For example, if a user repeatedly harassed the bot, Kai would respond with something like “I'm envisioning white sand and a hammock, please try me later!” “I really did my best to give the bot some dignity,” Feldman told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation in 2017.
Still, Feldman believes there’s an ethical imperative for bots to self-identify as bots. “There’s a lack of transparency when companies that design [bots] make it easy for the person interacting with the bot to forget that it’s a bot,” she says, and gendering bots or giving them a human voice makes that much more difficult. Since many consumer experiences with chatbots can be frustrating and so many people would rather speak to a person, Feldman thinks affording bots human qualities could be a case of “over-designing.”
This precise issue garnered a great deal of attention with the launch of Google Duplex, a technology now integrated into Google Assistant, which eerily mimics a human voice to execute tasks such as making restaurant reservations or setting up an appointment to get a haircut. Following a slew of accusations stating the technology was unethical and “horrifying,” Google stated the robot would identify itself as such when calling on behalf of users. In 2019, California became the first state to require bots to identify as such online, and though the law has been described as hollow and deeply flawed, in the US, it’s the only legal advancement in the matter.
To reimagine the future of the relationship between digital assistants and gender, companies must be willing to take a hard look in the mirror and ask difficult questions about how truly groundbreaking they are willing to be. As of this moment, 75 percent of professionals in the fields of artificial intelligence and data science are male. And it shows. Queering these products will only be possible if diverse women and nonbinary people play a significant role in the process of designing them. To think outside of traditional binary boxes, companies must be willing to understand that innovation cannot exist in the absence of difference. There are many ways forward, and exploring the numerous possibilities is precisely the point. “Queering is about diversity. It is not about saying, ‘OK, here’s the one solution that’s going to solve all of your problems,’” Strengers said. “It’s about representing a very diverse set of experiences and options that take us away from the norm and disrupt the heteronormative model that's been very embedded into these devices so far.”
