title: The New AI Marketing Playbook
author: Branded Content By
body:
The marketing world is undergoing the most profound shift since the invention of the internet. For the last 20 years, consumer journeys typically began with a search query and a page of ten blue links. Now, they increasingly start with a direct question to a generative AI-powered chatbot or browser, producing a single tailored answer.
It’s changing the way people shop—and fast. AI-driven traffic to US retail sites grew by 4,700% year-on-year in July 2025. Market research firm Gartner predicts that by 2026, traditional search volumes will fall by more than a quarter.
And some believe a bigger shift still lies in store: the rise of AI agents. This is AI that doesn’t just produce an answer, but can also use tools to complete tasks. Some believe agents will complete purchases on a user’s behalf—and in certain categories, like routine essentials, perhaps automate the whole consumer journey.
“For marketers, this steady shift is both a threat and an opportunity as prime placement on search pages is becoming less important,” says Scott Shepard, head of sales at Tremendous, which helps companies manage rewards and incentives for marketing programs.
Clearly, adapting to AI-mediated shopping—ensuring AI is likely to find and recommend products and services—is going to be important. But as the rise of AI changes the wider dynamics of retail, it also has implications for more traditional marketing methods. Mastering this new environment requires embracing new tactics and revisiting existing ones to consolidate discoverability, brand recognition and trust.
Here are three priorities…
Brand visibility used to mean landing on page one of a search engine. Today, it also means showing up in AI-generated answers. In the future, it could mean being found, selected and perhaps purchased by an AI agent. “AI is, in some cases, the most important audience you’ll never meet,” says Jack Smyth, Australia Country Lead at marketing technology group Brandtech, who has a speciality in the emerging discipline of “generative engine optimization” (GEO).
The first step is knowing what products and services the models are already recommending. Survey different LLMs directly: If you sell moisturizers, ask questions such as, “What’s the best moisturizer?” and then analyze the answers. Track which brands surface, which features are emphasized, and which external sites influenced the responses.
If brands don’t run this kind of survey, they’ll have no idea what options are presented to customers and what the LLM is saying about them. Smyth advises thinking about “share of model”, or how often your brand appears in AI answers and in what context.
To influence that share of model, many of the old SEO rules still apply: Deploy clear, descriptive, machine-readable content on pages that load quickly on mobile browsers (under two seconds, ideally); pepper in plenty of facts and data; and link to sources. But there are some specific tips for GEO. Rather than incorporating keywords, aim to fold in the natural language questions that potential customers could be asking, and incorporate text that a chatbot could extract to produce an answer. Also consider presenting information in formats that LLMs can lift directly, such as HTML tables of product information and bullet-point lists. Finally, include expert commentary written in a conversational way, broken up into short paragraphs—something chatbots are more likely to cite.
It’s not just about text—visuals are important too. Generative AI can interpret imagery and form views about the nature of products or services. If a business’ USP is that it’s more affordable than its competition, it shouldn’t create imagery that suggests luxuriousness.
The playbook mirrors SEO’s cycle of analyze, create, distribute and measure, but optimized for a new kind of gatekeeper which can judge color palettes, product formats and tone of voice.
Although the use of AI stands to reduce consumers’ exposure to conventional marketing, brand recognition is still important. It may determine what they ask a chatbot in the first place: If you are a running-shoe manufacturer, you want users to be asking which of “your” shoes is right for them. And even if a consumer doesn’t ask about your brand specifically, AI may include your products in the array of options the chatbot presents—and name recognition can be the decisive factor in which one the consumer chooses.
All of which means that, perhaps counterintuitively, traditional marketing could become even more important since it’s essential to building brand equity.
The good news is that, thanks to AI tools such as Midjourney and Google’s Veo 3, slick imagery and video is now in reach of almost anyone, and chatbots can directly help with writing copy. This not only makes it easier to generate high-quality marketing assets, but to also create potentially thousands of variants targeting different demographics in a way that once may have been prohibitively expensive.
One British Council campaign by The Brief, an AI ad creation platform, shows what this could look like in practice. Automation cut the cost of producing over 1,000 assets by 70 percent, and enabled rapid optimization for eight different geographies. But the base creative ideas still came from human designers. Distinctive visuals and storytelling remain irreplaceable. Without that, campaigns risk falling into the AI blandness trap.
Tammy Nam, CEO of The Brief, argues that soon, no one will ask whether a campaign used AI because the answer will always be yes. What will differentiate brands is precisely those things that can’t be automated. “Using AI is not about flooding channels with more content. It's about producing smarter, more relevant content that resonates,” says Nam. “Aesthetics, visuals, distinctiveness in tone of voice all still really matter a lot.”
The practical approach for getting the most out of AI tools, then, is to first design a bold campaign with human-led creative ideas. Next, use AI to generate tailored versions for different customer segments. Then use AI tools to localize the content and adapt that to different languages, geographies, and cultural norms so global campaigns don’t feel generic.
Smaller brands, free from bureaucracy, may be able to turn these new opportunities into an edge, testing and pivoting campaigns rapidly to keep them distinctive in a crowded field.
AI tools are valued for their perceived neutrality, but some shoppers remain cautious.
For expensive or highly personal items, this is especially pronounced. If an AI is recommending something within these categories, a consumer may seek validation from trusted external sources such as customer reviews and recommendations. Electronics, furniture, beauty, and travel consistently show the strongest demand for peer recommendations, says Tremendous’ Scott Shepard. “However good AI becomes, people still want that human validation before they click buy on a mattress or some big purchase.”
This is reflected in the accelerating search interest for Reddit content. For brands, this means that engaging authentically on communities like Reddit can be a productive strategy. This is not only because it can spark someone to embark on a shopping journey, or lead to positive conversations about your brand that others may use to validate their own purchases, but also because these conversations index strongly as sources used by AI models to shape their recommendations.
In the AI age, it’s essential not to overlook the power of word-of-mouth, either. As AI makes it possible to produce and scale marketing content infinitely—much of it not of the quality that The Brief’s Tammy Nam advises—audiences can grow cynical, placing ever greater weight on a recommendation from a contact. This puts renewed emphasis on schemes designed to spur such recommendations, such as referral programs, in which existing customers recommend a brand to their personal network.
Shepard says it can be a powerful strategy—studies show that referred customers are more likely to buy and stay loyal, representing 16 percent greater lifetime value, since referrals are highly trusted.
“There's just so much information out there, and it's really hard to know what to trust,” says Shepard. “But word-of-mouth is trusted highly.”
And, of course, referral programs can in turn be managed and optimized better than ever using machine learning-driven systems. Technology can help businesses make exactly the right ask of their customers—at the optimal time and with compelling incentives—to encourage them to take the desired action.
The shift to embrace generative AI is more than just a technical adjustment. It’s a wholesale rewrite for a decades-old playbook for how brands win attention and customers. To achieve success, marketers need to think about how their brand is being seen across every asset that an AI model may take into account. They can also use generative marketing tools to amplify what makes them distinctive, and double down on building human trust. “AI is giving us new channels, and changing the nature of traditional channels,” says Shepard. “Those handling this shift smartly are paying close attention to both—and it’s paying off.”
Tremendous helps businesses send gift cards and rewards, fast. From referral bonuses to cashback promos to loyalty rewards, marketers rely on Tremendous to deliver incentives at scale. Its free-to-use platform makes it easy to send payouts globally, delight recipients, and save money. Learn more at tremendous.com.

title: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?
author: Justin McCurry; Rebecca Bailey
body:
For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side.
Fast forward 12 years and dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia.
The New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea and has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby.
It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time between North Korea and Russia. The first road bridge across their short shared border, named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow.
“China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute.
Since late 2024, the North Korean leader has sent ammunition and as many as 16,000 troops to support Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, and has held two summits with the Russian president in the past three years. In 2024, the leaders signed a mutual defence pact that includes a clause requiring the countries to come to each other’s aid if attacked.
In return for arms and combat soldiers, Pyongyang is getting hard currency, real-time battlefield experience for its troops, weapons technology and the opportunity to extend political and economic cooperation beyond its traditional ally China.
North Korea stands to benefit from increased trade but for China, the bridge could be of more geopolitical value than economic given how little trade China does with its neighbour compared with its other partners.
However, the insular regime in Pyongyang is thought to be reluctant to increase its economic dependence on China, by far its biggest trading partner and aid donor, and may still resent Beijing’s previous support for UN sanctions targeting the North’s nuclear weapons programme.
In the past two years, however, Russian and Chinese support for UN sanctions has collapsed. “The main restriction on trade with North Korea is not the infrastructure but international sanctions,” says Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at Sydney University. “However, because China’s enforcement of UN sanctions has become desultory and Russia has actively repudiated their enforcement, North Korea is in a position to benefit from increased trade and weapons help (at least from Russia).”
The North’s “open” border with China contrasts dramatically with the one it shares with South Korea. In 2024, the North said it would sever all rail and road links with its neighbour, months after Kim said he would abandon the goal of peaceful reunification and declared South Korea his country’s “principal enemy”.
But Fyodor Tertitskiy, a North Korea expert at Korea University in Seoul, believes neither China nor Russia can influence North Korea in any meaningful way, citing Kim’s refusal to surrender his nuclear weapons or moderate his iron grip on power – two changes that would be welcomed in Moscow and Beijing.
“Both countries understand that Kim Jong-un would rather accept a complete breakdown in relationships than submit,” he says. “So I doubt we are seeing a straightforward struggle for influence. Kim is trying to play the two against each other, but China and Russia are not rivals like the Soviet Union and China were in the 1970s.”
Kim is more likely to turn to China improve his country’s struggling economy, while Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence, according to Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
“After expanding military cooperation with Russia … Kim Jong-un is leveraging his windfall from Moscow for additional gains from Beijing. China may seek to recover lost influence by increasing trade and people-to-people exchanges, but the Kim regime prizes autonomy and wants to limit foreign ideological and cultural influences.”
The South Korean government said last year that at least 17 active road and rail links connect North Korea and China along their 1,400 km-long border.
Tertitskiy is “not particularly optimistic” that the increased contact the bridges will bring means improvements to the lives of ordinary North Koreans or lead to a more western-style economy. “I think it will make reform even less likely. Why pursue reforms and take risks when you can just get what you need from abroad?”
Analysts say the expected rise in trade across the Yalu bridge is likely to be modest at first. But it could become a bellwether for the state of Sino-North Korean ties, says Easley.
“China remains economically indispensable to North Korea in ways that Russia cannot replace,” he says, adding, “In that sense, the bridge may offer an inadvertent window into bilateral relations if flows are visibly interrupted in the future.”

title: How Insolar is bringing solar power to the masses
author: Branded Content By
body:
When entrepreneur Henrique Drumond headed home to Brazil after travelling the world, he knew he couldn’t return to work as usual. “I already knew that I would not be able to readapt professionally in a traditional company,” he says. “Nor did I find a social organisation that reflected what I was looking for. Founding something new seemed to me the most natural way to move forward.”
Insolar was born from that need. Drumond’s startup is dedicated to bringing solar power to low-income families in Brazil. The social goal was inspired by his volunteer work in Mozambique using technology to help improve people’s lives, while he turned to solar energy in part thanks to his father. “My interest in solar technology must have been inherited from my father, who was an engineer,” Drumond says. “It was from him that I also inherited a photovoltaic-powered wristwatch.” Inspired by his travels and the timepiece on his wrist, Drumond had a goal. In his own words, it was “to democratise access to solar energy in Brazil, empowering low-income communities to generate their own energy from the Sun.” Brazil is the ideal place for solar technology.
In Rio de Janeiro alone, 1.4 million residents live in favelas with expensive, unreliable power, but across the country solar power makes up only 0.02 per cent of the energy mix, despite Brazil attracting 2,000 hours of sunshine annually.
Having the right idea – and plenty of sunshine – is not enough to guarantee success, of course. To help reach his goal of bringing solar power to Brazilian families, Drumond had a boost from two of Shell’s startup-supporting programmes. The first was Iniciativa Jovem, the Brazilian version of Shell’s LiveWIRE programme, which Drumond won in 2014. Now in its 35th year, LiveWIRE helps socially minded startups scale by linking up entrepreneurs, offering business support and contributing funding to local projects in countries where Shell operates.
Insolar also had a “big step forward” thanks to Shell’s #makethefuture Accelerator, Drumond says, with 100 entrepreneurs and The Founders Forum consultancy helping to perfect Insolar’s business plan, addressing both the commercial and social sides. Now, Insolar offers end-to-end commercial-grade solar installations to corporations, funnelling a portion of the profits to the Insolar Fund, which subsidises smaller solar projects in low-income communities.
“Then, Shell offered Insolar the opportunity to deliver a major project that could benefit a whole community in Rio de Janeiro that incorporated most of the insights we received from the entrepreneurs that attended the launch event,” Drumond says.
Drumond’s project is based in Santa Marta, a favela in Rio de Janeiro that’s home to 5,000 people who face unreliable, expensive power supplies – but enjoys year-round sunshine. Insolar’s mission was to install 150 photovoltaic panels across the favela, generating 185,000 days of low-cost power over 25 years for families and community organisations, including all four of its nurseries, letting them spend money normally allocated to energy on the children. The local samba school was also given solar panels, making it the first dance school in Brazil to convert the Sun’s energy into “the energy of Brazilian samba”.
Solar was chosen not only because it’s renewable and Santa Marta has remarkably sunny weather, but also because it changes how a community looks at power. “By offering our planet much more energy than we need, it fosters a more collaborative society,” Drumond says. “By looking at all corners of the world, it favours the development of local economies in a decentralised way.”
Indeed, Shell and Insolar wanted the solar-panel installation in Rio to last well into the future, rather than be left as soon as the cameras turned away. So, alongside helping nurseries, samba schools and families with their power bills, Insolar also trained local citizens to install and maintain the infrastructure. Training was such a success that Insolar added an extra 40 panels.
Solar panels can last up to 30 years, offering renewable energy for decades after installation – but they do require maintenance. “During the Shell #makethefuture project, we trained 35 Santa Marta residents in electric and solar installation, safety work and working at heights,” Drumond says. “The training offered the locals the opportunity to install panels in the majority of Santa Marta community spaces, such as nurseries, NGOs, sport centres and samba school. Moreover,they received ‘Insolar Ambassador’ titles and all the necessary certificates to work in the electric and solar fields. Some of them started their own businesses, found a quality job, or returned to school.”
Insolar’s ideas of sustainability and community are at the core of Shell’s #makethefuture programme, which kicked off in 2014 with Pavegen’s Brazilian project. That startup created the world’s first kinetic and solar-powered football pitch in Rio de Janeiro, highlighting #makethefuture’s goal of taking bright energy ideas and putting them into action in the real world – a mission that Insolar fits perfectly, says Malena Cutuli, group head of integrated brand communications and capability at Shell.
“The Insolar project is not just about utilising an abundant natural resource, it is also about collaborating with the local community to help create a long-lasting solution,” Cutuli says. “At its heart, this is what the Shell #makethefuture campaign is about: working together to develop solutions and initiatives that will help bring about more and cleaner energy for communities around the world.”
The Insolar project didn’t stop with solar panels in Santa Marta. Drumond toured with #makethefuture festivals, launching the company’s solar umbrella, which supplies shade while generating energy to charge devices.
As part of Shell’s #makethefuture campaign, Insolar further expanded its reach via the “Best Day of my Life” music video, starring Jennifer Hudson, Pixie Lott, Steve Aoki, Yemi Alade, Tan WeiWei and Brazilian artist Luan Santana. The video has topped 816 million online views.
“The fact that it was launched in Santa Marta, where Insolar delivered a major solar project in collaboration with Shell, certainly helped bring visibility to Insolar and to our social mission,” Drumond says.
Insolar received an extra boost from Luan Santana, a popular Brazilian singer witha huge social-media following. “I’m committed to make my voice echo Shell and the entrepreneurs’ social action,” he says. “Music produces an exchange of energy between audience and artist; I hope that #makethefuture rocks the five continents as it takes its energy relay around the world.”
Santana donates a percentage of the proceeds of his CD and DVD sales to projects such as Insolar, which supported the launch of the Insolar Institute. This will work with the startup to benefit social projects.
“As a social business, we work in the intersection between these two still-separate worlds,” Drumond says. “But as the concept evolves in Brazil, we expect to merge both structures, LTD and NGO, and operate with a single structure, setting up a benchmark of how we envision profit and social impact working together in the construction of a prosperous economy and society. It’s a win-win deal.”
INCEPTION: Henrique Drumond came back from his travels wanting to make a difference – but found he needed to launch his own startup to realise his dream of giving solar power to low-income families.
SHELL LIVEWIRE: In 2014, Insolar won Iniciativa Jovem, Shell’s LiveWIRE programme in Brazil, giving Drumond expert assistance in building a business plan and introducing him to a network for fellow socially minded entrepreneurs
SHELL #MAKETHEFUTURE: The next step was Shell’s #makethefuture accelerator, which saw 100 entrepreneurs and The Founders Forum analyse Insolar’s challenges and propose solutions. This helped to perfect his business plan to include both commercial and social sides.
COLLABORATING WITH SHELL: Plan perfected, Insolar trialled its ideas in Santa Marta, a favela in Rio de Janeiro that lacks a reliable energy supply for its 5,000 residents. The test run saw 150 photovoltaic panels installed across family homes and community organisations.
LAUNCHING TO THE WORLD: Shell helped spread the word about Insolar to the world via its #makethefuture festivals as well the “Best Day of My Life” music video, which highlighted the solar startup to millions of viewers.
For more on Shell's #makethefuture campaign, click here.

title: Live Updates: War returns to Iran with Israel, US strikes
tags: Your window to latest news, analysis and features from Pakistan, South Asia and the world.
body:
Pakistan hosts the first round of face-to-face talks between the US and Iran in 47 years in April; the talks end without a breakthrough, but also without a breakdown
US, Iran hold high-level talks in Switzerland on June 20 after signingpreliminary agreement to end the war; hold talks in Doha on July 1, with mediators citing “positive progress”
US launches strikes on Iran on July 8 in response to attacks on ships in Hormuz, Tehran retaliates as strait heats up again
Yemen’s civil war flares up after Saudi-backed government attacks Sanaa airport
US Senator Chris Van Hollen has called for an end to the war on Iran, saying, “Trump’s illegal Iran war is turning into our next forever war.”
In a post on X, Van Hollen has shared an article on US-Israeli plans to renew attacks on Iran after the US midterm elections.
“Eight months in, Trump and Republicans have deluded themselves into thinking the next strike or another bombing campaign will finally bring victory,” he writes.
“From Vietnam to Iraq, we know how this ends. This war must end NOW.”
The head of the Iranian parliament’s national security committee, Ebrahim Azizi, has sent a warning to Israel, saying it could be rendered uninhabitable within an hour, Al Jazeera reports.
“A single miscalculation is all it takes – the occupied lands rendered uninhabitable in under an hour,” he writes on his X account.
Azizi has published the warning in Hebrew, English and Persian.
In his Hebrew post, he has quote-reposted a video of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaking at an Israeli army graduation ceremony, where Netanyahu said: “There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all – to topple the regime in Iran. And that is my directive to the [army], the Mossad, and the security forces.”
Russia’s embassy in Tehran has denied reports that its diplomats and specialists working at the Bushehr nuclear power plant are planning to evacuate, Al Jazeera reports.
“Neither embassy staff nor Russian specialists at the Bushehr nuclear power plant have any plans to evacuate. Work continues as normal,” the embassy has said in a statement, adding that reports to the contrary were “FAKES”.
The Bushehr site, Iran’s only operating nuclear facility, has come under repeated attack during the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran, with satellite imagery released in July showing damage inside the complex.
More than 1,400 patients – including 1,110 with kidney failure, 192 in intensive care and 154 infants in incubators – face severe, life-threatening risks in Taiz as fuel and medical supply shortages intensify, according to Yemeni rights group Rasd, Al Jazeera reports.
In a statement carried by Yemen’s Saba news agency, Rasd says 98 health facilities were partially operational or had gone completely out of service, citing UNICEF data from October 11. It says 42 healthcare centres were battling acute shortages of medical supplies and oxygen, while critical fuel deficits threatened to halt or scale back operations across 12 hospitals.
The health crisis stems from the Houthi siege and supply route closures imposed on the city since October 4, 2026, leaving facilities struggling to provide roughly 120 required daily dialysis sessions, according to the statement.
It has added that World Food Programme assistance had failed to reach approximately 600,000 residents in Taiz as of October 14. This obstruction left 800,000 individuals across Yemen facing severe disruptions to humanitarian access.
The Muslim World League has strongly condemned Houthi attacks targeting the cities of Makkah and Madina, Al Jazeera reports.
In a statement, the Makkah-based organisation said the attacks were conducted “in disregard for the danger of frightening the feelings of more than two billion Muslims, and the violation of the values of our true religion, and the most basic principles of humanity”.
The league added that it stands in full solidarity with Saudi Arabia as it takes all necessary measures against the group.
Riyadh’s international airport says flights would resume on Sunday after a two-week closure following strikes from Yemen’s Houthis on the Saudi capital, though the Iran-backed group warned of more to come, AFP reports.
The Flight Radar monitoring site showed a plane taking off from Riyadh airport early Sunday, heading to the Saudi city of Jeddah.
“Please be advised that Terminal (1) will be designated for domestic flights and Terminal (2) for international flights operated by national carriers at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, effective Sunday, October 25, 2026,” King Khalid International Airport posted on X on Saturday.
Yemen’s Houthis have renewed their warning against using Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, hours after the airport announced it will designate two terminals for flights following a suspension earlier this month, reports Reuters.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the airport remained a “military target” and operations targeting the airport will continue, warning all airlines, airport staffers and travellers against using it.
Iran’s judiciary has said that its chief held a rare meeting with the country’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has yet to appear in public since being appointed, AFP reports.
Judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei and the supreme leader discussed issues including “securing public rights, and effectively combating corruption and its bottlenecks”, the judiciary’s Mizan Online website reported.
They held talks on “pursuing the recovery of rights and compensation for material and moral damages arising from the crimes of American-Zionist criminals”, it said.
The younger Khamenei has only communicated through written messages since his appointment, some of them published in handwriting attributed to him. No video message from him has been released, and the time and location of his meeting with Ejei were not disclosed, as has been the case with previously reported meetings.
Earlier this week, Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf also reportedly met with the supreme leader to discuss “the latest developments” in the war.
Yemen’s Houthi rebels have denied targeting the holy cities of Makkah and Madina after Saudi authorities reported responding to falling shrapnel from interceptions in those areas, AFP reports.
“What the Saudi enemy is promoting about our forces targeting towards the holy areas of Makkah and Madina is a great and huge lie,” said Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree.
Iran’s Ambassador to Pakistan Reza Amiri Moghadam has said that Tehran recently conveyed through Islamabad that it was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, The Associated Pressreports.
In his remarks at a seminar in Islamabad, the Iranian envoy also accused US President Donald Trump of rejecting the proposal by insisting the blockade of Iranian ports would continue.
Moghadam elaborated that Iranian officials had conveyed their willingness to reopen the Hormuz strait during CDF Field Marshal Asim Munir’s visit to Tehran, provided Washington ended its blockade.
Saudi Arabia’s Directorate of Civil Defense (DCD) says it intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by Yemen’s Houthis toward the Makkah and Madina regions, with debris falling in several locations including Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh, Reuters reports.
Yahya Saree, the spokesperson for Yemen’s Houthi rebels, claims that the group has carried out seven “specialised military operations” against Saudi Arabia over the past 24 hours, targeting facilities including Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and an Aramco facility in Yanbu.
In a statement posted on X, he says King Khalid Airport and Yanbu were targeted in “accurate” strikes, with the former targeted in two phases.
He adds that the Rabigh oil refinery was also targeted, along with a crude oil pumping station and the East-West oil pipeline. In both cases, the group “successfully achieved its objective”.
Najran Airport and King Fahd Airport in Dammam were also successfully targeted, Saree claims, adding that the group has also successfully hit an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
“Our operations will continue deep inside Saudi territory, enforcing the equation of blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation, and targeting the Saudi enemy’s troop concentrations until the aggression ceases and the blockade against our beloved country is lifted,” Saree adds.
Saudi Arabia has not immediately commented on Saree’s claims.
Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, and lethal plots by Tehran against American citizens have reached “advanced stages”, a senior intelligence official in the Trump administration warns in a memo seen by Reuters.
The alert from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton comes after Washington scaled back staffing at its mission in Saudi Arabia earlier this week in response to intensified attacks by Iran-allied Houthi forces.
“Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel,” Clayton wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a message dated October 23.
“The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries,” he added.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian says many Iranians are struggling to put food on the table, as the economic pressure from the Middle East war with the United States mounts, AFP reports.
“There are many people in this society who are struggling to put food on the table because of the war we have found ourselves in, because of the wartime conditions we are living under,” Pezeshkian says in a speech shared on his website.
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed an attack on a naval base and a military camp in Aden, the interim seat of the internationally recognised government, after blasts were heard there, AFP reports.
“Our armed forces targeted Saudi enemy concentrations at the so-called Al-Nasr camp and the naval base in Aden,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree says, adding that the sites were overseen by Saudi forces.
Explosions have been heard in Yemen’s Aden, the interim seat of the country’s internationally recognised government, a police source and an AFP journalist say.
A police official in Aden tells AFP he heard three explosions in the city, while an AFP correspondent also reports hearing blasts.
Another police source tells AFP the Houthis targeted a Saudi-led coalition position near Aden airport that was targeted last week, as well as the coast guard.
The United States has updated travel advisories for countries across the Gulf and Middle East, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Iraq, Lebanon and Israel, citing what it describes as the threat of increased Iranian-supported Houthi regional aggression, according to security alerts issued by US missions, Reuters reports.
Houthi media claims that Saudi strikes have killed 11 people in the Yemeni capital Sanaa, shortly after the Saudi-led coalition fighting them said it had intercepted two missiles targeting Saudi cities, AFP reports.
The Houthis’ Al-Masirah outlet reports a series of “Saudi enemy airstrikes” targeting Sanaa, including one on a house that reportedly killed at least four people and wounded several others.
A separate strike at a residential building for cement factory workers in the Sanaa governorate killed six women and one child and wounded three others, the broadcaster further claims.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in remarks broadcast on state TV, blames the United States for the failure of an interim deal with Iran, but says there should be a new attempt at concluding it, Reuters reports.
“We were having negotiations; the cowards (Americans) messed everything up … I still think we should go and conclude it,” Pezeshkian says.
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Tehran must exit the state of “neither war nor peace”, Isna reports.
He said at a ceremony: “But these cowards broke the rule. But I still believe that we must go and get out of the ‘no war, no peace’ situation, because Iran and our land are very rich and exceptional in minerals, geography, and human resources, and each of these is gold.“
Pezeshkian added that it was “necessary to correct our mentality and get on the right path”, and called for unity and cohesion.
“Let us compete with each other on this path and take useful, efficient, and effective measures.“

title: There's a chance your PlayStation 5 is plugged into the wrong HDMI port - Engadget
author: Thomas Godwin
body:
There's a chance your PlayStation 5 is plugged into the wrong HDMI port
The picture may look great, but that doesn’t mean you’re getting the full experience.
A PlayStation 5 can display a good picture even while connected to an HDMI port that's limiting its capabilities, which is a simple mistake to make. Most TVs and monitors come with multiple HDMI ports, each with tiny labels that are hard to read — assuming they're even present and situated where you can see them. If there is no label, you'll have to look up the specs for your brand and model. The PS5 console supports HDMI 2.1 for 4K output at 120Hz, among other gaming features, but accessing that requires both a compatible screen and the right output.
It's worse if you like to bring your PS5 around the house and set it up on different TVs, because each brand and model features different HDMI arrangements. Never assume that the same set of port numbers means the same specs, even if every TV in the house is from the same brand. For max benefit, check the specs for your exact model and look for an HDMI 2.1 input that supports 4K at 120Hz. On most TVs (not all), HDMI 2.1 ports are the third or fourth option.
Your choice of cable is also important. Sony recommends using the HDMI cable that comes with the PS5, or another high-quality Ultra High Speed (HDMI 2.1) cable. It's best to plug the cable directly into the screen or TV without a soundbar or similar between them. For the most part, that's all it takes. A PS5 console and TV can't provide peak signal support if the port, cable or intermediary equipment is getting in the way.
What the correct HDMI cable will unlock
The benefit of the correct HDMI port is access to the full breadth of output features the PS5 console supports. A 120Hz display can refresh its image 120 times per second, so compatible PS5 games offer smoother motion than a 60Hz setup can provide. However, the game has to support 120 fps output as well. This isn't always enabled by default, so check the game's video settings for an option like "120Hz output", "High Frame Rate" or similar.
Keep in mind that 120Hz gaming at a lower resolution (1080p or 1440p) can work through HDMI 2.0 on a compatible display. However, HDMI 2.1 is the relevant option for the PS5's 4K 120Hz output. Also be aware that few PS5 games run at 4K/120; most high frame rate modes lower the resolution to compensate.
If you're using a monitor with a high refresh rate, check which resolutions and refresh rates it supports with HDMI, as this might differ from any DisplayPort inputs. Alone, a high refresh rate is not an indication that any given HDMI port supports the PS5 mode you want.
Other important HDMI 2.1 features include Variable Refresh Rate (VRR), which syncs your screen's refresh rate with your system's output to prevent screen tearing. There's also Auto Low Latency Mode, which tells your TV to switch into its "Game Mode" — disabling picture processing features to minimize input lag.
Should I use HDMI 1 or 2 for gaming?
Neither input number on your TV is inherently better or worse than the other. "HDMI 1" and "HDMI 2" are simply designators, not necessarily version numbers like HDMI 1.x or HDMI 2.x. Plus, you could have a port that's clearly labeled HDMI 2.1, plug your HDMI cable into it, and still not get 4K 120Hz. Once the console is connected, check the TV/monitor's input settings, since HDMI 2.1 is not always the default option. Various manufacturers use different menu names and terms, like "Enhanced Features" or similar.
You also have to make sure to enable the feature on your PS5. On the main menu, open Settings > Screen and Video > Video Output. Set the resolution to Automatic for best results, leave Video Transfer Rate on Automatic and set Enable 120Hz Output to Automatic as well. Select Information for the Connected HDMI Device to see details about the screen's resolution, Variable Refresh Rate and HDR support. Current Video Output Signal also gives you information for troubleshooting.
If the console still fails to deliver the signal you expect, recheck the input, cable and display settings before assuming your PS5 needs to be shipped off for repair.

title: Azeri woman retracts rape allegations, gives suspect 'clean chit' in Lahore assault case
author: Mian Abid
body:
Published October 24, 2026
LAHORE: An Azerbaijani woman, who had accused three men of sexual assault in Lahore, has now retracted her claims in a new video statement, alleging that her earlier statement was given under pressure.
The victim, named Diana, had travelled to Pakistan for business purposes late September and was allegedly gang-raped by three men at a rented flat in Lahore's Defence area.
In a recent video, Diana mentioned one of the suspects, Ahmed Tanveer, saying that he had neither raped her nor taken her mobile phone. She said she did not understand why police had arrested Tanveer, insisting that he had no connection with the alleged assault.
Diana said she wanted to record her statement before a court earlier but was told that her life was in danger and that she had been "forcibly sent out of Pakistan".
“I was not given an opportunity to express myself or make decisions of my own free will,” she said, adding that she had also declared Ahmed innocent in documents submitted to the embassy.
Diana said she had forgiven Mohsin and Uzair as well and did not wish to pursue the matter further.
The video statement comes amid the ongoing investigation and court proceedings into the alleged rape case. The victim had recorded her account at the time of registration of the case, before a judicial magistrate under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, alleging that three men had sexually assaulted her after she was made to consume alcohol.
After the fresh claims, Deputy Inspector General of Investigation Zeeshan Raza said the woman's statement had already been recorded before a court and alleged that the video being circulated on social media was an attempt to influence the investigation.
He said the woman had accused three men in her judicial statement and that the two arrested suspects had also acknowledged the involvement of the third suspect, Ahmed Tanveer. He added that police would include Ahmed in the investigation and complete the probe on merit.
Separately, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said the government would closely monitor the case and revealed that the suspects' wealthy family had offered the woman between Rs15 million and Rs20 million to withdraw her allegations, despite her statement having already been recorded before a magistrate.
In a post on X, CM Maryam also referred to the allegations that the judge who granted bail to an accused had "allegedly been bribed", saying that, if proven, such claims would raise serious questions about the integrity of the justice system and the vulnerability of sexual assault survivors to financial pressure and the misuse of influence.
“I will continue to keep a close eye on such cases to ensure that no rapist or perpetrator escapes justice simply because he has money, influence, or connections,” Maryam wrote, stressing that justice must never be for sale and that nobody was above the law.
Meanwhile, Punjab Information Minister Azma Bukhari subsequently said the provincial government would pursue the case on the state's behalf.
Speaking on Geo News programme "Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath", Bukhari also confirmed the information concerning the allegation that a judge had accepted a bribe.
She said one of the co-accused had admitted in his statement that the other people nominated in the case were involved in the offence with him. She added that kidnapping and robbery charges had also been included in the first information report (FIR), alongside the rape allegations.
In view of the evidence, Bukhari said, it was not possible for the suspects in the alleged gang-rape case to be released, adding that the state would pursue the matter.
Separately, suspect Tanveer was produced before the Model Town kacheri court in connection with a related case involving the alleged abduction and torture of the Azeri woman.
Police requested that he be sent to jail for an identification parade, while the court reserved its decision on the request. A case has been registered against Tanveer and others at Ichhra police station.
It may be noted that 22-year-old Azerbaijani woman had earlier told a magistrate that she travelled from Istanbul to Islamabad, then visited Faisalabad before reaching Lahore to continue her journey to Skardu.
According to her judicial statement, she contacted two women, Nimra and Muskan, after finding it difficult to travel alone. She alleged that, after meeting them, a man identified as Mohsin took her to a separate room, where three men sexually assaulted her after she was offered alcohol.
She further alleged that the men withheld her Rs200,000 in cash and iPhone, threatened her against reporting the incident and later left her by the roadside without her belongings, prompting her to seek help and contact police.

title: From Fatherland to Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back: the week in rave reviews
author: Guardian Staff; Guardian staff reporter
body:
TV
If you only watch one, make it …
Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back
BBC iPlayer; available now
Summed up in a sentence Sixty years after the Welsh mining disaster, people tell their devastating stories – and their infuriatingly difficult fight to get justice.
What our reviewer said “Further indignities were caused to the stricken villagers, powerfully evoked in this restrained documentary by well-chosen memories from its interviewees. Gaynor remembers her father sitting puce with rage every evening in his chair as the NCB continued to fight liability for the deaths and deny the (expensive) need to remove the tips.” Lucy Mangan
Further reading I survived for a reason’: Aberfan fights to preserve memory of disaster 60 years on
Pick of the rest
Ellie & Natasia
BBC iPlayer; available now
Summed up in a sentence Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou are joined by a roster of brilliant comedy names in the second series of their hilariously weird sketch show.
What our reviewer said “There’s also a bit about a sack-wearing, trad wife-style content creator (White) who enjoys eating croissants, making collages and, er, keeping the woman her boyfriend cheated with locked up in her basement. So silly, so irresistible.” Hannah J Davies
The Experiment
Channel 4; available now
Summed up in a sentence In a shocking experiment, members of the public tour a fake “residential home” for disabled people that’s riddled with Nazi ideology – and their reactions need to be seen to be believed.
What our reviewer said “This is a show so disturbing, timely and surreal that within 90 seconds of viewing it alone, I am looking around for confirmation from an empty room that any of this is happening.” Frances Ryan
It Gets Worse
Channel 4; available now
Summed up in a sentence Comedian Leo Reich’s new sitcom, produced by A24, takes on gen Z houseshare life in London, with guest stars Lena Dunham and Andrew Scott.
What our reviewer said “It Gets Worse is, in many ways, a classic sitcom about surviving your 20s, complete with intensely awkward sex scenes (“Pull out!” “I’m not even in!”). And yet there’s a lot more going on here.” Hannah J Davies
Further reading ‘I’m lovingly making fun of everyone I’ve ever met’: on the set of Leo Reich’s gen Z sitcom
You may have missed …
VisionQuest
Disney+; available now
Summed up in a sentence Paul Bettany stars in a WandaVision spin-off that is visually striking and good fun – but it can’t help overdoing it on the dialogue and fight scenes.
What our reviewer said “VisionQuest is sometimes entertaining and always clever, yet if it does have anything to say about human nature, it is drowned out by dizzying plot particulars and the need for a big brawl every episode.” Rachel Aroesti
Film
If you only watch one, make it …
Fatherland
In cinemas now
Summed up in a sentence Hanns Zischler stars as Thomas Mann on his 1949 tour of Germany along with his daughter Erika, played by an extraordinary Sandra Hüller.
What our reviewer said “An impossibly elegant, poised historical vignette whose brevity and control can hardly contain its characters’ personal and historical pain.” Peter Bradshaw
Further reading ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four – or, possibly, five – of the year’s biggest films
Pick of the rest
Possible Love
In cinemas now
Summed up in a sentence Acclaimed Korean director Lee Chang-dong returns with an inspired account of an unhappy married couple befriended by a documentary-maker and her wealthy husband.
What our reviewer said “A finely judged, beautifully acted and rather novelistic work, in which a character at one point actually compares her surroundings to something from a novel.” Peter Bradshaw
Further reading ‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contender
Ghosts: The Possession of Button House
In cinemas now
Summed up in a sentence Spin-off from the warm and comforting BBC TV sitcom, that picks up not long after the events of the final episode of the haunted house comedy.
What our reviewer said “Breaking out of the 30-minute episode structure seems to have freed up the writers to unleash new levels of giddiness with added spoonfuls of silliness.” Cath Clarke
Scream
In cinemas now
Summed up in a sentence Thirtieth anniversary re-release of the Wes Craven meta horror with Neve Campbell and Courteney Cox – and a still alarming masked killer.
What our reviewer said “This film is brash and smart in that distinctive 90s way – and the title sounds like an order.” Peter Bradshaw
Further reading Scream: darkly funny, extremely meta horror and a 90s time capsule that never gets old
You may have missed …
Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom
In cinemas now
Summed up in a sentence Third cinematic adventure for Aardman’s resourceful ovine, in a spooky-season caper in which Shaun’s pumpkin-supersizing serum ends up in a balding farmer’s hair-growth bottle.
What our reviewer said “This is another excellent family film, crammed as ever with top visual gags, great throwaway references and, of course, a homemade Heath Robinson contraption, so often to be found in Aardman films.” Peter Bradshaw
Further reading ‘He goes to the dark side’: behind the scenes on the Shaun the Sheep horror movie
Books
If you only read one, make it …
On Another Planet They Can Save Me by Lieke Marsman
Summed up in a sentence The extraordinary posthumous memoir of a Dutch poet.
What our reviewer said “Marsman’s language is so beautiful … and her textual references so original … she cites Leopardi, Pasolini, Alanis Morissette, Robert Musil, Spinoza, Euripides, Wittgenstein and William James.” Edward Posnett
Pick of the rest
Gilgamesh by Simon Armitage
Summed up in a sentence The poet laureate takes on the ancient Mesopotamian epic about the adventures of a demigod king.
What our reviewer said “Armitage’s tactile, visceral version is a tour de force, combining careful scholarship with poetic verve and deft linguistic meldings.” Philip Terry
The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch by Thure Erik Lund, translated by David M Smith
Summed up in a sentence A long-thought-untranslatable portrait of a breakdown by the man Karl Ove Knausgård considers Norway’s best living writer.
What our reviewer said “This is a universal story of modernity and its discontents, but Lund is at pains to give it a specifically Norwegian dimension.” Sukhdev Sandhu
Emperor of Nothing by Blake J Harris
Summed up in a sentence The definitive biography of Seinfeld creator Larry David.
What our reviewer said “In 1992, just before it became the biggest show in America, [David] told friends: ‘Honestly, I would rather spend a year in prison than do another season of Seinfeld. It would be peaceful. Nobody would make me write anything.’ He was only half joking.” Dorian Lynskey
Under Fire by Humza Yousaf
Summed up in a sentence The former Scottish first minister on his family’s Gaza ordeal.
What our reviewer said “Under Fire is most powerful when Yousaf gives full vent to his anger at the unfolding genocide in Gaza and articulates not just the plight of his in-laws … but the barbarity of Israel’s actions.” Fiona Sturges
You may have missed …
We Love You, Bunny by Mona Awad
Summed up in a sentence This follow-up to the cult horror-satire Bunny has been shortlisted for the Wodehouse prize for comic fiction.
What our reviewer said “Awad is here to show us that romantasy can be serious literature, and nothing can really be too camp.” Sandra Newman
Albums
If you only listen to one, make it …
Shovel Dance Collective: Everything in Readiness
tak:til; out now
Summed up in a sentence The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its present.
What our reviewer said “The most immediate pleasure of Everything in Readiness lies in the head-spinning sonic surprises it delivers. As it lurches wildly around, you find yourself struggling to keep up, a sure sign that you’re in the presence of music that feels entirely fresh and different.” Alexis Petridis
Pick of the rest
Michael Kiwanuka: Fudge
Polydor; out now
Summed up in a sentence Its release delayed by ill health, Kiwanuka’s latest was made in tandem with 2024’s Small Changes – but it’s much more than a mere companion album.
What our reviewer said “It may have had experimental beginnings, but it sounds remarkably like the work of a man who knows exactly what he wants to do. You leave it hoping that he’s able to continue doing it at some point in the not-too-distant future.” Alexis Petridis
Further reading ‘Everyone can relate to pain and struggle. So I’m sharing mine’: Michael Kiwanuka on life after his devastating stroke
Bartók: Miraculous Mandarin Suite, The Wooden Prince
LPO; out now
Summed up in a sentence Edward Gardner and the LPO are taut and dramatically alert in fine performances of these two theatrical works.
What our reviewer said “As for The Miraculous Mandarin Suite, this is as fine a performance as any, sleek and sinister in its evocation of the honeytrap antics of the sex worker and her thuggish pimps, swaggering or shy in her encounters with the old rake and the young man.” Clive Paget
Basma and Temir Alcy: NAD
Stroom; out now
Summed up in a sentence Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tension.
What our reviewer said “On Ana Jaya, where the experimentalism peaks, the line between instruments and vocals blurs as the sound dissipates. The effect is bodily: tension you can feel, but can’t quite pin down. It’s a brilliant, heady formula.” Safi Bugel

title: Unlocking the Power of Interdisciplinary Teams
author: Branded Content By
body:
Shelley Zieroth, director, St. Boniface Hospital Heart Failure and Transplant Clinics; Beth Healey, doctor, Hospital Universitaire Geneve; and Scott Drawer, director of sport, Millfield School joined WIRED’s contributing editor João Medeiros in a panel to disrupt current thinking on the future of holistic patient care within the interconnected cardio-renal-metabolic space.
Interdisciplinarity is a difficult challenge to crack. Indeed, very few disciplines truly practice it. But those that do, find success in such an approach.
When treating patients, physicians tend to focus solely on their specific discipline—despite research showing how diseases of the cardio-renal-metabolic system are connected. “It’s easier for us to think about one issue, one problem, when they’re actually connected”, says Shelley Zieroth. However, “we’ve made such incredible advances in the last decade of what we can do to improve clinical outcomes and the functional status of our patients. Although, for a lot of clinicians, the evolution and change of heart failure therapies is thought to be very complex”.
In order to overcome these challenges, communication is key, as “it’s about creating dialogue and getting everyone talking to each other as often people are trying to solve the same problem” explains Beth Healey, doctor at Hospital Universitaire Geneve, particularly as we move to a more remote world post-Covid. “We've streamlined a lot,” Zieroth explains. “We’ve minimized a lot of work in terms of recognizing and trying to advocate for improvements in heart failure and care.”
Sports science is one sector that has successfully risen to the challenge. “In high performance sport, everything is measurable and visual, so you have something to anchor to. There wouldn't be a time any high performance athlete isn’t wearing a device to track their movement and physiological signals, which you can see in real time,” says Scott Drawer, director of sport at Millfield School. A typical Olympic athlete today is surrounded by a team of coaches and experts, from physiologists to nutritionists, whose sole task is to improve athletic performance.
Watch the full panel discussion above or on YouTube here.
In January 2011, Boehringer Ingelheim and Eli Lilly and Company announced an Alliance that centers on compounds representing several of the largest diabetes treatment classes. Depending on geographies, the companies either co-promote or separately promote the respective molecules each contributing to the Alliance. The Alliance leverages the strengths of two of the world’s leading pharmaceutical companies to focus on patient needs. By joining forces, the companies demonstrate their commitment, not only to the care of people with diabetes, but also to investigating the potential to address areas of unmet medical need. Clinical trials have been initiated to evaluate the impact of empagliflozin on people living with heart failure or chronic kidney disease.
This article was originally published by WIRED UK

title: The Promising Future of Seamless Global Travel
author: Branded Content By
body:
Underneath the colossal arc of London’s St. Pancras International train station’s glass roof, passengers shuffle towards the platform as the first glimpse of a sunrise yet to come casts glints of light from the rafters. It’s just after 5 a.m., and folks are beginning to queue up to board the high-speed train to Paris. It’s not surprising that a train station would feel sleepy and slow at a time like this, but this year, things have felt even slower than usual for those taking the first train of the morning out of the station and under the English Channel. And that’s because they are.
Following Brexit’s official enactment, border control at train stations and airports for passengers traveling between the UK and Europe became a new hurdle, that turned into a significant stumbling block for operations. Because all passengers must now have their passports verified between the two destinations, getting passengers through the check-in process became considerably slower than it used to be. So much slower, in fact, that at the beginning of the year, high-speed railway Eurostar was forced to cap ticket sales at 550 passengers for 6:01 a.m. train out of St. Pancras to Paris, leaving 350 seats empty in an attempt to prevent a bottleneck of queues that would undoubtedly delay the trains.
The issue at stations is not “impossible to tackle” Gwendoline Cazenave, the CEO of Eurostar, told the press. “We have to be better organized…We have to automize more than before.”
Since, Eurostar has done just that.
In just a few short months, the experience you can have as a passenger boarding a Eurostar train in St. Pancras changed drastically, thanks to the implementation of Smartcheck using Digital Travel Credentials (DTCs), which leverage biometrics. Once reserved for internal government use only (fingerprinting has been around quite some time), a revolution in applied biometrics has opened identification technology up to practical applications—like, say, opening our phone’s lock screen or allowing us to skip the ID check line at the airport. The new, everyday applications are making our lives simpler, while allowing us to stay in control of our ID and protect our privacy rather than endangering it. It’s only through identity and data security industry leaders like Entrust that such security around these everyday uses of biometrics is possible. By innovating applied encryption, Entrust is pioneering solutions that allow us to use the data we need to automize our travel, while still keeping that data secure.
According to the International Civil Aviation Organization (which is a specialized agency within the United Nations that outlines the principles of international air navigation), a DTC is intended to temporarily or permanently substitute a conventional passport with a digital representation of the traveler’s identity that can, “be validated using the travel document issuing authority’s public key infrastructure.” Which is a fancy way of saying that the data DTCs hold are derived from and verifiable through the electronic signatures of the government bodies that issue passports.
DTCs act as a supplement to a physical passport, reducing verification redundancies and allowing a passenger’s identity to be verified at eGates or using biometric lanes in a fraction of the time it takes at a traditional border control checkpoint. In a world where there are handfuls of passport control apps, private identification services, and online check-in options, a DTC stores the same information as the physical e-passport and can be associated with other travel data such as boarding passes or tickets to provide all of the information you need for each step of the traveling process.
“Typical statistics from an eGate show that you can process an ID verification in about 10 to 15 seconds on average,” says Gordon Wilson, Vice President and Global Lead of Seamless Travel at Entrust, the identity and data security company that partnered with iProov and Eurostar to find a solution for more efficient travel procedures. “Whereas at a traditional checkpoint with an officer, you're spending 30 to 45 seconds per person.” That may not sound like a huge differential, but when you multiply a few seconds by the hundreds of thousands of travelers using major hubs each day, it really adds up. It adds up to minutes saved, more passengers served, more secure border checkpoints, and — this may sound like an oxymoron — but a more relaxed travel experience for all involved.
Eurostar introduced SmartCheck, a contactless, fast-track facial biometric check-in system with a pilot starting in 2022 and has been in full production since July 2023. Entrust, in collaboration with SmartCheck lead partner iProov, and using Inverid’s ReadID, nurtured this program from its pilot stage to its full-scale launch. With SmartCheck, Eurostar passengers can securely enroll their ticket, passport and face before they travel, using their mobile devices whenever convenient. When traveling, they simply walk through the biometric lane, already verified by the contactless, ticketless, and secure verification process.
“This DTC-centered process saves time for both passengers — who have places to be — and security and border agents — who need to focus on high-risk individuals. This process facilitates the average person who's low risk coming to visit friends, go to a concert, or who’s traveling for business conferences, so agents can spend the time on persons of interest,” says Wilson. “So if they can remove 90 percent of the hay — being low-risk travelers — from the haystack, then officers are left with a small haystack that's needle-rich.”
DTCs, unlike traditional physical passports, are also able to act as living documents, which can enable data to help reduce instances of human bias instead of increasing it. As we all know, your driver’s license or passport has one picture on it. And, while passport and ID photos are rarely good, they can also be unreliable since they can be the only physical representation of a person for up to a decade. And let’s face it, most of us don’t look like we did 10 years ago.
DTCs allow you to electronically share the ePassport data and facial image in advance of travel and the IDV process that derives the DTC also captures the most current version of your likeness. When you walk up to the biometric lane or the eGate, your shared DTC supports verifying you using the picture from the passport as well as the photograph that was taken on your phone when your ticket and identity verification was confirmed. “That's where this advantage comes in,” says Wilson. “The data can be matched to more than one photo very quickly. And that photo can be your passport photo, but it can also be your current selfie that you took two or three weeks ago when you bought your ticket.” This ability to supplement data with your DTC without changing the core of the data can help reduce unnecessary ID checks with physical agents and documents.
Because the data within a DTC is controlled by the individual (just like how our passports are our own physical property), data sharing and protection aren’t concerns for users. Encryption protects the data stored, and sharing permissions can be temporary — ensuring that the airlines or government agencies who are accessing the information within your DTC don’t store it permanently. According to Wilson, “most organizations today don't want to keep that information” and would prefer to keep it out of a risk profile.
Because of the security and ease that a DTC can provide to make travel more efficient for travelers, industry professionals, and travel companies too, there’s a desire to adopt them more widely. In fact, 85 percent of travelers who took a survey about international travel use stated that they are: 1., willing to give their identification information in advance for check-in and verification; 2., are happy with their experience using a DTC and e-gates or biometric lanes; and 3., would use their DTC again for future travel.
So what’s the holdup with making virtual passports the norm while traveling? Uptake.
As all good things do, “it's going to take time,” says Gordon. “We’re probably talking at least two to three years before it becomes broadly available.”
Currently, we are learning from pilot tests how to use the technology, and how it impacts the travel industry’s core systems. There are already examples of how the ability to digitize a passport, even if it's just an optical scan of the data page, ensures that every passenger is verified without error, avoiding time-consuming mistakes like the expiry date of the passport or the passport number being wrong. This next phase is really about leveling up the confidence level between both travel service providers and the government. “I think it's really about connecting the dots across the whole of the process. So you have the consumer adoption side, you have government adoption, and you have travel service providers,” says Gordon. “We have to link them all. That takes time.”
But the time spent on making systematic changes within the industry is converting to big efficiencies on the other side, as evidenced by Eurostar. After seeing the success of the SmartCheck pilot, the railway has set its sights on being able to increase capacity by a third, or even 50 percent, without having to add any facilities to its network. That increased efficiency translates to everyone moving faster, with fewer tasks to be concerned with. That could look like border agents having to process fewer passengers that require more face-to-face attention. Or a passenger being able to make it to their meeting on time, or maybe even get to their hotel and take a nap before the meeting. In a game of, in Gordon’s words, “small continuous improvement,” it seems that a truly seamless day of travel could be a thing of the very near future.
This story was produced by WIRED Brand Lab for Entrust.

title: A New Approach to an Old Problem
author: Branded Content By
body:
Even for an organization as large and as accomplished as Orange—which has spent more than 30 years developing into one of Europe and Africa’s leading telecommunications brands—sometimes the key to achieving a core business objective is deciding to do things in exactly the opposite way you’ve done them before.
For Orange, that’s not an overexaggeration. As of a few years ago, the organization found itself wrestling with a persistent and central problem: how to promote the right product to the right customer at the right time, across a wide variety of customizable products and services. It wasn’t alone, obviously; thousands of enterprises across the world have been dealing with the same issue for years.
What has made Orange unique, however, was the approach it took in solving one of the industry’s most pervasive problems. It actually inverted its entire way of thinking about consumer marketing: Orange traded in product-centric strategies for AI-powered consumer-centric ones.
“What we were doing—and what marketing teams have been doing for ages—is that we had products, and we were looking for the customers for our products,” said Médéric Chomel, VP of data, AI and automation at Orange. “So we’d go to our data team and tell them, ‘Find me the most relevant customers for this offer.’”
“What we shifted to now is looking at a customer at one interaction point on one channel and asking, 'What is the most relevant offer we can show to them in that space?' It's totally the opposite [of before].”
“What’s in it for me?”
Bringing that new vision to life was more difficult than Chomel makes it sound. Appreciating how Orange was able to make it a reality takes an understanding of the effort’s somewhat humble roots.
The process originally started back in the summer of 2020, when a member of the data team had the idea for a new algorithm that would help manage other algorithms already in use—very data- and tech-centric stuff. The project was surgical in effort and impact, but still moving slower than was hoped for.
The conversation changed, however, once key business leads outside of the data team got involved. Their mindset was quite different: A new algorithm is fine, of course, but what’s the true business impact of the effort? That, according to Chomel, was when the end vision really began to take shape.
“When business teams [get involved], it becomes, ‘What’s in it for me?’ It took a bit of time to realize that it’s not the tech discussion we should have—it’s a business discussion,” said Chomel. “It’s business-driven, it’s tech-centric—but it’s a transformation process, led by business objectives.”
Those discussions quickly highlighted the true underlying business opportunity: to drive revenue via an AI-powered data system that makes product offers as relevant as possible for customers across all channels. This project was the opposite of surgical in scope: What was originally a constrained technical effort had suddenly become a five-year transformation.
Crafting the tech stack needed to truly personalize product offers across Orange’s entire marketing ecosystem was basically a full overhaul that required the strategic and technical skills of Boston Consulting Group (BCG) and BCG X, BCG's tech build and design team. The first step was creating a central data repository—a 360-degree data platform that consolidated all the available customer data and served as the basis for Orange's new AI-powered structure.
Once the data silos were eliminated, Orange and BCG X got to work creating the machine learning layer that would actually drive the recommendation engine. Over a roughly 18-month period, the team created more than 50 individual AI propensity models that utilize all known customer data to predict the likelihood of each customer-product pairing. They then merged these insights in real time, using a custom-made engine to detect the most appropriate product offer for each customer. Designing this engine with best-in-class optimization algorithms proved critical to preserve execution speed, and ensure that the marketing team keeps control over the product offering mix and the engagement rules. An integrated feedback loop means these models learn from previous interactions and detect and adjust to market changes, a level of sophistication that allows those models to be updated daily.
This setup also utilizes automated campaign simulation, taking a significant amount of the guesswork out of Orange's content creation needs. In other words, the engine not only pairs the right message to the right customer, but plays an integral role in shaping what each product's core message should even be in the first place.
Now three years in the making, the current state is already an achievement: Orange’s new AI-powered “next best offer” recommendation engine can evaluate user interactions in real time, providing highly relevant product or service offers to the right customers—in the right channels—based on the perfect blend of sentiment and business value. Bolstered by BCG’s ongoing training, Orange has also dramatically expanded the size of the data team managing the system: More than 150 full-time employees are now involved in the program. The ongoing challenge, though, will be refining the success measurement framework across so many products, customers, and variables.
“We’re not only doing upsell and cross-sell: We’re doing [customer] retention and satisfaction,” Chomel said. “Those kinds of value measurement questions, you can spend hours solving—hours squared—and we’re still doing it.”
A measurable impact
But granular measurement complexities aside, the top-line success is apparent: Between the new tech stack and BCG’s partnership, Orange has seen a 6 percent increase in existing client sales (upsell and cross-sell) across both digital channels and stores. At the enterprise level, increases like that can be hard to come by. If Orange ultimately wanted to tie this overall effort to business value, it succeeded.
But the work isn’t done yet. Chomel’s team is still refining the overall approach to personalize customer offers down to even individual price tiers or product features, a level of sophistication he hopes to see in place by the end of 2023. By 2024, Orange is hoping to use some of these same data strategies to triage and appropriately reply to inbound customer inquiries, as opposed to just sending outbound promotional efforts.
In other words, Orange still has room to expand upon an already profound impact to its business. The key to such big achievements, according to Chomel, was thinking big—and thinking business-first—from the beginning.
"We really defined a key group of people from day one," Chomel said. "We didn't say that we needed to start small: We thought big from the beginning. We put almost all the people who were working in personalization together, and so now that we were not different teams working in different directions, we had a common goal and common KPI—and that was enough."

title: An Eye for Innovation
author: Branded Content By
body:
Founded on Danish design principles, LINDBERG has been at the forefront of eyewear innovation since its inception in 1986. The brainchild of architect Henrik Lindberg and his optometrist father, Poul-Jørn Lindberg, the pair cemented a company ethos that took inspiration from architectural design, but remained laser-focused on the comforts and practicalities demanded by those relying on eyewear.
Awarded 112 internationally recognized design accolades since launch, LINDBERG has pioneered innovation, such as its cutting-edge manufacturing techniques that negate the need for screws or rivets within its exceptionally lightweight frames. In one special release, the company created a limited-edition series that was handcrafted from a unique oak log discovered in 1950 on the Danish island Møn. The National Museum of Denmark dated the bog wood at over 6,000 years old.
Its latest release, dubbed the Thintanium collection, does exactly what it claims, offering an evolution of its groundbreaking Thintanium technology. Here, LINDBERG has pushed the boundaries of innovation by incorporating acetate rims into its existing Thintanium construction, marking a significant leap in its eyewear design and customization.
Seeing as no two faces are the same, LINDBERG also offers unparalleled levels of personalization and customization thanks to its modular system that enables wearers to tailor the shape, temple, size, and color of their eyewear. To put that simply, the six new additions to the collection offer a minimum of 62,000 combinations across, size, fit, and color options per style—meaning there is a pair of spectacles to suit every face and sartorial taste.
This forward-thinking collection of eyewear features an ultra-thin titanium-plate front, which won it numerous design laurels, such as the The Red Dot: Best of the Best and the iF Gold Award, thanks to its delicate aesthetic and extraordinary strength-to-weight ratio. The addition of acetate rims takes lightness to new levels, while adding an extra layer of customization.
In essence, acetate rims—incorporated into the patent-pending ultra-thin titanium frames—allow for thinner lenses to be accommodated, enabling individuals with high prescriptions to enjoy lightweight eyewear without compromising visual clarity.
According to LINDBERG, this was only made possible by challenging the latest and most modern manufacturing technologies, resulting in frames that weigh as little as 3.3g and eradicate the requirement for screws within the hinges for a clean, uncluttered aesthetic.
“The evolution of the Thintanium collection exemplifies our dedication to continuous innovation and personalization,” says Roberto Vedovotto, Founder, CEO and President for Kering Eyewear, owner of LINDBERG. “Eyewear should not only reflect one’s style, but also provide unparalleled comfort. With the addition of acetate rims and the option for lighter lenses, wearers can now embrace a personalized eyewear experience that enhances both visual clarity and overall comfort.”
The latest Thintanium collection is offered in both men’s and women’s styles, with several frame designs offered to act as a springboard for customer personalization.
Available in selected LINDBERG partner stores now. Or visit lindberg.com for more.
