Our advice is simple: don’t do half measures. You won’t replace it again in a hurry, so you owe it to yourself to buy as specced-out a model as possible.
How to suss out the lay of the land? You could take a look through John Lewis & Partners’ technology category, which is carefully edited to showcase the products at the cutting edge (what’s more, all of them come with a five-year guarantee). Take, for instance, the [Samsung Q95T Flagship QLED 4K HDR 2000 Smart TV](https://www.johnlewis.com/samsung-qe55q90t-(2020-qled-hdr-2000-4k-ultra-hd-smart-tv-55-inch-with-tvplus-freesat-hd-black/p4913299){: rel=nofollow }, the manufacturer’s most advanced 4K TV this year.
The most important thing is the picture, which is not only pin-sharp in its detail – thanks to the 4K display – but extraordinarily vivid. That’s down to the “QLED” part of its name. This refers to a screen technology comprising LCD panels backlit by LEDs behind a quantum dot nanofilter. (Translation: it makes for extremely precise colours and high levels of brightness.)
Samsung has pioneered this kind of display, and for the Q95T has combined it with a system that adapts the brightness to your room and intelligently shifts power away from darker areas of the picture and towards lighter areas to heighten contrast. Which brings us to the “HDR 2000” part of its name. HDR stands for “High Dynamic Range” and seeks to capture brighter whites and darker blacks, so you can see detail even in shadows.
The Q95T’s HDR 10+ system can reproduce over a billion shades of colour, emulating the colour standard used by Hollywood films. So whether you’re watching a nature documentary or a sci-fi epic, the image packs a hefty punch – and the anti-reflection screen maintains that impact no matter your viewing angle or how much sunlight is streaming in through the window.
The design philosophy was all about showcasing that beautiful picture and removing as much as possible that which might distract from it. The bezel is therefore just 2mm wide on the top and sides, so whether it’s the smallest (55-inch) or largest (85-inch) model, from sofa distance it looks unbounded. The back is just as sheer as the front so it can be mounted flush with the wall, and it only requires a single “near invisible” wire to work. So what about all your HDMI cables? Well, they just run into the One Connect Box (tuck it away in a cupboard) on the other end of that wire. It’s an elegant solution.
Design, of course, is about software as much as hardware, and Samsung’s Eden smart TV platform is widely regarded as an industry leader. It’s compatible with every major app; while many of those offer 4K content, the Q95T uses its Quantum 4K processor to upscale a standard definition source to a much richer, far more detailed version than you might imagine possible. The interface is clean and intuitive, plus it integrates built-in Bixby, Alexa and Google Assistant, so you can continue using your go-to voice commands.
Now, let’s face it. If you’re buying a television this high-end, chances are it’s going to be teamed up with a surround-sound system or at least a soundbar. But Samsung isn’t taking that for granted. There are eight speakers in the Q95T, which combine with its “Object Tracking Sound” software to position audio accordingly. Imagine: you’re watching a plane loop from the bottom left of the screen to the top then to the bottom right. The TV locks onto its flight and shifts the sound of the engine’s roar accordingly. That’s not the only audio innovation. The TV can also detect background noise and use AI to recalibrate the audio profile accordingly – which it also does in response to what’s on screen. If you’re watching a stadium concert, you’ll get the full effect.
All of these features are obviously extremely appealing to gamers and, indeed, the Q95T has kept that customer firmly in mind. The “Real Game Enhancer+” matches the screen’s refresh rate to the console’s for a smoother picture, and “Dynamic Black Equalizer” technology increases the brightness of shadowy areas to help you spot enemies lurking in the dark. But it’s not just about what you can play today, it’s also equipped for the future. The Q95T has an HDMI port that can handle 4K HDR games with the frame rates expected of the next generation of Xbox and Playstation consoles. Because we know exactly what you’re thinking: it’s almost time to upgrade your gaming set-up too.

title: Technology and fresh thinking will help us reinvent teamwork
author: Branded Content By
body:
The last few months have been challenging for all businesses. As governments across the world took the step of enforcing lockdowns to confront the Covid-19 pandemic, most organisations went from gathering every morning in the office for a daily stand-up, to a new reality of working-from-home, conference calls and virtual-only interaction. In a strange paradox, staff members have ended up working scattered across multiple locations – in some cases even across various countries – at the very moment in which the upset triggered by the pandemic requires teams to be more cohesive and effective. How can they face up to this challenge? Can teamwork and team culture be preserved, and even reinvented, in the midst of the coronavirus emergency?
According to Margarete McGrath, chief digital officer at Dell Technologies UK, technology is already playing a key role in ensuring that teams keep working as smoothly and productively as possible. “Technology has an absolutely critical role, [and it’s] really ramping up,” she says. Although the working-from-home arrangement has had the positive effect of speeding some tasks up – with red tape and paperwork being slashed to a minimum and year-long problems solved swiftly out of sheer necessity – there are still issues that need to be addressed with fresh thinking and new tools.
Rana el Kaliouby, the founder and CEO of emotional intelligence-focused AI company Affectiva and author of Girl Decoded, explains how some emerging AI-powered tools can improve the cohesiveness and harmony of a team working from home. While on a video conference call, these tools can monitor each participant’s engagement and response throughout the conversation, helping to gauge how well the team is working together. “Our technology is able to track every person's expression [while on a call],” she says.
“We [can] aggregate people's responses, and show how positive or negative people are – you can see whether everybody's smiling Or you could visualise each person as a separate track.”
“My theory is: if you're able to quantify these [emotional] metrics, they will potentially predict things like trust, team motivation, team loyalty. Or, if empathy is really important, you can tie [empathy] to outcomes.”
Although video-calls have reached new highs of speed and sharpness, and other collaboration tools have exploded over the past several months, el Kaliouby believes that some elements of the “meatspace” office remain hard to replicate digitally. “One thing I think we have not figured out how to do with technology is brainstorming,” she says. “In a [physical] brainstorming session, you have a whiteboard, people are drawing ideas and riffing off each other. On Zoom, we're all staring at each other.”
That might possibly change in the near future, as cutting-edge technologies enter the mainstream. “We're seeing a real pivot moment to virtual experience. So Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality will get more elevated,” McGrath says. “That will continue to grow.” Meanwhile, other technologies – from biometrics, to advanced user interfaces, to real-time data analytics – are being harnessed to boost personalisation, safety, and privacy. In this way, companies keep workers engaged and reassure them about the increased role digital tools have taken up during the ongoing emergency. “We are seeing greater levels of collaboration on technology platforms, which requires people to trust those technology models. And this opens up a wider debate around the role of trust, data sharing, and privacy Ultimately, it’s about driving a positive online experience that is focused on creating greater and deeper connections based on trust” McGrath explains.
This increased – and, in a way, inevitable – reliance on digital poses a two-pronged challenge. On the one hand, not every team member will have access to last-generation devices and superfast broadband when working from home. Organisations will need to consider how to best support employees on this.
But the flip-side of the digital divide is the risk of burnout for employees that spend most of their time at home and online. Addressing that will take not only novel tools, but also fresh thinking among business leaders.
In a way, this is already happening naturally as a result of generalised remote working: hierarchies are turning looser, and employees feel more empowered to approach a given problem in a more creative and personal way. Autonomy is today’s watchword. At a deeper level, leaders will have to rethink not only their style, but their role.
“The leaders coming up today are different from the ones that we had before. This is not a nine-to-six job anymore: this is much more around autonomy and empowerment, greater focus on wellbeing and mental health, a clear sense of purpose and values. And also a greater sense of openness and honesty. I think authentic leadership and empathy is really going to stay the long course,” McGrath says. “And I think: bring it on.”

Pakistan on Saturday announced an initial 14-member Test squad for the upcoming two-match ICC World Test Championship series against Sri Lanka, with Sameer Minhas, Mohammad Taha and Mohammad Suleman receiving their maiden call-ups.

Babar Azam will continue to lead the Test side, while Abdullah Fazal, Arafat Minhas, Azan Awais, Mohammad Abbas, wicketkeepers Mohammad Ghazi Ghori and Saad Baig, Razaullah and Saud Shakeel have retained their places. Ex-skipper Shan Masood has been dropped.

The three uncapped batters earned their maiden Test call-ups following impressive performances in first-class cricket.
Left-handed batter Mohammad Taha, 26, is the leading run-scorer in the President’s Trophy Grade-I first-class tournament, which began in September. He has scored 730 runs in seven matches, including three centuries and a highest score of 225.
Mohammad Suleman ranks fifth on the tournament’s batting charts, having accumulated 652 runs in seven matches, also with three centuries.
Sameer Minhas, playing his maiden first-class season, has scored 405 runs in seven matches after an encouraging stint with Pakistan’s Under-19 side.

title: Governor rejects ex-health CEO’s plea in Jhang embezzlement case
author: Our Correspondent
tags: Your window to latest news, analysis and features from Pakistan, South Asia and the world.;pakistan
body:
TOBA TEK SINGH: The governor has upheld the Punjab ombudsperson’s order in a case involving alleged embezzlement of millions of rupees from the Jhang District Health Authority’s funds and directed the health secretary to initiate departmental proceedings against the former health chief executive officer (CEO).
A citizen, Haji Muhammad Hussain, had lodged a complaint with the ombudsperson, alleging misappropriation of funds through inflated fuel bills and vehicle maintenance expenses.
District Adviser to the Ombudsperson Chaudhry Almas conducted an inquiry into the allegations. In his written reply, the accused, Dr Shahzad, maintained that his official vehicle had been extensively used to monitor health programmes across Jhang and adjoining areas, arguing that the fuel and repair expenses were justified.
However, the inquiry report found him guilty of the charges. The Punjab ombudsperson subsequently directed the health secretary to conduct a regular departmental inquiry and take appropriate action.
  Upholds ombudsperson’s order, directs secretary to initiate proceeding against official
Dr Shahzad, the former health CEO of Jhang, challenged the ombudsperson’s order before the governor. The governor has now dismissed his appeal and upheld the original directions, requiring the health department to proceed in accordance with the order.
GARBAGE SITE: A garbage dumping site in Faisalabad’s Madina Town has been removed after remaining in the locality for two decades, following complaints by residents about its foul smell and alleged health hazards.
Residents of surrounding neighbourhoods had repeatedly urged the Faisalabad Municipal Corporation to relocate the dumping site.
Commissioner Dr Imran Hamid Sheikh visited the site a few days ago, where local resident Sardar Sajid Aleem informed him that the foul smell had caused health problems, including asthma, among members of his family.
He also told the commissioner that around 70,000 residents living in 2,100 houses near the dumping site had been facing difficulties because of the accumulated waste.
Taking notice of the complaints, the commissioner directed the immediate relocation of the dumping site outside the residential area.
Following his instructions, the site has been cleared, and work on the construction of a public park at the same location has also begun.
SENTENCED: An additional district and sessions judge in Shahkot, Nankana Sahib, Muhammad Mansoor Atta, on Saturday sentenced a drug dealer to nine years in prison and imposed a fine of Rs80,000 in a narcotics case.
Shahkot Saddar police had arrested the convict, Muhammad Nadeem, in 2025 after allegedly recovering a large quantity of narcotics from him.
According to the prosecution, the accused had brought the drugs to Shahkot for supply to local drug dealers.
After hearing the case, the court convicted him and awarded the prison term along with the fine.
WALK: The Punjab Institute of Nuclear Medicine (Pinum) Cancer Hospital, Faisalabad, organised an awareness walk to highlight the importance of early detection and timely treatment of breast cancer.
Doctors, paramedical staff, other hospital employees, members of the public, cancer patients and their family members participated in the walk.
The event was led by Pinum Cancer Hospital Director Dr Hafiz Khushnaseeb Ahmed Laghari and Regional Director Consultant Dr Asghar Butt.
Head of Oncology Dr Ijaz Khan, Dr Saira Zafar, consultant surgeon Dr Naeem, Dr Rabia Tanveer and other doctors and paramedical staff were also present.
During the event, Dr Saira Zafar and Prof Dr Saira Saleem of Madina Teaching Hospital delivered lectures on breast cancer.
They briefed participants on the symptoms of the disease, the importance of timely diagnosis, preventive measures and modern treatment methods.

title: Authorities investigating whether first Kenya and Nigeria Ebola cases crossed paths
author: Kate Bartlett
body:
Authorities investigating whether first Kenya and Nigeria Ebola cases crossed paths
JOHANNESBURG – The first Ebola patient confirmed in Nigeria may have crossed paths with the first Kenyan Ebola patient at a Ugandan airport, health officials said Thursday.
Nigeria announced its first case of Ebola in more than a decade on Tuesday. Nigerian health authorities said the patient is the Ugandan-born wife of a diplomat based in Abuja who had vacationed in Uganda in September and returned to Nigeria earlier this month.
She is being treated and 44 people she had close contact with have been quarantined, Dr. Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told a press briefing on Thursday.
Authorities are now investigating what the source of her exposure was.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, is the fourth on the continent to record an Ebola case during the current outbreak, but it's the first in West Africa and the furthest away from the epicenter in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Congo's current Ebola outbreak began in May in the country's east. It has become the fastest spreading on record. At least 4,600 people have died and about 9,700 have been infected in Congo.
Neighboring Uganda initially recorded about 20 cases but was declared Ebola-free in August.
The first case in Kenya was recorded in early October and since then eight other cases have been confirmed in the east African nation.
The first Kenyan patient, who has since died, travelled from Congo to Kenya, via Uganda.
Officials are now investigating whether that person crossed paths with the Nigeria case at the Entebbe International Airport in Uganda – as they were there on the same day.
Dr. Mankoula said the center was probing whether there had been "some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport."
Ebola is spread through direct contact with an infected person's bodily fluids or contaminated items. It causes severe fever and can be deadly. However, generally people are not considered infectious until they start showing symptoms.

title: Red Roses suffer back-to-back defeats for first time in 10 years as Canada make statement
author: Sarah Rendell
tags: Womens rugby union,Canada womens rugby union team,England womens rugby union team,Rugby union,Sport
body:
History-makers, era-enders, giant-slayers. Breaking England’s unbeaten run was a statement for Canada last Friday but they backed it up in a 31-22 win to deal the Red Roses their first consecutive loss in a decade, sending a formidable message to the rest of world rugby.
Some may view it as too early to call but Canada are serious contenders for the World Cup trophy in 2029, especially if they progress at the same rate that their performances have improved in just a year from that World Cup final loss to England in 2025.
On a cold Ottawa night, Canada played with freedom and pace to down England once again. The captain, Sophie de Goede, laid bare why she is the reigning world player of the year with a hat-trick and some excellent defensive work, and Julie Omokhuale also stood out among a good team performance.
England were looking for a response to that record-ending defeat but it never came. A strong and confident start ebbed into a scrappy and hesitant overall outing which they will want to put right for their final WXV Global Series match against the USA next Friday. But there were some positives for the visitors, namely Meg Jones. The captain, who turned 30 on Friday, was imperious in defence and Maddie Feaunati had another good game in the hour she was given.
An Owellian atmosphere was created for those watching from home with the pitch having a grey tinge to it, a dystopian world isn’t usually compared to that of the vibrant and action-packed women’s rugby sphere but it may have felt like another world for England players losing back-to-back games. It was their third loss in 74 matches, so the panic won’t set in, but this result will unsettle the Red Roses.
Jones said she told the team in the post-match huddle that they are “not broken, we just need to grow”. The captain added: “We’re a high-performing team in a high-performance situation. Our mindset is our biggest asset and it always will be. I genuinely believe we have the best players in the world and when we are firing we are genuinely unstoppable.”
The Tests between these two this autumn have been ferocious and it was an utterly brutal start. A key part of Canada’s win last week was their defensive set and keeping England from scoring for a long time but that was a different story with Feaunati over in the seventh minute.
Canada put England’s defence under its first proper stress test next and the white wall was impressive with a particular focus on double tackles, but it eventually buckled as Omokhuale dotted down. But the second Canadian try came all from England’s scrappy attack. A bouncing ball didn’t sit well for Zoe Harrison, who knocked on as a result and Gabrielle Senft pounced. De Goede tracked her run and was on her shoulder to receive the ball to finish it off with Canada’s secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, who announced new funding for Rugby Canada during the match, in the commentary box to celebrate the score and add: “I love it!”
Several knock-ons and a try being held up stifled England from hitting back and so it was Canada who held a 12-7 lead at the break. The Red Roses’ need for points was made very clear when they opted to kick a penalty to start the second 40.
England reverted to their deadly rolling maul from the 22 in an impressive score by Amy Cokayne. However, captain fantastic De Goede struck twice in quick succession for her hat-trick, with Savannah Bauder putting England out of sight despite a consolation score by Emma Sing.
Head coach John Mitchell was critical post-match and said the referee Aurélie Groizeleau did not have a connection to the television match official. “I think the game potentially needs an improved standard with TMO, there was no TMO connection tonight,” he said. “We have got to improve that. These games are so meaningful and there are going to be situations where there are going to be major turning points and I think the girls deserve quality decision making.”
 
Canada can ride the high of this victory into 2027 where their next games are slated to be in the Pacific Four tournament, while England have one more WXV match against the USA. The Americans are in form but they should heed a warning: this England team are not used to losing and they will be pursuing a big response.

title: Two Merseyside men face jail over £8.5m teeth whitening tax fraud
author: Web Desk
body:
Published October 24, 2026
Two Merseyside businessmen who funded lavish lifestyles through an £8.5 million tax fraud involving the import and sale of potentially dangerous teeth whitening products have been warned their prison sentences are “inevitable.”
Alastair Ramage, 44, of York Close, Formby, and Ian Barnes, 53, of Southport Road, Lydiate, admitted three counts of being knowingly concerned in the fraudulent evasion of VAT and one of evading income tax at Liverpool Crown Court.
The court heard the pair evaded £8,499,384.47 in tax between 2016 and 2023 through their business UK Teeth Whitening Ltd, later IBAR Trading UK. This included £5.3 million in unpaid VAT, while Ramage evaded £1.2 million in income tax and Barnes £1.9 million.
Many products breached UK regulations on permitted hydrogen peroxide levels, and money was routed through an account with Puerto Rico’s now-closed Euro Pacific Bank.
Prosecutor Nicola Daley described how the men “lived the high life,” spending £51,000 with Emirates and £155,000 with Virgin Atlantic in 2018/19 alone. Ramage boasted he was a “money-making machine,” while messages included “46K a month, long may it continue” and “F*** the peasants.”
Ramage’s Facebook flaunted holidays to Universal Studios and a private island in the Maldives, a selfie with Tyson Fury, and a Rolls-Royce Ghost chauffeur's ride to Wembley for the FA Cup Final.
The pair even drew up plans for swimming pools shaped like teeth.
Defending, David McLachlan KC said Ramage was “embarrassed and ashamed.” Judge Katherine Pierpoint remanded both men into custody, adjourning sentencing until next Friday due to lack of court time.

title: The iconic Campervan is getting an ambitious sci-fi makeover and this time it's electric
author: WIRED Insider
body:
The VW Microbus. The Bulli. The Campervan. The Kombi. The Hippy Bus. There are many monikers for Volkswagen's fabled Transporter, but this overtly practical and famously adaptable 70-year-old machine has achieved an iconic status, no matter the language you speak.
Which is why it came as such a surprise when chairmen of the board of management of the Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles brands, Dr Herbert Diess and Dr Eckhard Scholz, announced in 2017 that it would reintroduce the Microbus to the world… but in a very different guise.
"For us, the VW I.D. BUZZ is an important pillar in Volkswagen's future electric drive initiative, as it has such a strong heritage and evokes that sense of open-mindedness and freedom in fans of the original," explains Christian Senger, head of electric mobility at Volkswagen.
Slated for launch in 2022, the stunning I.D. BUZZ stylistically draws heavily on the original campervans and cargo vehicles, but will be built on the brand’s upcoming MEB modular EV platform.
On top of this, it will also feature an all-electric propulsion system that will see the vehicle accelerate from 0-100kph in around six seconds and travel for almost 1,000km on a single charge.
"The car will be built around the battery and the electric drive, which doesn't take up much space," explains Senger.
"The front and rear axles can be mounted very far apart from one another, which allows us to realise the iconic and emotional “one box design”.
"To add to this, the driving position is as close as possible to the front windscreen without sacrificing passive safety. It looks like a short compact van on the outside, even though it offers the generous interior space of a large van," he explains.
But where a generation that lived through the Swinging Sixties and enjoyed the experimental Seventies discovered a tool for exploration and freedom in the campervan of yesteryear, today's potential buyer is looking to stay anchored to the digital world, despite their geographical location.
As a result, I.D. BUZZ and fellow members of the upcoming VW I.D family, which includes an all-electric SUV and an affordable electric hatchback, will always be online and constantly connected.
"Our new generation of electric cars will be fully updated and upgradeable over the air," says Senger.
"We will also make pioneering technologies available in the range, such as an operating concept that features an AR-Head-up display.
"Information, such as the directions given by the GPS system, is projected as a virtual image from seven to 15 metres ahead of the car," he adds.
Using an innovative electric powertrain that forms part of the upcoming vehicle's basic underpinnings not only leads to impressive interior roominess (it boasts a 3.3m wheelbase and seating for up to eight), it can also power numerous devices, cool and heat the cabin without noise and offer a tranquil, lounge-like space for occupants to relax in when parked.
However, speak to any classic camper owner today and they will likely attest to the lack of power offered by these vintage machines – vehicles that thrived in a time when 100kph was plenty fast enough.
The Microbus of tomorrow must be able to keep up with the pace of modern life, so its proposed powertrain has been slated to develop an impressive 374hp.
This engaging performance is the culmination of a joint engineering project between Volkswagen's e-mobility technical departments in Wolfsburg and its motorsport outfit in Hannover.
The result of which has also lead to the formation of the ground-breaking all-electric I.D. R Pikes Peak vehicle, which develops a staggering 680hp that allowed it to obliterate the Pikes Peak International Hill Climb record at this year's gruelling event.
"Racing is fascinating," Senger exclaims. "Racing is always a good test bed to collect data about technology under extreme conditions.
"But it is also a reciprocal process. On the one hand, the I.D. R racing team benefited from the know-how of the technical departments in Wolfsburg but on the other hand, Volkswagen as a whole will get important information from the motorsport team about batteries and cells under extreme conditions," he adds.
It has been over four years since a Brazilian factory ceased manufacture of the VW Type 2 Bus, and those lusting after the open road have had to wait in hope that the German marque would resurrect it.
An electric powertrain, swivelling seats, an AR head-up display and interactive tablets for passengers might be a far cry from the original, but Senger and his team want to encapsulate the sense of freedom the Type 1 afforded.
"We want to reinvent the Microbus. Not just imitate it," he says.
--

title: ‘Horrific’: woman, 19, shot in head in drive-by shooting outside boxing event near Brisbane
author: Australian Associated Press; Guardian staff reporter
body:
Four people have been injured after a drive-by shooting outside a venue hosting a boxing event, including a 19-year-old woman who was shot in the head.
Queensland police Detective Inspector Ian Galpin said a group of people were gathered at the passenger drop-off zone outside Fitzy’s Loganholme, south of Brisbane, about 8.18pm on Saturday when a Mitsubishi pulled up.
Galpin said police would allege a “number of shots” were fired from the front window of the pub where two males wearing balaclavas and gloves were sitting, striking four people.
A Jimboomba woman, 19, was shot in the neck and head. She has undergone surgery and remains in a critical condition.
Speaking on Sunday, Galpin described her as an “innocent bystander”.
“It’s horrific. It’s something that her family should never have to go through.”
Three others were injured and remained in serious but stable conditions: a Browns Plains man, 38, shot in the abdomen and arm, a Salisbury man, 37, shot in the abdomen, and a Cornubia man, 27, shot in the abdomen.
Galpin alleged the Mitsubishi was set alight on Maloney Road at Waterford West, which was declared a crime scene, while a second car collected the occupants of the Mitsubishi and departed.
“It is possible one of these persons from the Mitsubishi was injured or burnt during this process,” Galpin said.
Galpin said it was too soon to say whether it was related to organised crime.
“This is a horrific event in a public space where adults and children were simply trying to enjoy a sporting event and this incident, it’s clearly not acceptable. We will not tolerate it.”
Speaking on Sunday morning, Logan’s mayor, Jon Raven, described residents in the area as frightened.
“This has sent a shock wave through Logan. We’ve never seen something like this in Logan before,” Raven told the Today show.
“Our hearts go out obviously to the victims and the staff and the people at this boxing event.
“I’ve been to one of these events before, they’re [a] really family friendly environment, and I know there’s lots of children who were there, and this will impact them for the rest of their lives.”
The deputy commander of Queensland police, Chris Stream, described the scene as “confronting”.
“A number of people had suffered gunshot wounds,” he told Today.
Raven said the event had been organised to help children steer clear of violence.
“[The organiser] will be devastated this has happened because he loves boxing and uses it as a tool to empower and reconnect young people who might be going off the rails, and this is the opposite of what he’ll want to see,” Raven said.
Logan City Titles shared a statement on social media on Sunday morning.
“We are heartbroken about the incident that occurred at the fight night,” it read.
“Logan City Titles was a family event, an event for our community, showcasing local talent, hard work and everyone’s skills inside the ring.
“These types of incidents have no place in the boxing community or any part of the broader community.”
The offenders were still at large on Sunday but police said they did not believe there was an ongoing threat to the public.
Police were urging anyone with information to contact them.

title: How 5G will revolutionise the future of mobile gaming
author: Branded Content By
body:
Video games have been a lifeline for many during lockdown, keeping us entertained with epic interactive stories or allowing us to remain connected to friends and family thanks to multiplayer experiences. Now, the entire games industry is on the cusp of a great change – not only are we about to enter a new console generation, but the advent of 5G technologies will fully unlock the potential of mobile gaming.
Thanks to the boost in raw speed that 5G offers – up to a staggering 10Gbps, ten times what even 4G LTE-A can deliver – players can expect faster downloads and streaming, but the bigger impact will likely come from massively improved latency. With response times as low as five milliseconds, this means in-game action will be smoother than ever, with no lag between your input and the game's response. With 5G's greater reliability, this should hold true, even with high numbers of concurrent players.
Imagine playing the mobile version of Call of Duty alongside thousands of others, with unnoticeable lag, all at speeds fast enough to compete professionally. That's the dream, according to Greger Blennerud, who focuses on 5G's opportunities for mobile operators at Ericsson, the Swedish networking and telecoms company helping drive the 5G revolution.
"If you take Fortnite or Call of Duty, the latest versions are free to download and free to play, but then it's all about having as many players as possible. Smartphones, in sheer numbers, is probably the broadest platform developers can find," says Blennerud. "The challenge there is of course [...] on the network quality. I think the key characteristics of 5G that really makes it relevant are the bandwidth and the low latency that we're getting. Gaming [is] maybe one of the most obvious beneficiaries of 5G."
Professional gamers are already reaping the benefits of 5G, with the faster technology having provided the backbone to tournament play.
"We have already held the grand finale of an esport competition over 5G during Milan Games week," says Santiago Tenorio, Vodafone Group’s Head of Network strategy and architecture. "The finals of the Asphalt 9: Legends and PUBG games were played on Vodafone Italy’s 5G network. This proves that our network is good enough for esport professionals."
The esports sector will potentially see twice the benefit from 5G, as the technology makes life better for both players and audiences. In April 2020, users of the game-streaming service Twitch racked up 3.1 billion hours watched, a hike of 17 per cent on the previous quarter – a spike partially attributable to lockdown viewership, but also tracking with the rapid growth in popularity of esports. As 5G improves the availability of high-definition video streaming on-the-go, fans will be able to tune into tournaments or just follow their favourite streamers, wherever they are.
The raw speed of 5G isn’t the only benefit it will offer gamers. Higher bandwidth and lower response times means cloud computing becomes more viable. This will allow developers to handle more arduous processing and rendering duties remotely, and stream a higher quality end result to players. This would lessen concerns over whether a game runs on older or lower spec phones – as long as the end user has a 5G data plan, they could enjoy higher quality games.
The key to this is mobile edge computing – effectively, localised cloud servers rather than larger, centralised ones. This basically means the devices in your pocket will communicate with more, smaller data hubs that are physically closer to them – on the "edge' of the network. Rather than games having to send data to a distant central server, process it, and ping back a response, all of which slows down overall communication speeds, they will be able to access more power, closer to their users.
"You can offload the processing of your devices into the network, while also improving the experience of the game," explains Carlos Bravo, who focuses on edge for Ericsson Group Function Technology. "Before edge computing, you had to send a lot of information between the players to make sure everything is fitting well together. This put high demands on the device processors and batteries. Edge servers can be dimensioned in a better, more efficient way, generating a synchronised gaming experience in the cloud. You won't feel any lag as you're moving around, which is critical for a good gaming experience, and you won't have to be hooked into a Wi-Fi network. Processing at the edge will also make your device battery last longer.”
The power and accessibility of edge computing is one part of the 5G rollout that's already exciting developers.
"With 5G, we're heading into a future where we will be able to do a lot of cloud-based gaming, where the processing power isn't necessarily on your phone, but it's on a server somewhere," says Tommy Palm, founder and CEO of Resolution Games, a Swedish developer that specialises in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) titles. "That opens up a whole range of new, very exciting possibilities. If you have cloud-based gaming, you can run all the calculations on the same machine, and you don't need to synchronise a lot [of individual players' phones]. This opens up [the possibility] for games that we could only dream of, where you have fully destructive worlds, for instance."
Augmented Reality games in particular could also finally see their potential unleashed by the combination of 5G and edge. For most players, games like Pokémon Go will be their only experience of AR, but at present such titles only offer the simplest uses of the technology – most commonly, tapping into your phone's camera and overlaying in-game characters onto a feed of the real world.
For committed players, it's often little more than a gimmick, but one that can contribute significantly to battery drain, which in turn reduces practical play time. 5G will help fix both of those problems, enhancing the overall experience and, if developers also tap into the benefits of edge computing, potentially improving battery life and overall performance too.
"A lot of people turn off AR functionality because either it consumes a lot of battery, or it doesn't contribute all that much to the experience. 5G could address both those major issues," says Alvin Jude, from Ericsson Research. "We can help with the battery issue by doing a lot more of the processing centrally. [Rather than] a lot of people huddled together in a park playing together and all of their devices doing essentially the same processing, you can do this once on edge, and then stream it down to players over 5G."
The high speed and low latency of 5G means that in future, games can do the grunt work of processing on the cloud and, Jude says, "people won't even realise that it's being done elsewhere. It's not going to consume all your battery, and the AR experience would be more accurate. We would have much better experiences."
5G may also be the tool AR needs to make the transition to wearable devices – dedicated headsets or glasses, rather than just apps on phones. The trick will be in the underlying technology powering them, which will share similar architecture to mobile phones and be able to benefit from the same network speeds and cloud computing to deliver better utility to users. Like all the best technology, its impact will be all but invisible, though.
"When it comes to successful headsets, they're going to be built on mobile technology," says Palm, "but a consumer is never going to know that unless they're very interested in what is powering them. We've released two proper games on the Magic Leap, which is an AR headset. Both that, and Oculus Quest for VR, are actually running kind of mobile phone technology in the background, and they're building on that type of hardware. It's very similarly performing devices, whether it's a mobile phone or if it's a next generation headset."
Ericsson's recent partnership with a leading football team gave a powerful example of what the future of mobile gaming, powered by 5G and AR, could look like – players taking to the pitch for a kick-around wearing a next-gen visor, playing against virtual recreations of real sports stars, all reacting in real-time to their actions. In time, this could evolve to include haptic feedback via synced wearables, delivering the same physical rush as kicking an actual ball into the goal. Such mixed reality experiences could be used for training the next generation of soccer stars, as much as entertainment.
"It doesn't have to be 100 per cent analogous to the real world," says Jude. "You already see benefits from, for example, people learning to ski in VR. It's not necessarily exactly how it is in real life, but you do the actions like you are – and that's perfectly fine. What that means is that we're changing the game, just a little bit. We're moving a little bit towards reality, but we also have to acknowledge that it's not exactly as in reality, so the gameplay has to change somewhat."
Jude calls it "breaking the mould", which is what 5G promises to do for mobile gaming, whether on your phone or in a new generation of portable devices. To fully realise the potential though, developers will have to think bigger than ever. Or as Jude puts it, "you have to break it even further – you have to shatter it completely."

title: Megyn Kelly reopens old celebrity feuds with blunt new claims
author: Web Desk
body:

Megyn Kelly is airing some very public celebrity grievances — and a former NBC colleague has made her list.
The 55-year-old conservative commentator spoke to the Daily Mail about the stars who left her with the worst impressions, naming Jane Fonda, Bruce Willis, Al Roker and Ellen DeGeneres.

title: Why electric cars are about to go mainstream in Europe
author: Branded Content By
body:
Every new technology, from radio and television to the internet and smartphones, takes a journey through the hype curve. A bold new technology begins its life with enthusiasm, before being weathered by overpromise and a sense of disillusionment, before reaching a make-or-break fork in the road. Here, the options are failure and obscurity – or success, rapid adoption and household-name status.
Over the last decade we have seen smartphones power their way up the hype curve and into billions of pockets the world over, while smartwatches took longer to build momentum, and virtual reality remains, for now, somewhat lost in the early stages.
A relatively new entry to this hype curve is the electric car. Discounting early-20th century efforts before internal combustion really took off, the electrification of the mainstream motorcar only really began a decade ago.
With growth slow at first – often blamed on the electric car’s initial chicken-and-egg problem when it comes to charging infrastructure – we are now seeing the market mature. Drivers which fit the description of trailblazers and innovators already drive electric, and soon the electric vehicle (EV) market will reach a key tipping point – where they account for more than 2.5 per cent of the global new car market.
This is where the early adopters get involved and momentum builds, soon reaching the early-majority phase of consumer adoption, before an EV can legitimately be adorned with the coveted ‘mainstream’ status.
In Europe, the electric car revolution is now moving beyond the nascent trailblazer phase. In some countries, the shift from internal combustion to battery power is nothing short of astonishing. Take Norway for example, long regarded as the world’s leader in EV adoption, and where in 2018 fully 52 per cent of new cars sold were electrified (meaning either hybrid or fully electric), and the Nissan Leaf as the best-seller.
Generational demands
It isn’t just the lure of shiny new technology which is promoting the electric car. Instead, a global shift in consumer spending habits, married to a growing sense of environmental responsibility, especially among younger drivers, is sending EVs mainstream. Research shows millennial and Gen Z buyers are more environmentally conscious than their predecessors – a mindset which makes an electric car with zero tailpipe emissions seem increasingly attractive.
But this desire to be green isn’t a byproduct of opting for an electric car in the pursuit of saving money. A recent report by Nielsen found that young consumers not only valued sustainable products, but were prepared to pay more for them, and opt for them over any other premium feature.
Such is the "greener and cleaner" mindset, that in the UK around half of younger drivers say they would prefer to buy an electric car over one powered by petrol or diesel, if purchasing in the next couple of years.
As well as being kinder to the environment, and potentially your bank balance, electric cars are luring buyers in because of the way they drive. Gone are the days when a milk float comparison would raise a laugh and a knowing nod; instead, electric cars offer a surge of instant power, a longer range and shorter charging time than many drivers realise, plus the fun of trying out a new technology.
And, before they truly reach mainstream adoption, electric cars carry with them a desirable sense of living in the future, and of sampling technology yet to be experienced by everyone else. “Once you’ve had a chance to drive an electric car, you’ve seen the future of driving, and you want it today,” says Helen Perry, Head of Electric Vehicles and General Manager for Nissan Europe.
The technology of tomorrow’s cars
Part of this living-in-the-future feeling is one shared across all electric cars. They operate in near-silence, with instant acceleration thanks to the motor’s smooth, linear power delivery – something even the finest internal combustion engines can’t match. Add in a sci-fi soundtrack and the sensation is often one of using a future technology ahead of its time.
The infrastructure too will change as electric cars speed along the hype curve towards the mainstream. Petrol stations will be replaced with banks of chargers, and plugs will be located in more convenient places – at home, at work, in the car parks of destinations like hotels and cinemas, or temporarily outside arenas ahead of a concert.
Charging technology also has the potential to go much further. A road is currently being built in Stockholm which charges modified electric vehicles as they drive along it. Called the eRoad Arlanda, the project is an example of how new technology – in this case, an electric rail to charge passing vehicles – can be embeddedƒne into existing infrastructure.
Another example of embedding EV charging tech into existing locations comes from the European Union-funded FABRIC, which investigates the feasibility of wireless charging spots at road junctions and where vehicles are stationary at traffic lights. Think of this as the same as resting your smartphone on a wireless charging pad at your desk, but for cars stood in traffic.
Meanwhile, in the US, scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology are working on wireless car-to-car communications, telling following vehicles whether to brake or coast up to a traffic light, opting for whichever will recharge the battery the most in those exact circumstances. 5G networks with their higher data speeds and lower latency – 50 times quicker than 4G – will play a key role in making this scenario a reality.
A sneak peak at the future
Electric cars also come hand-in-hand with new assistance technologies, which help to automate some aspects of driving. Such systems include Nissan ProPILOT and ProPILOT Park, which are available on select versions of the Nissan Leaf and help to keep the car in lane, automatically slowing the car when approaching the vehicle ahead, and maneuvering into a parking space at the press of a button.
The latest version of the Leaf, which is priced from £27,995, has a 62kWh battery pack, a motor producing 160kWh (217PS), and an expected range of up to 239 miles (WLTP) per charge.
The Nissan Leaf is the best-selling EV globally, with over 400,000 sold since 2010, of which 130,000 found homes in Europe. In 2018, the Nissan Leaf was also the top-selling EV across Europe.
A cleaner, greener and cheaper future
As much as younger drivers strive to make sustainable and environmentally-conscious purchases, cost remains an important consideration when buying a new car. The generally low cost of electricity means EVs can be cheaper to run than an internal combustion car.
This of course depends on individual circumstances and annual mileage, but the end result, after the cost of purchase or lease, plus tax and fuel, has been taken into account, is that electric cars can cost considerably less to run. Solar panels installed on the roof of your property can serve to cut these costs even further.
Perry, of Nissan’s Electric Vehicles division, said: “For me, driving a car like the Nissan Leaf is really about the intelligent driving experience. Do you remember the time before power steering, ABS, or even power windows – would you want to do without that? And who would swap their smartphone or flatscreen TV for a landline phone or a bulky CRT TV? We see this all the time with our customers. Once they’ve owned a Nissan Leaf, they don’t want to go back.”

title: The Future of Clean Air Lies in Hydroxyl Radicals—So What Are They?
author: Branded Content By
body:
Air quality is literally a matter of life and death. More than one in 10 deaths worldwide are attributed to dirty air, polluted through a matter of means and molecules, which makes the battle to clean up our atmosphere and make the air we breathe a significant, important goal to achieve. Millions more of us suffer from hayfever or allergies that are caused by molecules in our air that interact with our bodies in a negative way.
Finding ways to generate and maintain clean air is a challenge that many organizations and businesses are trying to reach—but it’s one that Panasonic has been meeting over the last two decades.
Since 2003, Panasonic has been utilizing its proprietary nanoe system in a range of products. Inspired by nature, its goal is to use technology to recreate the conditions that we see in our natural world, away from the tarnishing impact of human civilization. And at its core are little-known molecules called hydroxyl (or OH) radicals. Abundant in nature, hydroxyl radicals have the capacity to inhibit pollutants. Panasonic aims to scientifically bring these benefits indoors using nanoe X technology, so that soft furnishings and the indoor environment can be a cleaner and more pleasant place to be.
“The OH radical is a molecule contained in nanoe particles, which are nano-sized water particles, and can inhibit allergens such as pollen, and deodorize, sterilize, and inhibit viruses,” says Yohei Ishigami of Kurashi Living Appliances and Solutions Company within Panasonic, who was a key contributor to the development of the nanoe X technology. Ishigami labored to fine-tune the technology behind nanoe X, testing more than 100 different prototypes of varying shapes and materials to increase the amount of OH radicals—a mix of hydrogen and oxygen molecules attached to each other—in the air to 48 trillion per second. That’s 100 times as many radicals as the first nanoe technology.
First-generation nanoe technology uses electronic atomization, which condenses water in the air onto electrodes and applies high voltage to the electrodes to generate fine water particles. Those fine water particles are generated through electric discharges, and the water particles contain OH radicals, which are highly reactive substances.
“Electric discharges are interesting things, and their form changes depending on the configuration of the electrodes and the value of the current flowing through them,” says Ishigami. However, first-generation nanoe technology is relatively inefficient. An alternative, called spark discharge, which harnesses the power of an instantaneous discharge that occurs when a voltage exceeds a certain limit, is better at producing lots of OH radicals—but there’s an issue: “it also generates a lot of harmful substances and heat,” says Ishigami. “From the standpoint of safety, this type of spark discharge is not suitable for commercialization.”
So Ishigami toiled until he found a solution—a happy medium that combined safety and efficiency to produce the best possible answer. The moment between a traditional electric discharge and the spark discharge was the ideal—but maintaining that form of discharge, called leader discharge in the scientific literature, was a challenge.
But it was one Ishigami wanted to tackle. “We thought that it should be possible to maintain the system by stopping the application, so we assembled a circuit that would detect the discharge and turn off the application in microseconds, and continued to make adjustments,” he says. Ishigami approached experts within Panasonic for support on how to fine-tune his work. “What I appreciated was the breadth of Panasonic’s knowledge,” he says. “If there was something we didn’t understand, or if we had a problem, someone had the wisdom to give us a hint.” Ishigami tried different materials and methods, eventually settling on tungsten electrodes and tweaking his process to get the desired result.
It took eight years, but Ishigami had developed what became known as nanoe X technology. Not only was it world-beating in its production of the number of OH radicals, but it could also knock out of action an increased number of harmful substances: “The number of pollens [the system can tackle] has increased from four to 13, and the number of allergens has increased from three to 16,” says Ishigami. But it’s not just in helping hayfever sufferers that Panasonic’s nanoe X technology—which is used in its global air-conditioning units—excels. It’s also able to tackle tough smells in buildings and rooms, including cigarette smoke. Rooms equipped with nanoe X technology can get rid of that stale cigarette smell in a tenth of the time of other technology.
And it’s used worldwide. Since its commercial release in 2003, Panasonic has sold nearly 11 million units that are utilized in restaurants, vehicles and homes. They’re also miniaturizing the technology into deodorizing clothes-hangers and shoe deodorizers, tackling lingering smells where we’re most likely to encounter them.
It’s vindication for Ishigami, who has spent a huge chunk of his working life perfecting the product. Persistence helped through the challenging moments, as did a vision of the bigger picture. “There were many moments in the development process when we got stuck,” he says. “It is precisely at such times that I feel it is important to take a closer look at the product, work as a team to come up with many ideas, and try as much as we can.”
